learning_objectives: The ambition of the TU Delft and the faculty is to offer an intellectually stimulating study programme for a select group of academically ambitious, excellent students, in conjunction with the international, two-year Masters curriculum, with a focus specifically on academic research. This gives the TU Delft the opportunity to bind outstanding students with curiosity for research, and raise their interest in an academic career.

description:
Using the Netherlands as the point of reference, students question and develop standing theoretical knowledge (design concepts and methods) in discussion with different cultural, social, economic, and political contexts. This allows for the re-evaluation of the character and components of a design project, as well as of the role of architectural and urban design practices. Students theoretically question and redefine the conceptual and methodological components of a design project. Students explore the formats, mediums, contexts, and institutional frameworks that inform the disciplines of architecture and urban design. The main focus is on establishing a common language upon which to build in the two remaining terms.

The studio-based course aims to evaluate existing design methods and tools to perform in a cross-cultural design practice. Students are asked to comparatively test design approaches in diverse cultural conditions, thus exploring how specific methods and tools act in specific cultural conditions. Students will draw conclusions on the capacity of design methods and tools to act in a cross-cultural fashion.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student:

has awareness of potentials and limitations of a set of design approaches to perform within different cultures

is able to assess the validity of design methods and tools to perform

description:
In this seminar-based course, students focus on issues related to the transformation of the contemporary built environment, developing knowledge that better bridges speculative and actual architectural production. Students engage in a collaborative educational process in order to contribute to a deeper understanding of the themes at hand.

Through reading and seminar discussions students will be introduced to the literature on cross- and interculturalism. They will be asked to become familiar with the main concepts of the field of cross-cultural studies (transculturation, hybridity, mitigation, etc) and will relate these to contemporary theories from architects and urban designers (the generic city, the city of flows, critical regionalism, etc).
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student:

have gained knowledge of theories of inter- and cross-culturalism in relation to the built environment

have developed an intellectual framework of theoretical knowledge to reflect upon methods

description:
The course is a thematic lecture series focusing on scholarly research and critical approaches to architecture discourse. The aim is to provoke dialogue and debate, engaging students in linking architectural thinking and practice to the history of ideas and changing social and cultural conditions. Invited speakers consist of international emerging and leading practitioners, scholars, and experts.

The course is organized by the Berlage Center for Advanced Studies in Architecture and Urban Design. Each semester's theme relates to the education and research programs of the Department of Architecture.
learning_objectives: The main objective is to bring students in contact with leading and emerging practitioners, scholars, and experts. Focusing on scholarly research and critical approaches to contemporary architecture and urban design, the course provokes dialogue and debate. Students are encouraged to link architectural thinking and practice to the history of ideas and changing sociocultural conditions.

description:
This course explores different forms, methods, and instruments of inquiry, preparing students to perform advanced academic work in architecture and urban design. The aim is to strengthen the students background and refine their skills in research, historical interpretation, and critical analysis. Students will analyze architecture-related literature from a critical perspective, perform independent primary and secondary research, and present the results in written, visual, and oral forms.

First, students will receive an overview of the ideas that shaped European and Western cities, buildings, and landscapes during the twentieth century, followed by an investigation of the forces that are shaping the built environment in the twenty-first century. Topics will include the historical and contemporary contexts of architecture, landscape, and urban design in the Europe; architectural intentions in relation to shifting worldviews; the development of the architectural avant-garde in the twentieth century; the economic, political, and cultural circumstances with the larger framework of modernism, urbanization, and globalization; and leading figures of twentieth-century architectural thought.

Secondly, students will explore how architectural ideasor theoriesare not only disseminated through buildings, but also through words and images. As such, it is understood that clear communication is a vital skill and an integral part of architectural practice. Topics will include fundamental writing and research methods; the relations between architecture discourse and mediums; critical analysis of words and images; verbal presentation skills; and an introduction different forms of media.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student:

 has examined the relationship of architecture, architectural thought, and the architectural profession to different societies and contexts

 has a further knowledge in the field of theories in architecture and urban design, which enables to link theoretical skills in an adequate way to differing situations and contexts

 has an understanding of the way in which positions, intentions, and ambitions of architects and urban designers formulated in past and present architectural discourses and how these positions, intentions, and ambitions are related to the other design disciplines

 has an understanding of the intricate relationship between theory and practice within the disciplines of architecture and urban design

 has knowledge to delineate and analyze some of the key positions in the fields of architecture and urban design from historical and contemporary perspectives

 knows how to illustrate the operation of different architectural positions within contemporary research and design approaches

 has the knowledge of how architecture-related communication may be used as critical vessel to discuss, debate, and disseminate architectural ideas

 has understood that clear communication is a vital skill and an integral part of architectural practice

 has explored a range of formats, mediums, and techniques architects use express to their architectural ideas, ambitions, and positions

description: This course is an intensive two-week master class led by renowned architect, or professional from a related design discipline, and is themed around a design assignment.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student:

has the ability to gather and process information, in a short time span

has the ability to apply develop ideas an intense, short-time span

has the ability to communicate and cooperate within an international team

description:
Students will build on the knowledge they gained in the first term curriculum, focusing on the impact of societal, environmental, and economic determinants on contemporary architecture and urban design. Students will work on projects that take into account how design considerations relate to these determinants. Fieldwork will be an integral part of the curriculum, when applicable.

This studio-based course will focus on the ability of students to articulate their own methods and tools. Students will be given a design problem (dwelling for aging population, building for contemporary public life) that is anchored in particular a cultural setting, and will be asked to develop their own analysis and design approach. In doing so, students will be demanded to reflect upon the different aspects and components of a design approach, as well as on their relation to particular cultural settings.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student:

is capable of formulating an innovative research method and design approach that is suitable to answer a predefined cultural issue located in a particular cultural setting

can reflect critically on the research methods and design approach that he developed and its relation to a particular cultural context.

description: The course focuses on positions of practitioners operating in a cross-cultural fashion. Students will get acquainted with the methods and tools of practitioners in the field of architecture and urban design that operate cross-culturally. Through close analysis of these practices (plan analysis, text analysis, interviews) students will discuss the particular characteristics of the research and design methods that are employed by these practitioners.

The course is a thematic lecture series focusing on scholarly research and critical approaches to architecture discourse. The aim is to provoke dialogue and debate, engaging students in linking architectural thinking and practice to the history of ideas and changing social and cultural conditions. Invited speakers consist of international emerging and leading practitioners, scholars, and experts.

The course is organized by the Berlage Center for Advanced Studies in Architecture and Urban Design. Each semester's theme relates to the education and research programs of the Department of Architecture.
learning_objectives: The main objective is to bring students in contact with leading and emerging practitioners, scholars, and experts. Focusing on scholarly research and critical approaches to contemporary architecture and urban design, the course provokes dialogue and debate. Students are encouraged to link architectural thinking and practice to the history of ideas and changing sociocultural conditions.

description: This course is an intensive two-week master class led by a leading scholar or thinker and will be themed around a theoretical issue leading to the completion of a research assignment.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student:

has the ability to gather and process information, in a short time span

has the ability to apply develop ideas an intense, short-time span

has the ability to communicate and cooperate within an international team

description: In this course, students conduct in-depth, self-guided research, developing a critical and theoretically informed position on a design-related topic within the fields of architecture and urban design. Working closely with educational staff in an innovative and experimental setting, students will develop their critical thinking skills in order to identify appropriate resources for each individual area of interest within a collective framework. Students will use the course as the foundation for developing initial topics for thesis work to be undertaken in the third term.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student:

has selected a specific topic related to contemporary discourses on the built environment for further development as a thesis project

has further knowledge of the historical development of major theoretical concepts and models that influence contemporary discourses on the built environment

is able to interpret the broader and manifold context architecture, the city, society design concepts, and architectural and related practices

has the ability to apply the knowledge gained to the specific topics and case studies addressed in the course

has written a consistent report, containing a literature overview, a proposal outlining the research topic and questions to be explored, and a research plan for the completion of the thesis project during term 3

shows how the thesis project topic relates, and contributes, to broader discourse on the built environment

description: Students will develop a project in detail, demonstrating their capacity to critically synthesize knowledge in a relevant format. Students will engage in primary archival or scholarly research, conceptualize and shape content, and design and execute work in an innovative presentation (which could take the form of a book, an application, an exhibition, or a movie, among other formats). Students will be encouraged to perform fieldwork when applicable to their project.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student:

has learned to apply the skills and knowledge gained in the preceding two terms of study in a research and design project he has to carried out either independently or collectively.

course_name: Applied Spatial Analysis for Sustainable Urban Development
description:
Spatial analysis is a crucial part of projects carried out in urbanism and landscape architecture and a core application domain for the field of geomatics. After having encountered basic spatial analysis with short targeted workshops in the first three quarters of their MSc tracks, Urbanism and Landscape Architecture students following this intradisciplinary course work on an integrated, end-to-end analytical assignment, combining, advancing and extending their data-related skill- and tool-sets, while focusing on advanced workflows. The course offers the opportunity to MSc Urbanism Landscape Architecture, and Geomatics students to advance their technical skills required for scalable, automated and reproducible spatial analyses, practicing working in an intra-disciplinary setting with a real-world assignment. All students have the chance to learn skills from the other tracks and in the process strengthen their analytical skills for their upcoming thesis.

The course will start with an introduction to multi-criteria decision analysis, typology construction and their corresponding workflows suitable for a sustainable spatial development challenge. The higher-level principles of scalability, automation and reproducibility, as well as their implementation through computational notebooks, are also introduced early in the course. The course emphasizes data visualization as a way to explore data iteratively, generate new knowledge and communicate project results. Students learn about different types of thematic analysis, such as spatial analysis, network analysis, and landscape analysis which they can integrate in their analytical workflows. To apply the workflows and analytical methods introduced throughout the quarter, students work in intra-disciplinary groups on a given location.

The workflows presented in the course involve open-source tools using graphical user interfaces, such as QGIS, as well as programming in R and/or Python for spatial analysis. In the era of open data, the course emphasizes the importance of leveraging accessible and shared datasets to enhance the quality and depth of spatial analyses. In addition, the course underscores the significance of transparent and collaborative research practices by incorporating a dedicated segment on publishing datasets, workflows, and results. MSc Urbanism, Landscape Architecture and Geomatics students will be given the opportunity to contribute to the broader academic community through the dissemination of their work.
learning_objectives:
After following this course, students will be able to:

1. Construct analytical workflows in the context of spatial design and planning.

2. Employ spatial data visualization both for exploratory data analysis and for the presentation of their final project results.

3. Conduct integrated spatial analysis to understand and describe the complexity of urban environments and to inform spatial design and planning decisions targeting their transformations.

4. Adopt open science practices, including FAIR data publication, reproducible workflows, and usage of open-source software.

5. Report on analytical findings as part of a multidisciplinary team.

description: During the first weeks, we build the FOUNDATION of knowledge/skills regarding planting in the built environment. After this, we work with DIMENSIONS OF DESIGN, build upon the foundation and focus on planting strategies for gardens. Following, we strengthening PLANTING ENGINEERING strategies to improve ecosystem services. Finally, we integrate the knowledge gained in the past weeks into the design of (parts of) a park, while focussing on DRAWING REPRESENTATION.
learning_objectives:
By the end of this course, the student should be able to:

- recognize typologies that suit specific planting strategies.

- recognize planting potential.

- design with plants for climate adaptation, biodiversity and aesthetics.

- develop his/her own library with knowledge about a variety of plants, trees and shrubs.

course_name: Urbidata: Responsible Design for Fair Data Cities
description:
In this course we explore the main principles of data ethics, and the relevance of applied ethics in the domain of the data-driven city.

Eight billion people and their devices produce unimaginable amounts of data, seven days a week, 24 hours a day. Data on all aspects of human existence. Data, processed by AI and increasingly powerful computers, that promise mankind the opportunity to influence all aspects of life, especially in the urban setting. The concept of the 'smart city' assumes that big data leads to better (after all smart) solutions for planners, designers, industry and, at the end, citizens. Urbidata, the data-driven city of 2050, will be optimally planned, with smart mobility that allows for efficient and safe use of space and time, and citizens living in smart homes and working in smart offices that cater optimally their needs, based on their personal profiles.

Does this technology driven perspective provide the answer how we want the life in the future city of Urbidata to look like? Should all developments of data-driven solutions (e.g. by architects, urban planners and geo-specialists) and their use be permissible in the light of the consequences? The choices we make today determine our world of tomorrow.

Taking a critical, responsible design perspective it's clear that our data-driven future cannot be just a question of engineering and economic models. How about values as autonomy, privacy, transparency and consent?

At first sight this interpretation of the city of tomorrow appears to be a question of policy. Policy that might lead to a normative (legal) framework setting standards. However in this course we focus on the preceding fundamental discussion. What are the ethical concepts and principles that guide us to determine what solutions are right or wrong? And next: how to apply data ethics in a given situation? This in order to make the future city of Urbidata a fair data city.

course_name: Integrated Metabolic Design for Sustainable Neighborhoods, Cities and Regions
description:
In the course, students address sustainability challenges of society metabolism based on a systemic understanding, analysis and design:

through different spatial scales (from urban block and street to neighbourhood, city and region)

through different disciplines of engineering, design and governance

through interaction with different institutions and stakeholders

A theoretical foundation of society's metabolism and the methods used to improve it is introduced, discussed and applied through a methodological, multiscale, iterative cycle of analysis, design and assessment.

Presentations are used to share findings with stakeholders and gather feedback for further design iterations.
learning_objectives:
After the course, the student can:

Apply the concept of societal metabolism to analyse integrated sustainability challenges in a specific context

develop a multiscale design proposal based on their analysis.

Evaluate their proposal in the context of Dutch policymaking.

Communicate and discuss proposals with stakeholders in the concerned context.

Assess the effectiveness of design variants of environmental technologies through scales.

description:
Identity, continuity and transformation are essential notions of today's spatial design practice. In this course, you will learn how to analyze a given situation, interpret the characteristics of the transformative mechanisms and design a proposal that supports the (spatial) identity and narrative of the site in contact with the public. The scale of the assignment can vary from a historical garden to an (urban) landscape.

Your role is to participate actively in ongoing transformation processes from a multidisciplinary angle. You will prepare design proposals to modify a heritage site in cooperation with stakeholders and governmental bodies. The results will serve as the ground for discussion within these communities.

In preparation for the interactive workshop, you study literature on theory and methods of heritage transformation, landscape design, value assessment and participation with local communities in weekly assignments. You'll team up with students from different disciplines. You will debate theories on place-making. During the workshop you will work with experimental analysis visualization methods and techniques on heritage representation, like sensorial perception, tracing narratives, investigating historical sources, mapping space in various ways, experimental photography, etc. The results of the design workshop will be presented to local stakeholders.

In this course, the Landscape Architecture section wants to strengthen the interaction between landscape transformations and the role of (local) stakeholders in a multidisciplinary setting.

course_name: Metropolitan Regions in Times of Environmental and Economic Transitions
description:
The main aim of the course is to examine how metropolitan regions respond to, and navigate the impact of, the imperatives of sustainable and integrated development. The course is embedded in the field of spatial and environmental planning and design in TU Delft and builds upon urban and regional planning theories that are aligned with the UN sustainable development goals. These seek to effectively address environmental and social challenges facing cities and regions.

One of the courses primary goals is to advance a critical understanding of metropolitan processes within (post-)globalization, as well as their effects. It seeks to articulate these through both theory and design to move towards new urban and regional development paths that are better able to respond to the ever-increasing challenges faced by cities and city-regions. The course programme involves learning about current and upcoming challenges of sustainable development through a process of research and design. It focuses on urban and regional development models globally and develops an integrated approach, providing key skills that students can use as planners, designers, and landscape architects in different geographical contexts. It also enables them to work on different levels of spatial and temporal scales.

The students are trained in research methods relating to spatial planning, urban studies, environmental and urban design, with an emphasis on the diversity of planning cultures and the need to incorporate socio-environmental concerns into urban development. The course has a transdisciplinary ethos, and uses a series of different developing regions as case studies. Students have the chance to meet stakeholders from diverse backgrounds, including academics and governments, who act as teachers and trainers.

The course is also part of the International Forum on Urbanism (IfoU) and works in partnership with other universities from that network to deliver work that builds on theoretical knowledge in order to advance strategies for spatial and environmental planning. The results are location-sensitive strategies that outline real opportunities for moving towards more a sustainable future for the regions selected for study. Such regions include Greater Buenos Aires, Argentina, the Greater Bay Area in China (including Hong Kong, Guangzhou, Macao) and the Greater Paris region. Previous students work has been published and presented at several biennales (including Venice 2014, Buenos Aires 2016, and Shenzhen Hong Kong 2019).
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course the student is able to:

Critically understand and articulate metropolitan processes in the framework of globalization effects on urban and regional development.

Design metropolitan and local development strategies, considering infrastructural development, social integration, socio-economic wellbeing, and environmental adaptation.

Facilitate the articulation of urban and regional design within complex and multidisciplinary perspectives.

Understand and develop planning strategies and actions across scales and borders using a variety of methods.

Advance stakeholder analysis and translate diverse interests within local, regional and cross-regional scales.

Define a coherent communication perspective at various scales and levels of analysis to facilitate communication across a broader set of actors.

description: This course is designed for Architecture (A), Management in the Built Environment (MBE), and Building Technology (BT) students eager to (1) explore opportunities for starting their venture in the built environment (such as an architectural firm, development company, tech startup, etc.) and/or (2) discover how organisations within the built environment operate and function from an inside perspective. This course allows students to analyse how organisations (such as architectural studios, developers, contractors, and industrial construction companies) in the built environment operate, how they change in time, and how they can contribute to innovation. In the course students delve into the position of these companies in the built environment and learn how companies align their business goals with their surroundings. Moreover, the course provides students with the unique opportunity to analyse existing organisations and go beyond this. Students learn to identify how they can contribute to taking on challenges in the built environment using their personal skills, interests, and characteristics. To do so, students will develop an entrepreneurial attitude and investigate the opportunities for a (design) venture in the built environment. Students will focus on identifying the kind of impactful work they aspire and exploring how they can bring about meaningful change. The course is suitable for students of the tracks Management in the Built Environment (MBE), Architecture (A) and Building Technology (BT). The course contains a shared theory component focusing on fundamental elements of entrepreneurship, including theory about legal, financial, business modelling, market forces and organisational issues. In addition to the shared theory component, students can choose from several projects. For example, A and BT students can choose to explore the nuances of starting their architectural design studio. MBE , A, and BT students can create and defend a business proposal for an existing or new, innovative venture. For Architecture students the course also contains a design component.
learning_objectives:
After completion of the course the student will be able to:

- explain the key concepts of entrepreneurship and entrepreneurial behaviour
- explain and demonstrate the value and meaning of entrepreneurship in architecture and the built environment
- identify opportunities for entrepreneurship by analysing the relations between different organisations in the built environment.
- assess the influence of their personal characteristics on entrepreneurial opportunities
- develop and visualise a vision for a product and/or service and create a coherent business plan that combines business modelling, finance, legal, and market knowledge.
- critically evaluate and reflect on entrepreneurial skills and plans
- design and deliver a compelling business pitch

description:
In this elective course the interaction between spatial design, area and project development tools and social, economic, political, and environmental issues is at stake. Students from the MBE, Landscape Architecture and Urbanism tracks and the MSc CME Design en Integration Domain (from the coupled course Transformative Design), collaborate on the transformation of a peripheral urban area in the Netherlands. The pressure on these urban fringes is both urban and rural and characterised by urban sprawl, fragmented agricultural or industrial activity, remnants of natural and landscape values.

Working together in groups you will develop a master plan and elaborate individually a more detailed, imaginable transformation proposal. Students confront spatial qualities, opportunities, limitations and challenges of the chosen area with societal needs, transition goals, ownership issues and stakeholder claims. You design and define proposals on different scales and complexities including area, portfolio and project level. You will apply development strategies, feasibility criteria and research by design activities.

This course is organised as a multidisciplinary experience combining approaches, knowledge and skills from the viewpoints of management, urban design and landscape development and is therefore representative for area development practice in the real world. This collaboration provides insight in the complementarity of viewpoints, data, tools, vocabulary, methods and fun.
learning_objectives:
(1) students can analyse the characteristics, conditions, stakeholders, opportunities and potentialities of peri-urban transformation areas (using a theoretical framework)

(2) students can develop a tentative spatial perspective (e.g. spatial, social, economic, political, environmental) in a peri-urban context including primary notions of phasing: from initiative to implementation (masterplan version 0.5)

(3) students can elaborate a crucial, domain-specific aspect or component of the masterplan like a portfolio, structure, block typology or building

(4) students can synthesise varied input into an integrated, substantiated master plan for a peri-urban transformation area (masterplan version 1.0)

(5) students can reflect on the implications of the domain-specific theory on the application of the masterplan and its elaborations

description:
Initiated by the Building Audiences Group (Department of Architecture), this Q5 course invites students to develop their curatorial and editorial skills, with a focus on the built environment. Throughout the quarter, students will design and produce one exhibition and an accompanying publication that addresses pressing societal issues. The course is built around interdisciplinary collaboration, direct exchanges with industry professionals, the design and production of an exhibition that will open at the Orange Hall in week 1.10, and the organization of a public talk.  

Students will have the opportunity to engage with professionals from the Department of Urbanism (Faculty of Architecture and the Built Environment), the Faculty of Industrial Design Engineering, Stichting Archined (Rotterdam), Make Move Think Foundation (The Hague), Editoriale Domus SpA (Milan), and The New Institute (Rotterdam). These collaborations will take place at different stages and degrees of involvement throughout the course.  

The course equips students with critical, creative, and communicative tools to disseminate knowledge and engage broader audiences. Students will curate the content of an exhibition and design the physical space for it, displaying their work in an architectural piece they conceive themselves. The exhibitions are intended to spark public conversation. Future editions of the course may expand the formats of dissemination to include digital media, podcasts, and interactive installations.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- create an exhibition and edit a publication related to the built environment, learning to present a topic from a unique and well-defined perspective.

- analyse existing research on targeted topics, enabling them to create exhibitions and publications grounded in comprehensive, evidence-based insights.

- apply their critical thinking and reflective abilities through interdisciplinary collaboration, industry engagement, and project-based learning.

- evaluate interdisciplinary knowledge through collaboration, enabling them to familiarize with intersectionality for future professional endeavours.

- understand the importance of engaging with different publics and will be able to communicate their findings professionally to various stakeholders.

description:
The Q5 studio, a collaboration between the Building Knowledge groups Design, Data & Society (DDS), Complex Projects (CP), and Architecture Archives of the Future (AAF), is all about rethinking the future of higher education spaces.  In a world shaped by data and new technologies, students will explore how and where learning happens.

Students will work with real-world partners from academia and society to imagine what tomorrow’s universities might look like—and how they could better meet changing educational needs.  

The focus is on the very beginning of the design process: how do you even start to shape a brief for a place that supports future learning? Through hands-on design tasks, you’ll learn how to translate early ideas and ambitions into strong, visual concepts.  

Students will use a mix of lectures, workshops, and group research to explore how space and education connect. They will investigate a real site and create future scenarios through collaborative workshops and smart data visualizations. The studio sees the input from experts working on TU Delft Campus Rotterdam and at the Nieuwe Instituut, a cultural centre in Rotterdam, focusing on architecture, design, and digital culture. The goal is to better understand how space shapes learning—and how a client figures out what they want from a new learning environment.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to: 

- discuss the evolution of learning spaces and their architectural expression by collecting and interpreting information through lectures, seminars, and archival research.  

- analyze social, environmental, and technological data by collecting data from open sources, questioning, interpreting, and reorganizing them.  

- evaluate the quality and fit of collected information from data analysis, design studies and input from experts about the design brief projects and innovative visualization techniques. 

- create a design brief in a team, by compiling information and proposing several design scenarios and options of innovative spatial solutions for a new learning environment.

- collaborate in a transdisciplinary education environment by bringing together individuals from diverse academic disciplines, professional backgrounds, and societal sectors.

description: Initiated by staff members from the Department of A, this research and design project is a collaboration with the Faculty of Design Sciences of the University of Antwerp, and other Belgian societal partners. It explores new grounds and methods in architectural education. Students learn to work in-situ: ‘reading’ places, engaging with real-life issues, working with existing sites and conditions. The studio promotes experimental methods in ‘doing’ architecture by using film, drawing, photography, model making, writing, and performance. By locating architecture in real-life settings, the studio aims to explore multi- and interdisciplinary collaborations with other fields of knowledge, both within the school and with external partners and institutions. The studio will culminate in an exhibition.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

develop a fieldwork study that explores real-world contexts using observational and notational techniques, fostering curiosity, improvisation, and engagement.

implement experimental research methods to analyse and interpret the physical and social fabric of an urban context in relation to specific urban and architectural design themes.

correlate historical, cultural, and spatial information by synthesizing layers of time and space.

translate real-world experiences into compelling visual stories and objects, using a variety of media such as sketching, filming, model making, photography, and script writing.

collaborate within an interdisciplinary group to integrate and cross-fertilize diverse knowledge and skills from multiple fields, producing a cohesive project that reflects collective insights and interdisciplinary innovation.

description: Initiated by staff members from the Department of A, this research and design project is a collaboration with the Faculty of Architecture at Politecnico di Torino and the Cultural Heritage Agency (RCE). Designers – whether in architecture, art, industrial design, or civil engineering – have long travelled to gain insights from different cultures, with Italy being one of their favourite destinations. The concept of the travelling architect provides a lens to explore the evolution of design across disciplines and its cultural context. This course aims to deepen knowledge, foster collaboration in multidisciplinary teams, and do research by creating models and using various visual/sculptural means to present findings. As part of the course, students travel to Italy for on-site research.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

analytically explore their chosen project, formulate a research question (for Research Booklet and for Model), and conduct on-site research (during study trip) using a variety of documentation tools and a transdisciplinary approach (FALs 1, 2).

understand the complexity of different types of information and show this by writing a Research Booklet with a relevant title, a clear goal, a well-defined methodology, a comprehensible structure and a scientific conclusion (FALs 1, 2).

process various research data into a design program, create a design, and develop a proficiency in using and constructing digital, graphical, and physical models to represent at least two architectural elements (FALs 2, 3, 4).

present a coherent, significant, detailed, accurate, and analytical exploration of a research and design project (Model and Suitcase), and communicate abstract themes visually (FALs 3, 4).

learn to work in teams composed of diverse cultural backgrounds and disciplines, and contribute to the group process through specific tasks, determining individual roles within the group, and aiding in the creation of an integral group product (FALs 2, 5).

description: The 21st century is an era of unprecedented technological acceleration, climate change, environmental degradation, resource scarcity, and intensive societal transitions. The Anthropocene has made evident the impact of human intrusion on living and Earth’s systems, manifesting as “wicked problems”. Tackling these problems from monodisciplinary perspectives is counterproductive. What is needed is a transdisciplinary approach that works towards the development of sustainable design strategies for environments and ecosystems in transition. In this end, the Theories, Territories and Transitions Section of the Architecture Department of the Faculty of Architecture has developed this interdisciplinary Q5 course in cooperation with staff of the Faculty of Technology, Policy and Management, the Delft Deltas, the Infrastructure and Mobility Initiative, and the European Association for Architectural Education. Every academic year we will collaborate with our partners, and with domain and site-specific experts, to explore constructed ecologies and human altered environmental systems and landscapes across European contexts. Students will develop analytical research tools and develop strategies and methods that leverage the spatial disciplines and interdisciplinary design for transitions.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

develop interdisciplinary approaches and methods in research and design

to evaluate and synthesize information from sources across multiple design domains

to critically analyze relationship between organizations, processes, stakeholders, and industries in complex eco-social and techno-social systems

to communicate and collaborate with different societal stakeholders across disciplinary domains

to produce holistic and sustainable strategies and design interventions for environmental problems in natural and altered contexts

description: Initiated by staff members from the Department of AE&T, this research and design project is a collaboration with the Faculty of Industrial Design Engineering, and the Board of Government Advisors. Technological developments, the high demand for affordable housing and sustainability goals for the built environment appear to create an unstoppable trend towards industrial production. The current but also historical developments of industrial building systems in housing construction prompt discussions on the role and responsibilities of architecture and the architect in this process. Students are asked to reflect on the possible constraints of design for serial production, but also to explore its opportunities to create qualitative architecture for the masses.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- understand and analyse industrial building systems (for housing) - as historical cases and current development - from the various disciplinary perspectives involved.

- evaluate case study documentation, and argue its architectural qualities.

- create an architectural innovation for one case study example.

- argue a series of statements and develop a personal and academic position on the topic in the temporal, social and interdisciplinary context.

- create and formulate innovation in architecture.

description: This course explores robotics technologies within the creative industries, particularly those closely relevant to spatial design. It is a research and design project taught through collaboration between the Architecture and Built Environment, Mechanical Engineering, and Industrial Design Engineering faculties and involves RoboHouse and TU Delft Science Centre. It aims to enhance students’ understanding of robotics through applied, critical, and speculative approaches focusing on the relationships between robots, humans, and environments. In this course, the students will work in interdisciplinary teams to develop innovative concepts and applied solutions by using robotics. They will develop skills and knowledge in human-robot interaction, computer vision, machine learning, coding, and digital crafting. They will integrate them to create tangible projects addressing the design, production, or use of built environments.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- understand the state of the art in robotics within a built environment context.

- develop innovative applications that integrate robotics in the design, production, or use of the built environments.

- apply computational methods and integrate digital technologies toward solving a design and engineering problem.

- create a prototype to present the envisioned relationships between robots, humans, and environments.

- apply interdisciplinary teamwork in defining, solving, presenting, and assessing a design assignment.

description:
The Future Materials course is a cross-faculty initiative led by an interdisciplinary team from Architecture, Industrial Design, Mechanical Engineering, Civil Engineering and Aerospace Engineering. The course takes a hands-on approach in which designers, engineers and materials scientists collaborate in the conception, design and application of novel materials that support a radical transformation to a more sustainable and resource-efficient built environment. The teaching and mentoring team includes external international design and engineering offices including Arup, Octatube, NPSP, ABT, Foster & Partners, MVRDV and Eckersley O'Callaghan.

In the first phase, students from a conceptual design background will develop an understanding of the basics of material science and structural design, whilst students from a technical background will be exposed to conceptual design studios. Building on this, students will work in interdisciplinary teams and apply systems-thinking to define a design brief which is informed by key performance and sustainability criteria. Through the use of systematic design methods, digital tools and physical prototypes, students will design and develop the next generation of material-(cycle)s through a process of: conception – elaboration – making – testing, to address a performance-based design brief. The environmental, financial and social sustainability of the proposed design solution will be evaluated throughout the design process.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- Understand the fundamental principles of sustainable material selection, systems-thinking, resource-efficient design strategies and whole-life-assessment methods.

- Apply these principles to develop an inter-disciplinary performance-based design brief that accounts for environmental, technical, financial and social factors.

- Create methods, employ digital tools and construct physical prototypes to design and evaluate sustainable material solutions and cycles of use for real-world applications.

- Evaluate and reflect on the environmental, financial and/or social sustainability of the proposed design solution.

description: This course is a collaboration between the Faculty of Architecture and the Faculty of Industrial Design Engineering. It offers a unique learning trajectory to master the art and science of lighting indoor and outdoor spaces. Students learn to combine daylight and electric lighting to achieve optimal visual performance, communicate architectural and branding expressions, and keep environmental footprint from lighting at a minimum. Through hands-on workshops, a group assignment rooted in the town of Delft and pitches to mentors from industry, students acquire new knowledge from first-hand experience that can be immediately applied in practice.

Initiated by staff members from the Departments of A and U, this research and design project is a collaboration with housing association Habion, and knowledge and network organisation Platform 31. It will look into the role played by neighbourhoods in promoting health, changing lifestyle, and preventing future diseases. To elaborate on the relationship between space and health, this course will use suburban neighbourhoods as testing grounds – areas predominately built for families and often lacking public facilities like neighbourhood centres and medical care facilities. The course will explore the role of public architecture and dwelling in dealing with these issues, in order to create more accessible and just environments.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of this course, the student will be able to:

Present and discuss convincingly a coherent, significant, elaborated, correct and innovative design proposal.

Conduct research by employing quantitative and qualitative methods.

Approach design issues according to a multi-scalar perspective, implementing holistic solutions to specific problems by working simultaneously on the urban scale, the building scale, and the scale of dwelling.

Explain and reflect upon the relationships between analysis, conceptualisation, method, and composition of a design proposal.

Analyze questions of health, well-being, access to resources and publicness through a multi-disciplinary perspective that involves collaboration with different scientific fields and societal partners.

description:
This interdisciplinary design studio explores the future of the TATA Steel plant and the North Sea Canal area, addressing the challenges of industrial legacy, environmental toxicity, and the transition toward a circular economy. Students from architecture, urbanism, landscape, industrial ecology, civil engineering, and sustainability fields will collaborate on long-term spatial strategies that balance environmental, economic, and cultural concerns.

Working closely with partners — the North Sea Canal Area (NOVEX), College van Rijksadviseurs, and Havenbedrijf Amsterdam — students apply systemic design methods such as backcasting and tipping point analysis to envision resilient transformations. Site visits, expert lectures, and workshops on systemic design, heritage, and industrial transition will support students' research and design processes.

The studio emphasizes innovative media use (3D modeling, animations, point cloud scans) to communicate complex systems and future scenarios, culminating in a public exhibition and online campaign. Final projects bridge design, policy, and public engagement, addressing urgent real-world challenges at the intersection of infrastructure, climate, and societal change.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- investigate the lifecycle and spatial footprint of commodities from extraction to re-use in relation to a given region (NZKG) and related industrial ecology and heritage, combining interdisciplinary perspectives with a metabolist and system-thinking methodology (linked to GFAL2, GFAL4, GFAL5).

- analyze (through texts, interpretative drawings, diagrams and/or models) the complex challenges systemic transition to circular flows of the investigated commodities, through integrating interdisciplinary, technical and cultural perspectives on contemporary economies across various scales (linked to GFAL1, GFAL4, GFAL5, GFAL6).

- design an integral intervention supporting the regional transformation of the NZKG towards a circular and sustainable economy, which is anchored on a specific place (spatial), institutional framework (governance and policy), and interdisciplinary knowledge (linked to GFAL3, GFAL5, GFAL6).

- reflect on the complexity of globalized economy and on how design proposals supporting a systemic transition toward a circular economy may impact the extant built environment and vice versa (linked to GFAL1, GFAL4, GFAL6).

- demonstrate skills in communication and project management in an inter-/transdisciplinary and multi-sector context (linked to GFAL4, GFAL5).

course_name: Delta Infrastructure and Environment Design/Delta Futures Lab
description: Initiated by staff members from the Department of U, this research and design project is a collaboration grounded in the Delta Futures Lab, with the Faculties of Civil Engineering and Geosciences, and Technology, Policy and Management. It aims at reparative interventions in deltaic areas where the environmental crisis is apparent due to imbalance between environment and infrastructure. In the course, students with backgrounds in spatial design and in engineering rethink these infrastructures from an interdisciplinary design perspective, integrating the genius loci of the spatial assembly of the system to reach a resilience in relation to natural hazards. The course will respond directly to societal challenges (working for a ‘client’).
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- identify and discuss the tension between public and private in urban environments in the context of political ecology.

- identify and discuss the synergy between natural conditions and technological possibilities in urban environments.

- formulate their design perspective that is based on a conceptual or theoretical framework.

- apply methods concerning the appraisal of what a sustainable future is of an urban environment and connect this to a value system.

-  demonstrate by interdisciplinary design (integration of solutions from different disciplinary natures) the connection between the natural system and technical possibilities in urban environments.

- perform inter-disciplinary work by understanding the dependency between the participating disciplines, creating a shared value system and goals, draw shared conclusions.

description: Initiated by staff members from the Departments of U and AE&T, this research and design project is a collaboration with the Faculties of Industrial Design Engineering, Civil Engineering & Geosciences, and Technology, Policy and Management, and the Municipality of Rotterdam. In this course, a group of students with different disciplinary backgrounds work together on climate adaptive solutions (both spatial, technical, and strategic) in an urbanized area in Rotterdam. Based on a challenge-based approach, issues related to urban heat, drought, air pollution, and flooding are addressed integrally, uncovering possible conflicts and synergies, and taking multiple spatial and temporal scales into account.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- explain the fundamental characteristics of climate change and its impact on urban areas (FAL1&7)

- implement a project management plan (including data generation plan) in collaboration with peers from different disciplines, with a distinct contribution to the team effort (FAL2&6)

- identify the main spatial, technical and social goals in relation to the climate challenges from a complex brief commissioned by an external client (FAL4)

- apply spatial measures and strategies into a design proposal at different scales to address the identified climate challenges (FAL3)

- reflect on the climate performance of the design according to the previously defined goals through software modelling and evaluation (FAL5)

description: Initiated by staff members from the Departments of AE&T, U, A and MBE, this research and design project is a collaboration with the Faculties of Industrial Design Engineering, Civil Engineering and Geosciences, and Technology, Policy and Management, the Municipality of Delft, and other universities of the Bauhow 5 European Alliance for Architecture and Built Environment. The course equips students to become socially responsible engineers, integrating academic innovation with hands-on societal impact in urban environments. Through a transdisciplinary engagement studio, students tackle real challenges in post-industrial cities (Delft-TUD, London-UCL, Munich-TUM), co-creating sustainable urban solutions with community partners.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- design innovative, socially responsible urban interventions that are contextually responsive and sustainable.

- effectively collaborate in transdisciplinary teams, leveraging diverse expertise to develop cohesive, integrated solutions for urban challenges.

- underpin their design interventions with rigorous, scientifically grounded research, ensuring that solutions are informed by data and analysis.

- propose interventions/design/methods that respond to societal needs and ethical concerns, aiming for tangible, long-term urban improvements.

description: Initiated by staff members from the Departments of U, MBE, A and AE&T, this research and design project is a collaboration with the Faculty of Civil Engineering and Geosciences, the TU Delft Campus Real Estate & Facility Management, the TU Delft Hortus, the Municipality of Delft, and other societal partners. In the course, students explore the development of a sustainable working and living environment, by using the TU Delft campus as a realistic case study. The course aims to develop a transdisciplinary learning environment where students from different disciplines work together with societal stakeholders. ECO- campus is seen as a canvas for identifying the complex interdependencies and synergetic potential of three domains: circularity, society, and ecology.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- understand/analyze the three-domain [circularity-society-ecology] interdependencies

- contextualize/evelop a shared/holistic assessment criteria framework to evaluate circularity-society-ecology interdependencies at different scale levels

- elaborate holistic approaches to tackling complex circ-soc-ecology challenges by engaging in futuring processes

- navigate scientific-societal exchanges in knowledge production and meaning-making processes with engagement of stakeholders

- communicate and present their work of the stakeholder based circular ECOcampus in a coherent manner to students, staff and stakeholders.

course_name: Sustainable Finance: Valuation Techniques Going Beyond Monetary Value
description:
Valuation and value are the keys to any decision. Explore the future of valuation by looking beyond traditional financial metrics. This innovative course teaches you to integrate social, environmental, behavioral, and technological factors into real-world valuation scenarios. This will empower you to create valuations reflecting today's complex world. Transform how you see value and how others see value. Learn how to make convincing arguments favoring sustainable (investment) decisions.

Discover valuation through an engaging mix of dynamic lectures from different faculties and departments (Industrial Design, TPM, MBE, Architecture, …), expert guest speakers, interactive workshops, and hands-on simulations. Redefine value in the modern world and discover the drivers that influence value.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- identify advanced valuation methods: through lectures, students will learn multiple valuation methods and identify where to use which method.

- evaluate economic and sustainability factors influencing valuation.

- assess the applicability of valuation methods in decision-making with different sustainability contexts.

- defend the appropriateness of the applied methods in a real-world case.

- compile knowledge to substantiate and compose a comprehensive new value proposition.

description:
Initiated by staff members from the Departments of MBE and U, this thematic package is a collaboration with the Faculty of Technology, Policy and Management, and the IHS Institute for Housing and Urban Development Studies at Erasmus University Rotterdam. It applies a multidimensional understanding of the concept of sustainable development, which goes beyond the technical and environmental aspects. Through a three-pronged thematic structure - the interrelationship between equitable distribution and consumption, liveability, and societal relations -, the course aims to equip students with an integrated and critical understanding of the social, cultural, and political aspects of sustainability in the built environment, leading to an intervention case.

The learning objectives follow a stepped approach whereby students are enabled to first explain the main challenges of social sustainability in human habitats across the globe, followed by their ability to apply theory to explain and assess these challenges and ultimately their ability to examine critically an “intervention” (i.e., a policy, programme or practical approach) applied to solve a social sustainability challenge. The course adopts an interdisciplinary approach, which is embedded across all learning objectives. Furthermore, this interdisciplinary character will be tested and assessed through its inclusion in the evaluation rubrics of the course’s assessment methods.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- explain the main problems and challenges related to social sustainability in
human habitats in different parts of the world.

- apply key concepts and theories to explain and critically assess social
sustainability challenges in human habitats.

- critically examine an intervention applied to the address of a social
sustainability problem in a given context and provide recommendations for its
improvement.

- design an alternative or improved intervention (policy/physical/institutional) to
tackle the problem.

course_name: Entrepreneurial Engineering and Design for the Built Environment
description: Initiated by staff members from the Departments of MBE, A, U and AE&T, this entrepreneurship project is a collaboration with the Faculties of Technology, Policy and Management, Civil Engineering and Geosciences, and Industrial Design Engineering, the BK-Launch Community and The Green Village. The aim of this studio is to tackle urgencies in the world around us, such as climate adaptation, energy transition, urban inequality, conservation of building materials, and biodiversity for buildings and cities. It cultivates interaction between knowledge-based design and entrepreneurship. A diversity of students together will develop products, designs or services that have the potential to initiate new ventures and possible solutions, and have a tangible, positive impact in the built environment. In general: Science, society and technology are not isolated phenomena. Opinions and methods have a background; decisions have social consequences over time. Students of this course learn and use this and can integrate these insights into their academic work, by means of an iterative development process between design and entrepreneurial planning.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

- create a significant design, product, service or prototype for a societal (local or global) challenge in the built environment. (Linked mainly to T.3, T.7)

-develop an entrepreneurial plan or implementation strategy for realizing the design, product, service or prototype. (Linked mainly to T.1, T.6, T.7)

- evaluate on collaborating effectively with students and parties from other disciplines (Linked mainly to T.1, T.2, T.3, T.4)

- formulate evidence informed argumentation why their project can have societal value and impact. (Linked mainly to T.4, T.5, T.6, T.7)

- defend their proposal and implementation strategy by presentation and discussion. (Linked mainly to T.6, T.7)

description:
Port-Cities: People, Projects, Paradoxes

At a time of climate change, new design strategies are needed at the edge of water and land. Scheveningen as a fishing, yachting, regional port city serves as an example for this investigation and its opportunities and challenges for analysis and design.

Like port cities around the world, Scheveningen, struggles to align multiple values—liveability for citizens, logistics for port transportation, spaces for tourist parking, places for beach goers, and swimmers. Spatial designers—architects, urban designers, landscape architects, industrial designers, and managers—need to develop new strategies, establish new tools, and build upon current research and societal debates. 

How will the port work with sea-level rise, what do we do with the dune areas?

Students will explore the particular history of Scheveningen and its multiple stakeholders; they will identify a topic and collaborate with the City of The Hague/Port of Scheveningen and the Deltametropolis Association, to develop and test tools of engagement. In the first part of the course, they will collectively identify a challenge, do research, and develop a design vision/policy recommendation. In a second part they will individually prepare design solutions (such as design of public spaces, public buildings, public facilities, public amenities) and discuss possible impact with stakeholders.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will be able to:

Conduct on-site research and analyse the complex relationships of Scheveningen based on multiple sources and formulate a value proposition/guiding theme.

Condense the information into a well-structured research booklet that features a guiding vision, a policy recommendation, and design concept, including a meaningful title, clear methodology, and a scientific conclusion.

Process relevant data into a policy recommendation or design concept as part of a group exercise as a foundation for individual output, including careful analysis of the unique conditions and intervention/design needs at the edge of sea and land.

Present a comprehensive proposal for intervention (policy, urban design, architectural design, engineering) with specific details and convincing visual and/or textual communication.

Work in a transdisciplinary setting, including multiple professional, disciplinary, cultural background and facilitate both collaborative processes and individual output.

description:
Master honours students from the Faculty of Applied Sciences work in multidisciplinary teams of 3-6 persons on a company project. The project deals with actual question of technical or more future scenario oriented problems.

During the project, the teams will use expertise from their own fields of studies, to deliver a final advice or product (depending on the assignment). A final report and presentation will be given to the company after the assignment is finished.

The content of this series of Honours Classes supports the Company Project of the Master honours students of the Faculty of Applied Sciences. In these Honours Classes, students reflect on the challenges they meet in working on their Company Project.

The content of these Honours Classes relate to both company and student team sides. On the company side important aspects like corporate identity and image, company vision, mission and strategy, new product and process design and development targets and methodologies, marketing approaches, advertising and promotion.

For communication within and outside the student teams aspects as team roles and personal en team profiles, project and time management, idea generation, creativity, analysis, evalation, reasoning, argumentation, reporting, presenting and negotiation, and credibility.

Depending on the needs of the students and their assignments, the theme order and priorities may vary. These Honours Classes depart from theoretical backgrounds on these themes, which are made practical during five consecutive interactive sessions.

1. Intro: course overview and The Company and Project

- The Company:

- Corporate identity and image, company vision, mission and strategy, new product and process design and development targets and methodologies, marketing approaches, advertising and promotion.

- Innovation and industry

- The Project - BOSCARD

- Background

- Why this project, how does this fit into company strategy / innovation portfolio

- What problem will be solved - what are alternatives to address

- What are the effects (SHEETS) when design solution is in place.

2. The Team

- Personal Quality Quadrant

- Belbin

- Team Roles - SWOT analysis

- Different project phases call for different team role to take the lead

- Personal feedback - receiving and giving.

3. Executing the Project

- Innovation through design - design methodologies

- Design methodologies linked to Innovation classes and types

- QFD, VDI2221, Total Design (Pugh), Product Design and Development (Ulrich, Eppinger), V-model (Prorail?), Sustainable Design (cradle to cradle, blue economy, Ellen MacArthur Foundation

- Design methods for (chemical) products

- Choice of design methodology, phases and activities

- Project and Time Planning approach, methodology, phases and activity and time planning

- Creativity for synthesizing various options (design, project execution, communication)

- Communication within the team, reporting design activities;

- Set report and presentation formats early on; organise communication and cooperation.

- Discussing/convincing/negotiating within the team (roles, tasks, planning, design approach, design solutions, communication)

- Develop and use presentation on the go

4. Communicating and Reporting (to stakeholders)

- Within the team - activity reports - tables/figures - text - ppt slides (see point 3.)

- Report: Key parts - Summary, - Main Report , Appendices;

- Presentation: Key parts: Title Page, Introduction en Project Objectives, Supporting evidence for Conclusions en Recommendations, Conclusions en Recommendation

- Quality control on communication (FOOFI's list)

5. Reflection and lessons learned - report and present to lecturer and peers

- Write personal reflection on Company Project - Personal lessons learned for each of the 4 lessons/themes (max. 1 A4 per theme)

- Present personal reflection on Company Project to peer group - personal lessons learned for each of the 4 lessons/themes in two formats: elevator pitch (1 minute - no slides); presentation max 10 slides.

- Topics to cover:

- What did you do differently for this project in comparison from previous projects?

- What will you (again) do differently in future projects?

description:
Course contents

This course covers several basic transferrable skills and knowledge that are central to becoming an effective scientist or engineer. It contains a range of aspects related to setting up an effective scientific argument and producing a scientific text (article, MSc thesis) while upholding the rules related to research integrity. The following aspects will be covered:

1.       The absolute basics of the philosophy of science (The scientific method, Popper, Kuhn)

2.       How to set up an effective argument:
a.       Critical thinking
b.       Levels or argumentation

3.       Scientific writing:
a.       The scientist/engineer as a professional writer
b.       Structure of scientific stories (OCARstructure, story arcs)
c.       Flow: how paragraphs and sentences connect
d.       Targeting your audience

4.       Research integrity
a.       Ethics and integrity in science and scientific publishing
b.       Presenting and discussing data with integrity
c.       Fraud and integrity violations in science
learning_objectives:
1.       The students understands and can explain the scientific method
2.       The student has a basic knowledge of the philosophy of science
3.       The student is familiar with different levels of reasoning and can implement them in their own writing
4.       The student can recognize and comment on different story structures in scientific writing
5.       The student can design a story structure for a text targeting a specific audience
6.       The student is familiar with the principles of research integrity and can recognize when
these principle are violated.

description:
Art is a sophisticated activity binding the conscious and unconscious, the rational and emotional counterparts of our species. It makes a unique contribution to society by offering various means of expression and exchange and it is a powerful investigation tool for complex human issues. It plays an important societal role in expanding the public imagination by engaging them in a challenging sensorial - intellectual dialogue, increasing the perception of themselves as individually and collectively.

This course invites you to experience and produce art rather than simply broaden your knowledge in contemporary art or history of art.

Using various tools and media, you will develop an art project around an ethical or a societal problem related to the design and use of technology. You will be led to perceive and portrait some relevant aspects of a chosen societal problem, questioning in a completely open and creative way, the consequences, limitations, advantages or any other aspect associated with a chosen technology, as perceived by those who experience the problem or the (mis)use of a that (imagined) technology. You will examine the situation through the eyes of your inner artist, connecting with society through an empathic pathway.

As examples of tools and media we can cite, not exclusively, the case of visual arts: painting, printing, photography, installations, graffiti, films, etc. As examples of global societal problems, we can cite boat people, misuse of big data, consequences of genetically modified organisms, facial recognition, etc.

This empathic and aesthetic exercise is to be complemented by a systematic conceptual reflection on the chosen ethical or societal problem, both carried out in parallel. That is achieved via lectures, debates and self-study of proposed material where you will explore the ethical, cultural and other societal aspects of problems related to new technologies. You will then write an Ethics essay on a topic of your choice that is coupled to your art trajectory and Final Art Assignment.

No previous art experience is necessary.

Course attendance is compulsory.
learning_objectives:
After having completed the course, students can:

recognise their own way to develop a concept or reasoning that has an emotional or empathic origin

reflect on the role of art in expressing and questioning risks associated to new technologies

understand how people immersed in societal problems perceive that problem in their daily lives

communicate via own artistic production, emotions, questions, ideas related to the risk associated to new technologies

reflect on and anticipate the emotional reaction of society or specific social groups to new technologies

empathically participate in the emotional-moral debate associated to state-of-the-art science and technologies

make use of divergent thinking strategies that incorporate creative (artistic) approaches

interpret various aspects of avant-garde art in order to challenge their personal responsibility (position) as engineers

description:
ArtScience is a Research - Education MSc project designed to provide students with a broader experience relating their technical education to the short and long term impact of new technologies on the living and non-living planet, society and human kind itself.

ArtScience is Transdisciplinary in nature and it aims to generate new knowledge trough combined approaches between the Sciences and the Arts, providing an opportunity to achieve a more complete and universal understanding of all that "is" or "will be".

It involves understanding the human experience of nature through the synthesis of artistic and scientific modes of exploration and expression. ArtScience is experiential by nature blending subjective, sensory, emotional and personal understanding with objective, analytical, rational and collective knowledge where students learn how to develop and explore various artistic approaches coupled to scientific approaches to generate their own interpretations and questions on the complex relations between human activities and the planet.

This program is based on making art in small groups of 3-4 students from various faculties to provide them with a first hand opportunity to develop an ArtScience project which either translates the state of the world, community, ecosystem, etc. into an art piece or concept of an art piece. Through this process, students gain new insights on how to translate, critically assess or identify the various ways our technological society interact with humans and non-humans.

In order to illustrate typical projects without being exhaustive:

Music of Heavens - Sonic artistic translation of processes taking place in the atmosphere:

Climate change takes place at time and spatial scales far larger than the human scale. How to translate such complex processes taking place in the planet atmosphere into a sound/visual installation that communicates the state of the change and explores the future as a function of our now a days technological choices ?

Futures in our present - A visual media translation of possible futures

Futures in our Present explores how and where scientists and engineers project their own bias with unconscious scientific procedures and technological choices into products and technologies that will be used in large-scale, or, on the contrary, limited to a small privileged social or geographical group. For instance, what are the possible futures of humans and societies when access to genetic enhancement or brain implants are either limited to a few or imposed to the many ?

These are just a few examples.

Teachers are also open to students' ideas on topics and media.

For questions or more information, email to : e.mendes@tudelft.nl (Eduardo Mendes)
learning_objectives:
After completion of this project, the students can:

LO1: Think beyond their field of education through analytical, critical and creative skills.

LO2: Think divergently to investigate complex problems to obtain original solutions.

LO3: Develop, research and evaluate ideas, concepts and processes as appropriate within a transdisciplinary (ArtScience) domain.

LO4: Work in partnership and make an independent artistic / conceptual innovative contribution to a joint product or process.

LO5: Recognise, analyse and communicate the material and emotional impact of innovative technologies on society and on the planet using a holistic ArtScience approach.

LO6: Better relate their profession, societies and the planet by being equipped to participate in emotional-moral debates, reflecting and acting upon personal responsibility.

description:
Coaching is a key factor for successful innovation. Leading teams, particularly in dynamic and high-stakes environments, places unique and demanding expectations on coaches and leaders.
Different contexts require tailored behaviors and approaches, and this course is designed to prepare you for coaching and leading teams effectively across various settings.

This hands-on course will equip you with the knowledge and skills necessary to become a successful innovation coach and leader. The course learnings will be delivered in an interactive way, with a focus on experiential learning. You will be able to take note of relevant theories and understand how these may work in practice, through exercises and role-plays. Moreover, the course will include multiple sessions of coaching training. The objective of these sessions is to equip you with the necessary skills to coach and manage multidisciplinary project teams. The course is open to both RSM (Rotterdam School of Management - Erasmus University) and TUDelft students, which will further contribute to your skillset in working with people from different backgrounds.

The lectures and coaching training provide foundational skills - taking place in Q3. In Q4 - you will apply these skills intensively in practice. You will coach multidisciplinary teams of Bachelor students (BSc Business Administration and International Business Administration students from RSM and BSc Applied Physics) who are enrolled in the Technology Management course. These coaching sessions, which require significant commitment, offer the unique opportunity to practice your leadership and coaching in a safe learning environment.
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course students should be able to:

1. Understand the leadership/coaching theories that are central to leading for innovation
2. Utilize coaching techniques and skills to inspire and motivate others to innovate
3. Coach interdisciplinary teams in a coaching team to successfully complete (technological) innovation projects
