Orally present and defend project execution and results [ILO 9].

description:
The base module CIEM1000 aims to equip students with both structural engineering design competence and a deeper understanding of construction materials and their mechanical behavior. By combining complementary units from the Structural Engineering (SE) and Structural & Materials Engineering (SME) tracks, the module provides a well-rounded foundation in both structural design principles and construction materials engineering.

Together, these units provide a robust framework for analysing and designing safe, efficient, and sustainable structures. Students completing this module will be well-prepared to address the challenges of modern structural engineering, combining material insight with design expertise.

The module is composed of three interconnected units spread over two quarters:

Unit 1: Sustainable Construction Members and Systems (8 EC – 5 EC in Q2, 3 EC in Q3) - also see CIEM5000 unit 1 syllabus.

Unit coordinator: Dr. ir. A. Tsouvalas
This unit broadens SME students’ structural engineering capabilities by guiding them through six core themes over two quarters.

In Q2, the focus is on loads in structural design, sustainability aspects of construction, and the design and analysis of steel and timber structural members.

In Q3, students advance to the design and analysis of prestressed concrete systems and detailed connections in steel and timber structures.
Throughout, the unit emphasizes sound structural reasoning, design intuition, and the application of sustainability and circularity principles in modern engineering practice.

Unit 1 focuses on loads and sustainability aspects of structural design and design and analysis of steel, timber and concrete members. More specifically, the following topics are covered:

Identification and quantification of loads on structures. This includes short-term, long term, and moveable loads, and the combination of different types of loads.

Design of steel cross sections and members. Influence of properties of base material, production routes and execution tolerances on verification of critical steel cross sections loaded in bending and shear, members loaded in compression and steel bolted and welded connections.

Design of timber cross sections and members. Identification of material properties and their use in the design and verification for strength, stiffness and stability at member level. Design and verification of timber joints and connections.

Analysis and verification of response of prestressed concrete members exposed to forces, i.e.: axial, bending and shear, in order to meet requirements for ultimate and serviceability limit state.

Application of the principles of sustainability and circularity in civil engineering structures. The content on sustainability covers general

LCA approaches and system boundaries supported by specific environmental product data, fabrication processes used in construction of structures, railways and roads. Main principles of circularity and reusability will be covered supported by examples of real structures.

Unit 2: Science and Selection of Construction Materials (4 EC – Q2)

Unit coordinator: Dr. O. Copuroglu
This unit introduces the chemical and physical foundations of construction materials and their influence on mechanical performance. Students learn how manufacturing processes, microstructure, and environmental conditions affect material properties. The unit also trains students in material selection methods, emphasizing the relationship between composition, sustainability, and performance for various construction applications.

Introduction; Chemistry of Construction Materials; Phases and Microstructures

Thermodynamic concepts and electrochemistry

Earth Materials and Aggregates

Portland Cement

Building Physics Fundamentals

Glass, Wood and Timber, Bituminous Materials

Polymers and Organic Additives, FRC

Materials Selection Workshops

Unit 3 Fracture Mechanics (3 EC – Q3)

Unit coordinator: Dr. F. Messali
This unit deepens students’ understanding of failure mechanisms in construction materials. It introduces fracture mechanics concepts and experimental methods to characterize crack formation, propagation, and failure. Theoretical insights are paired with lab-based examples to connect microscopic material behavior with macroscopic structural performance.

Theory of Griffith

Elastic-plastic fracture mechanics

Cohesive zone model and FEM

Quasi-brittle failure

Fracture mechanics in timber

Fracture mechanics in glass and masonry

Fracture mechanics in metals

Environmental influences on fracture
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to

Explain the chemical roots of mechanical behavior of construction materials

Categorize and select construction materials based on functional requirements, economic, environmental and ethical considerations

Design and predict engineering properties of construction materials based on composition and production methods

Identify and quantify the most important loads on structures, roads and railway and schematize and combine them as input for the determination of the force distributions and deformations.

Design, analyze, and optimize steel, timber, and prestressed concrete structures and connections under various load combinations, ensuring structural performance through understanding of material behavior, force flows, and environmental effects.

Analyze, model and predict failure of construction materials and structural elements

Apply fracture mechanics principles to develop materials more resistant to cracking

Understand and apply the principles of sustainability to identify, analyse and evaluate negative effects of civil engineering structures at component and system level on natural environment and society and to use circularity strategies to reduce the environmental impact of structures, railways and roads.

description: Use of materials for structural applications requires quantification of the material performance. Such quantification is related to two scientific disciplines: experimental characterisation and numerical modelling. Safe engineering with construction materials requires that material behaviour has been experimentally tested under controlled conditions and that the performance of the material under expected conditions can be predicted with simulations. In materials science, the two disciplines meet when numerical simulations are used to interpret laboratory experiments and when experiments are used to calibrate and validate models. This module provides students in the construction materials track with a solid basis in both disciplines of measuring and modelling. Students will learn about using advanced experimental techniques that can be used in the laboratory and on-site to monitor and characterise construction material performance. Furthermore, they will be trained to interpret measured data and determine consequences for their short and long-term performance in the specific application. This module will also prepare students for the development and application of multi- scale and multi-physics modelling techniques to study the behaviour of construction materials and to explain deterioration and damage accumulation.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to

Set up a computational model for simulation of the behaviour of materials

Perform linear and nonlinear finite element analysis for mechanical and transport problems

Calibrate and validate computational models with experimental observations

Set up a testing plan for characterisation of materials to define input parameters for structural analysis

Analyse experimental measurements to characterise the performance of construction materials

Advise structural engineers on characterisation and modelling strategies for describing material behaviour

Quantify uncertainty in models and measurements

course_name: Module B1: Technology, Durability, and Performance
description: Module B1 is designed to offer students the opportunity to develop in depth scientific insight into the development of construction materials and their behaviour under various environmental and loading conditions. Specifically, students will learn about construction materials technology (5EC), degradation mechanisms and durability (5EC) and imposed deformations (5EC).
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

1. Design mixture of concrete, asphalt and other composite materials for application-related requirements

2. Define durability concepts of construction materials, describe material properties and their effect on durability.
3. List and explain physical, chemical and biological degradation mechanisms of construction materials.
4. Perform service life design of structures based on material properties.
5. Set-up repair and maintenance strategies for degraded structures
6. Analyse and predict the influence of eigenstresses in materials on the behaviour of structural elements and components
7. Explain how environmental effects and different gradients on material level and structural level impose deformations and stresses

course_name: Module B2: Technology, Durability, and Modelling
description: Module B2 is designed to offer students the opportunity to develop in depth scientific insight into the development of construction materials, their durability, and modelling. Specifically, students will learn about construction materials technology (5EC), degradation mechanisms and durability (5EC) and constitutive modelling (5EC).
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

1. Design mixture of concrete, asphalt and other composite materials for application-related requirements

2. Define durability concepts of construction materials, describe material properties and their effect on durability.

3. List and explain physical, chemical and biological degradation mechanisms of construction materials.

4. Perform service life design of structures based on material properties.

5. Set-up repair and maintenance strategies for degraded structures

6. Formulate constitutive models to describe the linear/nonlinear response of materials and implement them in FEM codes

7. Select and apply constitutive models for various physicochemical material behaviours.

description:
The course is composed of three thematics relating to advanced computational mechanics concepts: multiphysics, multiscale and optimisation.

The first three weeks will consist of lectures to give an overview about each of those concepts which includes:

Multiphysics: physical equations coupling, interface coupling (such as fluid-structure interaction)

Multiscale: homogenisation methods, mixed-dimensionality (such as Discrete Fracture Network)

Optimisation: softening regularisation, machine learning

During those weeks, you will decide on one of those topics for your project. In the following weeks, you will gather a literature review on the method selected, and run simulations implementing the method. The project is kept on track with a weekly follow-up by the project supervisor. Eventually, a report in the format of an academic paper needs to be submitted for the assessment.

The last weeks of the course consist of presentations of the projects to the whole class.
learning_objectives:
In this course, you will study advanced numerical Finite Element Method that is used to simulate complex mechanical phenomena. On completion of this module, you should be able to:

LO1. Identify which numerical method to apply in case of complex physical behaviour.(ILO 2, 4)

LO2. Explain the algorithms needed to implement one selected method of your choosing in a Finite Element simulation. (ILO 2)

LO3. Run Finite Element simulations implementing the selected method. (ILO 7)

description:
This course is offered for the students who are interested in forensic construction materials engineering, which comprises techniques and protocols to associate construction damage and failure to the materials characteristics and design. The course is especially suited for those students who would like to work in the field of consultancy.

The main focus of the course is on concrete, reinforced-concrete, masonry, glass, natural resources, asphalt concrete and other bituminous materials. However, the techniques discussed can be considered equally useful for steel, composites and bio-based construction materials.

The content covers the following topics. Each week, a workshop session is devoted to the applications of the forensic techniques on various construction materials.

Week 1. Introduction and damage types

Week 2. Sampling and specimen preperation

Week 3. Optical microscopy

Week 4. Corrosion techniques

Week 5. Electron microscopy and microanalysis

Week 6. X-ray techniques

Week 7. Selected topics

Week 8. Practical aspects, reporting and communication
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

Define activities in a forensic engineering research. Recognize the need for a forensic research in civil engineering cases. Classify damage types in structures and compare damage and failure examples. Evaluate and select in-situ testing methods, laboratory tests and numerical methods to identify the causes of damage and failure. [ILO 7, 8, 10]

Associate damage features with durability problems. Compose a protocol by choosing the suitable forensic tools for a case. Evaluate and criticise forensic reports from other parties. Develop a systematic approach (preliminary investigation-hypothesis-data collection-evidence analysis) to analyse the causes of damage and (premature) failure. Communicate forensic investigation details with the (multidisciplinary) stakeholders. [ILO 2, 3, 6, 9]

Illustrate working principles of different analytical tools for forensic engineering research. Classify analytical techniques based on their use i.e., chemical composition, phase analysis, pore analysis etc. Compare and explain these techniques to show they are not alternatives but complementary to each other. [ILO 8, 10]

Summarize forensic research tools and protocols for commonly used construction materials e.g.; reinforced concrete, asphalt concrete, masonry, glass etc. Distinguish advantages and limitations of in-situ testing over lab testing. [3, 6, 8]

course_name: Upscaling Techniques in Construction Materials Design and Engineering
description:
This course on upscaling techniques in construction materials, design and engineering will consist of the following topics:

Introduction to computational upscaling techniques.

Introduction to homogenization and viscoelasticity.

Micromechanical aspects of response focusing on the interplay between adhesion and cohesion mechanisms, the effects of moisture, aging etc.

Numerical simulation based on homogenized properties.

Back-calculation of stress/strain response at individual components based on numerical simulation results.

Linear poroelasticity for the determination of elastic properties of composite-like materials.

Microporofracture mechanics (linear poroelasticity and linear fracture mechanics).

Multiscale modelling of the transport properties of concrete, the deterioration process under coupled service conditions (multi-action).

Obtaining the microstructure of cement paste numerically as well as experimentally.

Upscaling of mechanical properties of cement paste.

Modelling of rheology, time-dependent response on creep, shrinkage, and fatigue of concrete.

These topics will be supported with several workshops and guest lectures.

The course may suit students with different specializations having the below-mentioned prerequisites. Within the Civil Engineering MSc programme, the course is recommended for students from the tracks Construction Materials, Structural Engineering and Geo-Engineering.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

Explain microstructural modelling and upscaling approaches of multi-component materials. [ILO 2, 10]

Analyse the influence of microstructural features on the (mechanical, transport) properties of building materials. [ILO 2, 3]

Select an appropriate upscaling technique (computational, numerical or analytical homogenisation) for a given multiscale problem. [ILO 2, 5]

Apply microstructural modelling and upscaling approaches to predict engineering properties for multi-component materials (e.g., asphalt, concrete, metal composite). [ILO 2, 10]

description:
Glass plays an ever more prominent role in structures through its application in facades, roofs, floors, beams, columns, walls and complete glass constructions. Consequently, there is an increasing emphasis on glass technology both in engineering practice and in research, resulting in a strong need for engineers in this field.

This course therefore focuses on the application of glass in structures and covers the state-of-the-art in glass research and engineering. Through lectures, workshops, analyses and a hands-on design of a glass structure, students learn about the engineering and research aspects of glass, such as its mechanical behaviour, manufacturing processes, testing procedures, design standards, connection typologies, safety aspects, sustainability considerations and innovative glass structures.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

Design a glass structure, including the verification of structural glass components, stability measures and the detailing of glass connections.

Implement safety and sustainability considerations in the design of a glass structure.

Analyse the latest developments in glass research and engineering.

Apply the latest glass developments in the design of a glass structure.

Analyse the material behaviour of glass in structures.

Assess the influence of production and processing techniques on the performance of glass in structures.

Evaluate the effects of loading and environmental conditions on the performance of glass and address these in the design of a glass structure.

description:
The Geotechnical Engineering Track Base Module includes three units, Theory and modelling of geo-processes (3 ECTS), Testing and modelling of soil behavior (6 ECTS), and Foundations and Excavations (6 ECTS).

Students will learn how to describe mechanical behavior (stress-strain response) of soils and rocks based on laboratory testing and data analysis. The concepts of constitutive modelling will be introduced, and the applications are discussed. The observed soil behavior from standard geotechnical laboratory tests will be presented and students will learn to analyze and interpret the test data to translate them into mathematical formulations and model parameters needed for engineering design. Formulation, assessment, and evaluation of the soil coupled hydro-mechanical response in engineering applications will be covered. The students will use the derived soil parameters in common design approaches to predict the behaviour of foundations and excavations. Case studies where the actual response of structure was measured will be used to promote reflective learning.

Moreover, the interaction between the subsurface and geotechnical structures as well as the impact of the environment on the design, construction and performance of geotechnical structures, and vice versa will be presented. Topics such as communicating with stakeholders from all relevant backgrounds about geotechnical problems and solutions will be presented and discussed.

In Track Base, the learning line of Monitoring and Data Science is covered within all three units. The basics of topics related to the monitoring of geotechnical structures will be introduced in Foundations and excavations. Additionally, all three units provide opportunities for elaborating the data, and development of models for predicting soil and geotechnical structures behavior. Such elaboration is guided throughout the module for students to learn how to process/visualize/present information for clients and stakeholders.

This module will add to the learning line on Ethics related to design of geotechnical structures considering issues such as usability/safety of geotechnical systems, evaluation, and assessment of the interaction between the subsurface and geotechnical structures as well as effective Communication with stakeholders.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

C-LO1: Describe the mechanical behavior (stress-strain response) of soils and rocks based on laboratory testing and data analysis

C-LO2: Recognize and apply the concept of constitutive modelling

C-LO3: Analysis and interpret laboratory tests and derive and apply mathematical formulations for engineering design

C-LO4: Evaluate and assess the interaction between the subsurface and geotechnical structures

C-LO5: Recognize, and determine the impact of the environment on the design, construction, and performance of geotechnical structures, and vice versa

C-LO6: Communicate the results with experts from other disciplines and other stakeholders

C-LO7: Assess the impact of hydro-mechanical coupling on the soil response

description:
The module covers two complementary processes in geotechnical engineering: Engineering Geology and Numerical Modelling. A geological perspective is a prerequisite of a complete geotechnical analysis. Once this interpretation of the geology in an engineering context is established in the Engineering Geology unit, the resulting ground model provides the starting point for geotechnical analyses and predictions by numerical models. The Numerical Modelling unit covers the theory and application of these models to come to quantitative predictions, as well as the interpretation of the results in the geotechnical context, because after all a number is not an answer.

Parts of this module follow the learning line on Data and Monitoring by covering 1) the manipulation of both sparse and dense data, and both soft and hard data to highlight ground related risks and opportunities, 2) the interpretation of numerical analysis results in the context of data- and model uncertainty, 3) uncertainty propagation in (numerical) models.

Parts of this module follow the learning line on Ethics by considering ethical aspects in feasibility studies conducted in Engineering Geology. This allows students to apply moral frameworks to the allowable actions as a CE Engineer. The Numerical modelling unit covers modelling techniques which are at the heart of various value sensitive methods for CE designs to be understood in the learning line on Ethics.

Keywords:

Engineering geology; desk study; soil and rock properties; conceptual ground and ground water flow modelling; anticipated ground conditions; geo-hazards and geotechnical issues; feasibility study; finite element method; numerical models; engineering solutions; sensitivity analysis;

The module covers the design, monitoring and assessment of geotechnical structures. It addresses the measurement, characterization and numerical modelling of spatial variability, the evaluation of risk and uncertainty in geotechnical engineering, the interaction between soil layers and the geotechnical structure, and the impact of geotechnical structures on other structures in an urban environment. Applications include the design of geotechnical structural elements (e.g., tunnel lining, soil reinforcement).

The learning line on Monitoring and Data Science is included through the analysis of conventional and innovative geotechnical monitoring, and the evaluation of data from site investigation and physical modelling (Site Investigation modelling, Risk and variability in geotechnical engineering).

Parts of this module follow the learning line on Ethics by considering ethical aspects in geo-risk management. In the Site Investigation and monitoring unit, students will gain understanding into approaches used to reduce risk in geotechnical engineering. Ethical aspects associated with human factors and risk communication in geo-engineering will be also covered.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

B1-LO1: describe the nature, impact and characterisation of soil spatial variability.

B1-LO2: explain the relationship between soil spatial variability and geotechnical design and risk assessment.

B1-LO3: evaluate advantages and shortcomings of different alternative choices for the design of infrastructure.

B1-LO4: evaluate the design and construction methods for different types of infrastructure.

B1-LO5: identify suitable site investigation techniques and critically analyse the results of a site investigation survey.

B1-LO6: analyse geotechnical problems based on physical and numerical modelling techniques.

description:
The module includes three units, namely Mechanics of Deltaic Soils, Experimental Soil Mechanics, and Soil Dynamics. Students will dive into non-standard aspects of Soil Mechanics, both in terms of analysis/modelling techniques and geotechnical applications. Deltaic soils are soils that are found in deltaic areas, such as normally consolidated soft clays, organic clays and peats, and loose to medium dense sands. From a methodological standpoint, the module covers advanced topics regarding the testing and constitutive modelling of soils, up to the solution of boundary value problems through both physical and numerical modelling techniques. Relevant applications include the analysis of geotechnical problems in soft deltaic soils, and/or in the presence of cyclic/dynamic loading conditions.

In this module the learning line on Monitoring and Data Science is enriched with further content. In particular, the unit on Experimental Soil Mechanics addresses topics related to the monitoring of physical geo-models during small-scale centrifuge experiments, including the selection of the most suitable sensors for real-time measurements.

Overall, the three units provide opportunities for elaborating the data, often of big size, returned by physical and numerical models. Such elaboration is guided throughout the module for students to learn how to process/visualise/present information for clients and stakeholders.

Ethical aspects associated with Advanced Soil Mechanics subjects are discussed throughout the module. Given the emphasis on experimental and numerical analyses as essential input to geotechnical design, important implications are pointed out regarding the impact of (i) selection of testing methods, (ii) identification of soil model parameters, (iii) validation of physical/numerical models on the usability/safety of geotechnical systems. Particularly, conflicts of interest, and their potentially catastrophic consequences, between (financial benefit of) service providers and (satisfaction/safety of) clients is discussed throughout the three units from a mechanics-oriented perspective.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

B2-LO1: analyse the role of advanced, time-dependent features of soils' hydro-mechanical behaviour

B2-LO2: identify and integrate testing and constitutive modelling strategies for soils subjected to environmental and man-induced perturbations

B2-LO3: select and perform advanced analyses of geotechnical problems based on most appropriate physical/numerical modelling techniques

B2-LO4: critically reflect on benefits and limitations of advanced physical and numerical modelling strategies in geotechnical engineering

B2-LO5: effectively report in writing the outcome of advanced experimental and computational analyses in relation to geotechnical engineering applications

description:
Geotechnical Engineering in delta areas, in the Netherlands and worldwide, must face challenges associated to soft, and possibly unstable, soils. Such challenges must inevitably be tackled at different levels, i.e., from fundamental understanding and simulation of deltaic soil behaviour, to their in-situ characterisation for geotechnical design. More specifically, the module covers the design, monitoring and assessment of geotechnical structures. It addresses the mechanics of deltaic soils, the interaction between soil layers and the geotechnical structure, and the impact of geotechnical structures on other structures in an urban environment. Applications include the design of geotechnical structural elements (e.g., tunnel lining, soil reinforcement).

This module includes three units, namely Geotechnical Design, Site Investigation and Monitoring, and Mechanics of Deltaic Soils.

The learning line on Monitoring and Data Science is included through the analysis of conventional and innovative geotechnical monitoring, and the evaluation of data from site investigation and physical modelling (Site Investigation en Monitoring).

Parts of this module follow the learning line on Ethics by considering ethical aspects in geo-risk management. In the Site Investigation and Monitoring unit, students will gain understanding into approaches used to reduce risk in geotechnical engineering. Ethical aspects associated with human factors and risk communication in geo-engineering will be also covered.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

B3-LO1: describe testing and constitutive modelling strategies for soils subjected to environmental and man-induced perturbations.

B3- LO2: explain the role of advanced, time-related features of soils' hydro-mechanical behaviour.

B3- LO3: evaluate advantages and shortcomings of different alternative choices for the design of infrastructure.

B3- LO4: evaluate the design and construction methods for different types of infrastructure.

B3- LO6: analyse geotechnical problems based on physical and numerical modelling techniques

description:
A number of countries have ambitious targets to develop offshore renewables projects. There are many technical challenges to be solved. From a geotechnical engineering perspective these include: (i) characterising unusual soils, (ii) considering the impact of irregular loading, including earthquakes, typhoons, impacts etc. (iii) developing frameworks to understand the response of soils to cyclic loading, (iv) updating design models developed from the oil and gas sector to the foundation systems deployed in renewables projects and (v) the consideration of installation risks.

A series of short lectures will be by researchers and practitioners involved in developing and implementing state of the art design procedures (see content below). The lectures will be supplemented by small-group workshops on real-world problems:

Marine Geology and Site Characterisation

Offshore Soil Behaviour including cyclic response modelling.

Design of Shallow Foundations (incl. mudmats, suction caissons, GBS).

Development of the new ISO Pile Design Method for Axially Loaded Foundations

The PISA model and alternative approaches for monopile design

Anchor Systems for floating wind

Installation of foundation systems

On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

Describe the response of marine soils subjected to monotonic and cyclic loading [ILO 1,4]

Plan and implement an offshore site survey for soil characterisation purposes [ILO 1,4]

Analyse/design foundation systems for both bottom-fixed and floating offshore structures [ILO 1,4]

Explain the application and limitations of design codes [ILO 4,9]

description:

It is meant as an addition to other specialist courses and the topics studied here can also be applied in other courses. The course will cover aspects of:

The technique of Horizontal Directional Drilling (HDD)

Boring equipment

Technical calculations for stresses in pipelines

Renovation of existing pipelines

Research on trenchless technologies and innovative applications

Role of the contractor and engineering office

Influence of contract types on project execution

Risks and risk management

Case discussions

identify and describe the methods available for trenchless installation and rehabilitation of cables and ducts [ILO 1,4,9]

make a preliminary design for new pipe line installations [ILO 1,4]

description:
The course covers the fundamentals of rock mechanics and rock engineering. It deals with the following:

characterisation and laboratory and in situ testing for the determination of properties of intact rock, discontinuities in rock, and discontinuous rock masses

mechanical behaviour of rock masses, including dynamic, time-dependent, and post peak behaviour.

basic principles of flow through discontinuities and discontinuous rock masses.

weathering and susceptibility to weathering of rock masses.

principle of excavation methods. Excavatability, wear and performance of cutting tools. Influence of blasting and other vibrations. Influence of stress and stress changes.

principle of support methods.

rock mass classification systems. Possibilities for analytical and numerical modelling of discontinuous rock masses.

application of principles of rock mass excavation and support to slopes, tunnel, dam, foundation, rock dredging or sea water breaker design.

monitoring, analysis, prediction and mitigation of subsidence due to solid removal.

application of engineering tools such as Total Geological Approach and function (system) analysis to projects case histories.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

explain how to characterize, test, and monitor rock material, rock discontinuities and rock masses for a wide range of geo-engineering- and environmental applications [ILO 2, 3, 4]

select models that capture the essentials of the rock behaviour observed in the lab or in situ and highlight limitations of these models. [ILO 2]

appraise ground conditions and evaluate ground parameters, even from sparse and incomplete data sets, and formulate ground risks associated to projects. [ILO 3, 4, 5]

evaluate analytically the stability of various structures founded in or on rocks. [ILO 3, 5]

design basic stabilization measures and recommend more advanced methods for critical situations. [ILO 1, 9]

apply to construction projects lessons learned from case histories and engineering tools such as the Total Geological History and Function analysis. [ILO 1, 5]

Work on rock mechanics and rock engineering problems independently, compile results in written reports, and defend them orally. [ILO 2, 7, 9]

course_name: Base: Hydraulic Engineering Fundamentals and Environments Part I
description:
The Hydraulic Engineering Extended Track Core of 24 EC consists of two parts. Part I (15 EC) contains three units: Hydraulic Engineering Solutions in a Changing Environment (6EC); Waves (5EC); and River Systems and Interventions (4EC).

The unit Hydraulic Engineering Solutions in a Changing Environment considers physical processes, design of structures, ecological and societal components. The focus is on the most pressing issues and building with nature solutions at a system scale.

The unit Ocean Waves covers the dynamics of wind-generated waves in the open ocean and in coastal waters.

The unit River Systems and Interventions covers: (1) the characteristics of a river system,(2) the morphodynamic behaviour of these systems (including the response to human interventions) based on the underlying hydrodynamic and sediment transport processes, and (3) typical river engineering problems and methods design interventions.

The Hydraulic Engineering Solutions in a Changing Environment unit presents modern challenges in hydraulic systems that cover coastal, river and port environments, and covers fundamental knowledge required to design nature-based and hard engineering solutions in these systems (e.g., flow and transport fundamentals, design of bed protections, interactions with ecosystems). In order to effectively propose and design solutions both engineering and ecological design principles are discussed.

The Ocean Waves Unit focuses in the first part on the description of regular (monochromatic) waves before extending the results to realistic wind-generated wave fields that consist of wave components of varying frequencies and directions. It starts with linear wave theory which gives the interrelation between physical characteristics as the surface motion, the wave-induced pressure in the water and the motion of water particles. Commonly used nonlinear wave theories are then briefly introduced. We then discuss how the main properties of regular waves change when they propagate over varying depths and how they are affected by currents. In the second part of the Unit, we transition to irregular and directionally spread wave fields. We discuss how such wave fields can be measured and subsequently characterized, both in the time- and frequency-domain. We finally discuss how the wave field develops in the open ocean and coastal waters, and how an energy balance can be used to predict spectral wave evolution.

The unit River Systems and Interventions covers three main topics:

(1) The characteristics of a river system. Here we address river systems, river response to change and associated time scales, catchment hydrology, rainfall-runoff, and climate aspects.

(2) The hydraulic and morphodynamic behavior of these systems. Here we address flow properties (normal flow, backwater types, flood waves, flow structures), sediment transport, and initial, transient and equilibrium morphodynamic response.

(3) River interventions. Here we address river-related problems, (inter)national river management, flood safety, navigation and other river functions, as well as river interventions.
learning_objectives:
On completion of the Hydraulic Engineering Extended Track Core (Part I and Part II combined), the student will be able to:

Explain the physical principles behind flow, transport, turbulence, mixing, sediment transport, surface waves and hydraulic loads.

Design solutions for typical hydraulic engineering problems regarding scour, contamination, sediment transport, bed stability.

Integrate building with nature concepts and principles in the design of hydraulic systems covering coastal-, riverine- and port domains by considering physical, engineering, environmental, ecological and societal aspects.

Explain the characteristics of rivers, coasts, estuaries, ports and waterways in hydraulic engineering systems.

Predict and assess the behavior of rivers, coasts, estuaries, ports and waterways in hydraulic engineering systems in response to natural and anthropogenic change taking uncertainties into account.

Identify the range of functions of rivers, coasts, estuaries, ports and waterways in hydraulic engineering systems.

The specific Learning Objectives for the unit Hydraulic Engineering Solutions in a Changing Environment are:

Describe how physical, biological, sedimentary and chemical processes are connected and interact in hydraulic systems.

Assess the impact of engineering interventions on ecosystem sustainability and climate resilience across a range of spatial and temporal scales in the design process.

Apply physical principles to design engineering measures for scour protection, bed stability, and sediment management in dynamic hydraulic systems.

Integrate building with nature concepts and principles in the design of hydraulic systems by considering physical, engineering, environmental, ecological and societal aspects.

The specific Learning Objectives for the unit Waves are:

Explain the rationale behind the definition and computation of the wave spectrum and calculate spectral wave characteristics.

Characterize wind-generated waves in a statistical framework.

Explain the physical processes driving wave transformation in oceanic and coastal waters and evaluate which processes dominate in a given situation.

Calculate the evolution of wind-generated waves in oceanic and coastal waters.

The specific Learning Objectives for the unit River Systems and Interventions are:

Explain the role of the river system in the hydrological cycle, the controls of a river system, time scales of change of the controls versus time scale of system response (catchment to reach scale), and phases (initial, transient, quasi-equilibrium, equilibrium) of river response

Derive and apply simplified forms of the one-dimensional shallow-water equations (i.e., normal flow, flood waves, and backwater curves);

Predict and assess (initial, equilibrium, and transient) river response to natural and anthropogenic change of controls

Identify and assess the range of river functions (e.g. flood safety, navigation, nature restoration, freshwater supply, ecology, port operability, water quality, and construction in water), system-related problems (from catchment to reach scale) in national and international river management, and possible solutions or interventions

Apply (inter)national safety standards in flood risk management.

course_name: Hydraulic Engineering Fundamentals and Environments Part II
description:
The Hydraulic Engineering Extended Track Core of 24 EC consists of two parts. Part II (9 EC) contains two units: Coastal and Estuarine Systems and Introduction to Port and Waterway Systems. Together with the unit River Systems and Interventions of Part I, they cover the Hydraulic Engineering Environments or systems.

1. Coastal and Estuarine Systems (6EC). This unit covers: (1) the characteristics of a range of coastal systems (seas, open coasts, estuaries and tidal basins), (2) the morphodynamic behaviour of these systems (including the response to human interventions) based on the underlying hydrodynamic and sediment transport processes, and (3) typical coastal engineering problems and methods for coastal protection.

2. Introduction to Port and Waterway Systems (3EC) This unit explains the importance of port and waterway systems in supporting waterborne supply chains at different scales, and discusses performance optimization from an infrastructure perspective. The unit is organized around three themes: (1) Ports and terminals: challenges for port development, port planning, port layout, terminal development, (2) waterways: challenges for waterway development, waterway dimensions, waterway elements, ship and ship-waterway interactions, traffic management, (3) system performance: analyzing the performance of systems of ports/terminals and waterways (queueing theory).

Various topics will be considered in this module. An overview per unit is provided below.

Topics per week for Coastal and Estuarine Systems (and corresponding chapter in textbook):

Week 1: Introduction (Ch1) and large-scale geographical variation of coastal systems (Ch2)

Week 2: Wind waves and tides (Ch3),

Week 3: Global wave and tidal environments (Ch4), Coastal hydrodynamics  wind waves (Ch5)

Week 4: Coastal hydrodynamics  wind waves (Ch5), Coastal hydrodynamics  tides (Ch5),

Week 5: Sediment transport (Ch6), Cross-shore transport and profile development (Ch7)

Week 6: Cross-shore transport and profile development (Ch7), Longshore transport and coastline changes (Ch8)

Week 7: Exam questions Cross-shore and Longshore, practical Ch8, Coastal inlets and tidal basins (Ch9)

Week 8: Coastal inlets and tidal basins (Ch9), exam questions Tidal, Coastal protection (Ch10)

Topics per week for Introduction to Ports and Waterways:

Week 1: General introduction to ports and waterways; Port-city interaction and Corridors

Week 2: Integral port planning and Port layouts; Planning and design of port water areas

Week 3: Queuing theory; Terminal planning and design (within port layout)

Week 4: Container terminals + Port economics and investment analysis

Week 5: Evaluation assignment, Inland Navigation

Week 6: Ship-waterway interaction, Dimensioning of waterways and waterway elements

Week 7: Environment, Lecture Wrap up and Beyond

Week 8: Q&A session

Coastal systems (Ch2, Ch4)

Wave and tidal climate (Ch4)

in the oceans (Ch3); and

along open coasts and in tidal basins (Ch5).

longshore transport (Ch8)

The specific Learning Objectives for the unit Introduction to Ports and Waterways Systems

LO 01 - general:

Describe the environmental issues relevant to ports and waterways and explain the importance of integrating environmental considerations in (stakeholder inclusive) port planning and design.

LO 02 - ports/terminals:

Explain the principles of port master planning and develop basic port layouts based on principles of robustness and adaptability in an uncertain future;

Develop functional designs of port terminals (number of elements and their order-of-magnitude dimensions) using state-of-the-art design methods and rules (Module A focuses on container terminals, Module B04-01 will address other terminal types);

LO 03 - waterways and port water areas:

Discuss the importance of inland waterway transport corridor policies/plans and perform a basic capacity analysis taking into account forecasted traffic volumes and waterway infrastructure in place or planned;

Explain the basics of ship motions, ship-ship interaction and ship-fairway interaction;

Develop functional designs of inland waterways and port waterway areas using state-of-the-art design methods and rules (canals, locks, bridges, approach channels, turning basins, berths).

LO 04 - system behaviour:

Analyse relevant processes influencing capacity;

description:
Central to this B-module are coastal engineering problems and interventions and specifically the assessment of the impact of these interventions and their technical design. Impact assessment and design require advanced system knowledge and proper application of tools. These three elements in connection (interventions, knowledge and tools) are the basis of this B-module. Ethical issues and the role of the engineer will be addressed in the model assignments, which are  part of the second two units described below, by addressing conflicting perspectives of various vocal and non-vocal stakeholders.

The module consists of three units of equal weights, which run in parallel (with especially strong connections between the first and second units):

1. Advanced Coastal and Estuarine Systems

2. Coastal and Estuarine Modelling

3. Shore protection en Breakwaters

Advanced Coastal and Estuarine Systems treats, in-depth, coastal and estuarine processes and system behaviour (a.o. waves, tides, currents, coarse and fine sediment transport, morphodynamic change) and response to interventions (a.o. storm surge barriers, groynes, dredging and nourishments). A wide range of coastal systems is considered: deltas, estuaries, beaches and dunes, tidal plains, barrier and lagoon coasts. Not only the physical principles but also their complex interplay in the built and natural environment is discussed. This process knowledge is linked to coastal engineering problems and interventions.

Coastal and Estuarine Modelling combines knowledge on prediction, modelling and monitoring concepts with a hands-on approach. Students apply various state-of-the art models in order to solve complex coastal engineering problems taking into account its uncertainties. Students (functionally) design and evaluate coastal engineering interventions related to amongst others coastal safety or sediment management. Students collaborate in the group assignment.

Shore protection en Breakwaters treats the mechanisms of (in)stability of protection layers under wave loads. Aspects needed for practical implementation of these protection layers are introduced, like construction, environment, uncertainty, maintenance, boundary conditions, and modelling techniques. The technical design of all parts of a breakwater cross-section is treated in-depth.

(B1-5) Account for uncertainties in relation to monitoring, modelling and data analysis for research and design

(B1-6) Clearly present and report design and modelling results

description:
This course is on integration of the natural system in engineering thinking and design, called Building with Nature. You will learn to analyse and design with natural processes and the natural system and everything that lives in it. Lectures will focus on providing you with the basic skills to do a system analysis by improving your understanding of the interaction between abiotic and biotic processes and Building with Nature principles.

The central element in this course is a case study of the Oosterschelde. Students work in groups to disentangle abiotic and biotic processes in this area and to describe functioning of the system on different scales. This analysis constitutes the basis to evaluate the problem at hand from the perspective of different stakeholders and to formulate objectives to serve these different stakeholders. Interventions to meet the objectives will be formulated and evaluated using a multicriteria analysis. For a single intervention a more detailed design will be made in an individual assignment. For this design simple wave-vegetation models will be used. The work will be captured in a report.

Guest lectures will inform students on implemented Building with Nature practices and bring students in contact with companies that work with Building with Nature. Problem analysis, objective setting and intervention evaluation will be done in groups. The modelling exercise is an individual assignment. During tutorials the students can work on the assignments. A field visit of a day to the Oosterschelde area is part of the course and during the field visit a stakeholder game will be played. Reports will be delivered and graded individually.
learning_objectives:

Make a qualitatively underbuilt Building with Nature design. [ILO 1]

Evaluate long-term and large-scale effects of their proposed design considering climate change effects and ecological objectives. [ILO 1, 3, 4, 5]
