course_name: Advanced Modelling of Turbulent Flows and Transport
description:
1. introductory lecture on the course

2. statistical description of turbulence (mean flow, higher statistical moments, (auto)correlations, Taylors hypothesis)

3. experimental techniques (single point vs. field measurements, flow visualisation, measurement techniques)

4. balance equations I (continuity equation, Navier-Stokes equations, turbulent kinetic energy)

5. Reynolds decomposition (ensemble averaging, Reynolds equations, closure problem, energy transfer, Kolmorogov scales, energy spectrum, Kolmogorovs 5/3 law)

6. balance equations II (2DH/3D shallow water equations for free surface flows, scaling, hydrostatic pressure, wind stress, bottom friction, horizontal mixing, vertical mixing, constituent transport)

7. numerical techniques for 2DH shallow water equations (recap computational modelling, staggered schemes, time marching, momentum conservation, rapidly varied flows, flooding and drying)

8. turbulence modelling (mixing layer hypothesis, eddy viscosity concept, k-epsilon, LES)

9. numerical aspects of 3D turbulence modelling (regular vs. flexible meshes, sigma layers vs. z-layers for free surface flows, artificial vertical mixing, finite volume method, higher order upwind schemes+flux limiting)

10. turbulent flows in practice (boundary layers, law-of-the-wall, wall roughness, free surface flows in complex geometries, separation and recirculation)

11. turbulence diffusion (Reynolds analogy, dispersion, spreading)

12. non-hydrostatic flow modelling (vertical acceleration, subgrid, lock exchange, high performance computing)
learning_objectives:
On completion of this elective, the student will be able to:

Identify different concepts to describe turbulence and characterize various turbulence processes as well as discuss the statistical description of turbulence, the various measurement techniques, and computational modelling concepts. (ILO 2, 4, 10)

Describe the balance equations for turbulent flows and discuss the necessity of the Reynolds decomposition and appreciate the closure problem. (ILO 2, 4, 10)

Identify the various numerical modelling concepts and discuss the abilities and restrictions of these concepts as well as categorise typical numerical issues, e.g. numerical properties and possible artefacts. (ILO 2, 4, 10)

To analyse observed problems and suggest solutions supported by his/her findings with evidences or examples for a given case. (ILO 2, 4, 7)

To execute a CFD model for computations, invocation of special functions, and performance of some other technical work. (ILO 2, 10)

To identify the various turbulence models and explain their abilities and limitations. (ILO 2, 4, 7, 9)

To make estimates of length and velocity scales characterizing the turbulent motions and judge the impact of turbulence on bed material, structures and the transport of matter (ILO 2, 4, 10)

To develop an engineering problem and select software packages, and the turbulence models in particular, in the context of applications with open water bodies as seas, estuaries, rivers, lakes and channels. (ILO 7)

To compose a view on new developments in the field of turbulence research and in the field of CFD. (ILO 2, 9)

description: This course is an introduction to physical oceanography for civil and offshore engineering students, introducing them to the basic physical concepts behind oceanography. The aim of the course is to provide an understanding of the basic physics governing our oceans, from our estuaries and coasts to the deep ocean. Therefore, in this course emphasis is placed on the fundamental physical processes occurring in the ocean. This provides a basis for understanding geostrophic flows, tides, internal waves, estuary and river plume dynamics, the wind-driven ocean circulation and the thermohaline (density-driven) deep ocean circulation and its role for climate.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this elective, the student will be able to:

explain the influence of Coriolis and stratification on a number of coastal and ocean flows. - ILO2,3

explain the basics of tides, wind-driven circulations, thermohaline circulation. - ILO2,3

derive the key equations governing the ocean circulation on coastal and basin scales and apply them to gain insight into the fundamental concepts and balances. - ILO2

explain the concepts of buoyancy and mixing and their role in coastal oceanography. - ILO2,3,4,5,8

evaluate the properties of internal waves, instabilities and stationary flows. - ILO2,3

analyse the role of the Coriolis force for the wind-driven circulation and in particular for western boundary currents. - ILO2,3

analyse the thermohaline circulation and its role for climate - ILO2,3,5,8

description: The CE HOS track addresses the challenges associated with the design, construction and operation of hydraulic and offshore structures by unifying the knowledge from structural, hydraulic, and geotechnical engineering disciplines. The role of the Track Base Module is to equip students with the fundamental knowledge necessary to tackle the engineering challenges associated with the structural design, construction and operation of structures in river, coastal and marine environments.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of this module, the student will be able to:

MLO-1. Analyse fluid- and soil-structure interaction processes, as well as structural mechanics principles, Relevant for the engineering of hydraulic and offshore structures.

MLO-2. Analyse scientific knowledge on fluid- and soil-structure interaction, as well as structural mechanics, that contributes to solving complex hydraulic and offshore structures.

MLO-3. Perform, statistically model selection and identification for fluid- and soil-structure interaction analyses.

MLO-4. Quantify uncertainty in models and measurements for fluid and soil-structure interaction analyses.

MLO-5. Evaluate uncertainty propagation for fluid-and soil-structure interaction analyses.

description:
HOS-A1 Hydraulic Structures: 9ECs

HOS-A-1 Ultimate Strength en Fatigue: 33%

HOS-A-2 Design of Hydraulic Structures: 67%

The module enables students to produce a conceptual engineering design of common hydraulic structures, building on already acquired skills. Students learn to analyse a problem to formulate a design objective, which leads to a functional-spatial design. This is followed by a structural design where next to stability and strength checks, constructability plays a major role. The student further develops skills to motivate assumptions, methods and values of design parameters, using basic sketches. Hydraulic, geotechnical and structural aspects are addressed in coherence to understand the behaviour of these structures.

The content of the module contributes to the MUDE and Ethics learning lines.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

MLO-1. Generate sound preliminary designs for hydraulic structures based on current natural and societal needs, accounting for its interaction with the environment its life-cycle aspects, using available scientific knowledge. (HOS-1,2,3)

MLO-2. Analyse principles of ultimate resistance and fatigue relevant for the design of hydraulic structures, using available scientific knowledge. (HOS-2,3)

MLO-3. Perform statistically model selection and identification for the analysis and verification of the structural health of hydraulic structures. (HOS-3,4)

MLO-4. Effectively collaborate and communicate with the aim to generate and optimize the design of hydraulic structures. (HOS-4)

MLO-5. Critically reflect on the design and reliability of hydraulic structures and its structural components. (HOS-2,4)

MLO-6. Translate current natural and societal needs into possible technical designs of offshore structures by accounting for relevant moral values, norms and principles. (HOS-4)

description:
The module Offshore Structures of the Hydraulic and Offshore Structures (HOS) track, is worth 9 ECTS and consists of the following units:

Ultimate Strength and Fatigue = 3 ECTS (this unit is shared with the module CIEM4110 Hydraulic Structures

Design of Offshore Structures = 6 ECTS

This module enables students to produce conceptual engineering designs for fixed offshore structures accounting for ultimate strength and fatigue criteria. During this course, students gain a thorough theoretical understanding of the design process, its structuring, available design methodologies and the philosophy behind the design codes. Furthermore, this module addresses offshore, geotechnical, structural and reliability aspects in coherence to analyse the behaviour of offshore structures.

The ultimate strength and fatigue unit specifically focuses on the ultimate strength and fatigue assessment of steel and concrete structures. The provided knowledge and skills are required to be able to perform the verification of offshore structures design and are therefore directly applied in the design component of this module.

Throughout the module students work on a group design project, where each student team designs an offshore support structure from scratch up to a preliminary design by performing a full design-cycle. This design-cycle includes:

The design and assembly of the structure geometry and the structural configuration, including a natural frequency analysis,

Determining and assessing the permanent and environmental loads, including both hydrodynamics and wind, on the structure,

The design, analysis and evaluation of its foundation,

The analysis of the jacket structure by using structural mechanics approaches, and

The evaluation of the jacket structure against ULS and, if applicable, FLS design criteria.

Through this group design project, students will not only learn to judge their design against ULS and FLS design criteria, but they will also develop an instinct on how to best modify and improve their design based on both static and dynamic structural analyses. Thereby, students will learn how to analyse and evaluate the dimensioning and performance of structural components for strength and stability. Furthermore, students learn to predict how changing (parts of) their design will influence the corresponding loads and based on their insight in these loads, be able to defend their design choices. Moreover, students will learn what the practical implications of their design choices are for operations and other feasibility and life-cycle aspects. To reinforce the understanding of these aspects, the course program also includes a visit to an offshore structures fabrication yard.

During this course, students will additionally learn how to collaborate effectively in a team and develop skills and competences to motivate their assumptions and provide argumentation of their design choices by accounting for relevant moral values, norms and principles.
learning_objectives:
On successful completion of this module, the student are able to:

Define the design space and generate sound preliminary designs and design solutions for new or modified offshore structures based on functional requirements, its interaction with the environment and accounting for the full life-cycle of the structure, and to do so in a methodological and transparent manner.

Analyse principles of ultimate resistance and fatigue relevant for the design of offshore structures, using available scientific knowledge.

Evaluate the limit states of designs of offshore structures, using an applicable safety philosophy (deterministic, probabilistic) based on valid design standards.

Perform statistically sound and context-based analysis and verification of the structural health of offshore structures, including possible mitigation measures.

Effectively collaborate and communicate with the aim to execute a design project based on principles of project and time management, and to generate and optimize offshore structures designs.

Critically reflect on your own design and that of your peers, and the reliability of offshore structures and its structural components in general by articulating assumptions, boundary conditions and limitations of (design) methods to put results, conclusions and recommendations into perspective.

Translate current natural and societal needs into possible technical designs of offshore structures by accounting for relevant moral values, norms and principles.

description: The module concerns the design, monitoring and assessment of offshore wind and ocean energy farms, in general, and different technologies (both bottom-fixed and floating), specifically, in an integrated manner, including control, installation, maintenance and economics. Regarding the development of offshore energy farms, this means that all relevant aspects and stakeholders are addressed and their implications for design assessed. From a structural perspective, this implies that the different technologies should be understood as a system as a whole and the varying environmental interactions aerodynamic, hydrodynamic and soil be considered in conjunction. The content of the module contributes to the MUDE and Ethics learning lines.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

MLO-1. Create offshore renewable solutions based on future natural and societal needs, using available scientific knowledge (HOS- 1, 3).

MLO-2. Evaluate offshore renewable structures in interaction with the surrounding environment, using available scientific knowledge (HOS-2, 3).

MLO-3. Convey quantified uncertain outcomes corresponding the design of hydraulic and offshore structures (HOS-4).

MLO-4. Propose new ways for dealing with ethical issues within the field of hydraulic and offshore structures from the perspective of different relevant moral frameworks (HOS-4).

MLO-5. Conduct a solution-oriented debate with stakeholders about ethical issues within the field of hydraulic and offshore structures, while acknowledging real-world constraints in terms of technological possibilities, governance and institutional options (HOS-4).

description:
The module aims at the engineering design of hydraulic structures that protect against the effects or impact of waves, currents and high-water levels, starting with understanding the underlying processes and related systems. It concerns the design of breakwaters, dikes and closure dams; flood risk reduction strategies, and structures to protect beds, banks and shorelines.

The content of the module contributes to the MUDE and Ethics learning lines
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

MLO-1. Create solutions for dams, dikes and breakwaters based on future natural and societal needs, using available scientific knowledge (HOS-1, 3).

MLO-2. Evaluate dams, dikes and breakwaters in interaction with the surrounding environment, using available scientific knowledge (HOS-2, 3).

MLO-3. Convey quantified uncertain outcomes corresponding to the design of dams, dikes and breakwaters (HOS-4).

MLO-4. Consider ways of dealing with ethical issues within the field of dams, dikes and breakwaters from the perspective of different relevant moral frameworks (HOS-4).

MLO-5. Conduct a solution-oriented debate with stakeholders about ethical issues within the field of dams, dikes and breakwaters, while acknowledging real-world constraints in terms of technological possibilities, governance and institutional options (HOS-4).

description:
The module addresses the design, monitoring and assessment of floating and (semi)-submerged civil engineering solutions for infrastructural and urban development applications, for instance floating bridges and moored tunnels, including control, installation, maintenance and economics. This implies that the structure should be understood as a system as a whole and the varying environmental interactions aerodynamic, hydrodynamic and soil be considered in conjunction.

The content of the module contributes to the MUDE and Ethics learning lines.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

MLO-1. Create floating and submerged solutions solutions based on future natural and societal needs, using available scientific knowledge (HOS-1, 3).

MLO-2. Evaluate floating and submerged structures in interaction with the surrounding environment, using available scientific knowledge (HOS-2, 3).

MLO-3. Convey quantified uncertain outcomes corresponding the design of hydraulic and offshore structures (HOS-4).

MLO-4. Propose new ways for dealing with ethical issues within the field of hydraulic and offshore structures from the perspective of different relevant moral frameworks (HOS-4).

MLO-5. Conduct a solution-oriented debate with stakeholders about ethical issues within the field of hydraulic and offshore structures, while acknowledging real-world constraints in terms of technological possibilities, governance and institutional options (HOS-4).

description:
The principles and practice of hydropower engineering is introduced in this course. Focus is on design of dam, diversion, and run of river powerplants, including the civil (structural, geotech, hydraulic), mechanical (turbines), and electrical (generation) components of these facilities. Newer technologies to be introduced in this course include low-head hydro, small hydro, in-conduit pressure recovery hydro and pumped hydro storage. Practical in class exercises are included which range to finding optimal hydropower sites based on GIS-tools to Assessing the stability of different types of dams. A major component of the course evaluation will be a group design of a hydropower project. The main topics of the course are:

1. Hydropower fundamentals

2. Small hydropower

3. Low head hydropower

4. High head hydropower

5. Dams

6. Dam Safety

7. Spillways

8. Foundations

9. Power waterways

10. Powerhouses and electromechanical equipment

11. Turbines

12. Project planning and costs

13. Pumped storage

14. Tidal Barrages and Hydro-kinetic Hydropower

15. Reservoir Operation
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

LO1: Review the principles of hydro power-based energy generation and storage [ILO 1,4].

LO2: Identify key components of a hydropower development project [ILO 1,4]

LO3: Evaluate the technical and economic feasibility, viability, and desirability of old and more recent hydro power projects [ILO 1,4].

LO4: Design a hydro power development project considering local and global environmental conditions [ILO 1,4].

After completing this module, you will be able to:

Analyse the physics, mechanics and thermodynamics of ice.

Predict expected ice features and ice regimes in different cold regions.

Account for material behaviour in cold environments.

Classify cold region structures and developments.

Assess static ice-induced loads on port, coastal, marine and offshore structures.

Analyse and select optimal structure types and structural designs for performance in cold regions depending on local conditions.

Characterize and model dynamic ice-structure interaction.

description: The Flood Risk Elective Module aims at the engineering performance of flood risk analysis, and evaluate flood risk reduction strategies and measures for flooding prone areas as well as flood defence systems that protect against the effects or impact of waves, currents and high-water levels, starting with understanding the underlying processes and related systems. It concerns the Quantitative flooding risk analyses of flood prone regions (polders) with and/or without the flood protection system which serve for addressing and quantify risks, anticipate changes and to continuously optimise risk mitigation measures and flood risk reduction strategies for the regions.

The course consists of preparatory lectures and workshops during the three weeks preceeding the actual measurement week (usually the last week of September). The weeks after the measurements are used to process, analyse and present the results. The elective is offered to a limited (25 to 30) number of students. The application procedure is announced on Brightspace in Q4 of the academic year preceding the fieldwork.

There are two options for the execution of the fieldwork. It is announced in Q4 preceding the fieldwork which option(s) will be organised. Depending on the number of applications and the interests of the students, it is decided what option(s) will take place.

Option 1:

A design-oriented fieldwork. This type of fieldwork acquires data for the evaluation of an existing configuration (like a nourished beach), or for the design of a new structure like a breakwater, marina or artificial island. Typical components of such a fieldwork are beach profile measurements, echo sounding for bathymetry measurement, sand sampling, observation of instantaneous wave conditions, inspection of breakwaters. The emphasis of this version is on the entire measurement campaign rather than on operating advanced instruments.

Option 2:

A research-oriented fieldwork. Measurements are done on the beach, like profile measurements, sand sampling, sediment transport measurements, etc. The collected data will have to be checked to the deep-water boundary conditions (waves and currents) which are available via the routine measuring devices.

The introductory lectures are given in collaboration with the Coastal Remote Sensing elective within the MSc program Applied Earth Sciences, organised by the Department of Geoscience and Remote Sensing.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

plan and execute a measuring plan needed to solve problems in the field of hydraulic engineering [ILO 2,3,7].

decide what types of data have to be collected, according to what method, with a useful number of samples (with respect to resolution and frequency) and of sufficient quality [ILO 4,7].

process raw data and organize them into a measurement record, including metadata [ILO 2].

analyse these data and draw conclusions relevant to hydraulic engineering. Uncertainties like weather changes, unexpected circumstances, unknown environment and lacking local background are dealt with [ILO 1,2,3,8,10].

organize and operate in a group performing a measurement campaign [ILO 9,10].

Present the findings in a report and in an oral presentation [ILO 9].

description: This course introduces students to the offshore renewable resources of the ocean environment and the technologies for renewable energy conversion, with the main purpose of developing comprehension of the first principles of offshore renewables engineering. In addition, students are trained on transferable skills, relevant for their professional development.
learning_objectives:
Formulate the renewable energy principles in the ocean environment for the analysis of marine renewable energy systems.

Determine the renewable energy potential in the ocean environment and be able to design and assess the working principles of offshore renewable energy systems.

Assess the power production by different marine renewable technologies, and compare the technological solutions for wind, wave and tidal energies

Handle constructive feedback, both in provision and reception, to define individual goals for professional development.

Infer logical conclusions based on deductive, inductive and abductive reasoning, distinguishing basic elements of arguments and recognizing different types of arguments, cognitive biases and fallacies in reasoning.

Build international, multi-cultural and multi-disciplinary collaborative environments, based on established considerations, and recognizing the value of diversity, equity and inclusion in teams.

Identify societal and environmental impact of own work on the basis of principles of morality and integrity.

description:
In this module, the learning line on Modelling, data monitoring and sensing and Uncertainty and risk analysis is continued from the Faculty base module. Modelling of structures is central in the SE Track, since both mechanics and codes are in their essence models of real structural behaviour. Data and sensing is addressed sideways when it comes to the determination of mechanical properties and behaviour of materials and structures from laboratory experiments. Experimental results are discussed to illustrate e.g. failure phenomena during lectures and to explain the basis of codes and design models. Ethics is reflected through sustainability and circularity that are the major aspects that future structural engineers need to develop in order to preserve environment. Designing skills are important for all structural engineers and in this module the goal is that students embrace principles and good feeling of structural design with traditional construction systems and materials. The module is composed of 2 units: Unit 1 - Sustainable Construction Members and Systems (8EC) and Unit 2 - Mechanics of Slender Structures (7EC).

Unit 1 focuses on loads and sustainability aspects of structural design and design and analysis of steel, timber and concrete members. More specifically, the following topics are covered:

Identification and quantification of loads on structures. This includes short-term, long term, and moveable loads, and the combination of different types of loads.

Design of steel cross sections and members. Influence of properties of base material, production routes and execution tolerances on verification of critical steel cross sections loaded in bending and shear, members loaded in compression and steel bolted and welded connections.

Design of timber cross sections and members. Identification of material properties and their use in the design and verification for strength, stiffness and stability at member level. Design and verification of timber joints and connections.

Analysis and verification of response of prestressed concrete members exposed to forces, i.e.: axial, bending and shear, in order to meet requirements for ultimate and serviceability limit state.

Application of the principles of sustainability and circularity in civil engineering structures. The content on sustainability covers general LCA approaches and system boundaries supported by specific environmental product data, fabrication processes used in construction of structures, railways and roads. Main principles of circularity and reusability will be covered supported by examples of real structures.

The content of Unit 1 is divided into 6 themes offered over 8 weeks in Q2 and 8 weeks in Q3 with a workload of 5EC and 3EC, respectively. In Q2, loads and sustainability aspects of structural design and design and analysis of steel and timber members are covered. In Q3, the design and analysis of prestressed concrete systems and connections in steel and timber structures are covered.

Unit 2 treats the mechanics of slender structures. In Q2, simple cases are treated in which analytical solutions of single elements are possible. The goal is to explain physics and the basics of the methods. In Q3, the focus is shifted towards more design-type assignments in which the students apply the solution methods in more complex systems consisting of combined one-dimensional structural elements and plates together with complex boundary/interface conditions. The unit covers:

Formulation of governing equations of one-dimensional and two-dimensional slender structures.

Statics and dynamics of cables, rods, shear beams and beams in bending.

Statics and dynamics of plates in bending.

Statics and dynamics of combinations of one-dimensional slender structures.

Statics and dynamics of plates undergoing in-plane deformations.

Statics and dynamics of combinations of one-dimensional and two-dimensional slender structures.
learning_objectives:
After completion of this module, students will be able to:

Identify and quantify the most important loads on structures, roads and railway and schematize and combine them as input for the determination of the force distributions and deformations.

Design critical steel cross sections, members and joints with optimized dimensions and reliable performance against structural and environmental requirements under the influence of single and combined bending, shear, torsion and axial loads.

Design and verify structural performance of timber members and connections subjected to single and combined bending, shear and axial loads through understanding of fundamental material properties and force flows in timber joints.

Design, analyse and optimize prestressed concrete structures, considering influence of internal stress distribution, time dependent effects, type of pre-tensioning, boundary conditions, prestress losses, cracks and reinforcement details.

Understand and apply the principles of sustainability to identify, analyse and evaluate negative effects of civil engineering structures at component and system level on natural environment and society and to use circularity strategies to reduce the environmental impact of structures, railways and roads.

Formulate the governing equations of motion of a class of one-dimensional slender structures (beams, cables, rods) and plates subjected to static and dynamic loads in- and out- of plane.

Analyse 1D slender structures subjected to static loads and dynamic loads and evaluate the structural response.

Analyse plates subjected to static and dynamic loads in- and out- of plane and evaluate the structural response.

Create mathematical models of complex structures consisting of one-dimensional elements and plates subjected to static and dynamic loads and evaluate their structural response.

description:
The A1 module on Mechanics and Dynamics of structures and structural components provides the students with advanced knowledge on mechanics and dynamics of structures which are typically encountered in civil engineering. The structure of the module balances a strong theoretical basis with application cases relevant to the structural engineer. By following this module, students will learn how to analyse the stability of structures to both static and dynamics loads. They will get acquainted with the various computational techniques used in the static and dynamic analysis of complex structural systems and they will learn how to deal with measurements and analysis of vibrations of engineering structures.

The learning line on Modelling, Data and Uncertainty is continued from the Faculty Base and Track Base module. In the third unit of this module (SE-A1-3), the student will extract modal parameters from spectral estimates obtained using measurement data from self-designed set-ups in the laboratory, quantify and interpret the uncertainty in these estimates and modal parameters, and statistically judge consistency between mode shapes. Also comparisons will be made between the estimates and their modelled equivalents as obtained in the second unit. The learning line is addressed explicitly in the LO's 2, 3, 7 and 8 of the third unit.

In the first unit, the learning line on design will be continued from the preceding modules. In this unit students will learn to explain the criteria for designing stable structures. A range of instabilities that needs to be considered in a conceptual design phase is considered, including buckling, plastic collapse of frames, galloping, flutter, and vortex-induced vibrations.
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

Analyse the stability of structures subjected to both static and dynamics loads.

Explain the theoretical background of finite element formulations for structural analysis.

Perform finite element analysis to analyse the force distribution, stability and dynamic response of frame structures.

Analyse and interpret vibration measurements to identify modal parameters, including their associated uncertainty.

Design a measurement set-up for vibration analysis, with the purpose of quantifying modelling and measurement uncertainties.

description:
The A2 Module focuses on the Design of Structural Components. Potential for reducing environmental impact of structures and achieving an optimum structural design lies in integrating construction materials in structures where they best fit, given their mechanical and functional properties. By successfully completing this module, you will learn to understand the possibilities and limitations of both conventional and innovative construction materials, select and or adjust their properties according the functionality of the structures. You will learn to design structural members which combine the advantages of various materials such as steel, concrete, FRP or timber. Designing future structures, using innovative construction materials, optimised for circularity (prefabricated and demountable constructions) will be emphasised. The module consists of two units: (1) Prefabricated and composite structures and (2) Design with innovative materials . You will learn to design prefabricated and composite structures made of conventional construction materials, and will also explore improvements with novel construction materials, (composite) systems and fabrication methods.

A2-1: Prefabricated and composite structures:

The content is divided into 4 themes offered in Q3. More specifically the envisioned content is as follows:

Theme 1: STEEL

Design verification of steel members (beam-columns) exposed to interaction, axial force and transversal load

Hollow section steel structures; Main topology of joints

Steel-concrete composite structures; Principles of design; prerequisites and consequences of full and partial composite action;

Theme 2: TIMBER

Engineered wood products

Massive timber buildings and timber frame housing

Connections in prefabricated timber structures

Timber trusses and portal frames

Timber concrete composite structures

Theme 3: CONCRETE

External prestressing

Strut-and-tie models and detailing

Prefabricated elements for building and infrastructure

Theme 4: RAILWAY

Conventional track structures and innovations, such as prefab concrete slab tracks; prestressed concrete sleepers, timber sleepers, composite sleepers; composite ballast bed

Modular in railway infrastructure: current experiences and perspectives

A2-2: Design with innovative materials:

The content deals with a wide overview of innovative construction materials, their applications, functional, sustainability and safety benefits and basic principles of design. The unit is offered in Q3. More specifically the envisioned content is as follows:

Theme 1: HIGH PERFORMANCE CONCRETE

Introduce new types of cementitious materials ((SHCC), UHPFRC, Geopolymer concrete, auxetic, phase change, self-sensing, self-healing, 3d printed, recycled)

Theme 2: RECYCLED MATERIALS

Introduction of recycled construction materials and their circularity

Adaptive design for easy dismantling and reusing structural materials

Challenges and opportunities.

Theme 3: HIGH PERFORMANCE STEEL AND COMPOSITE STRUCTURES Weathering and stainless steel; High strength steel Composite materials and members

Theme 4: STRUCTURAL GLASS

basic information on how structural glass is used and what the material properties are, basic calculations Theme 5: DIGITAL MANUFACTURING

3D printed steel (material, members, connections) 3D printed concrete; Wood -plastic composites. Theme 6: INNOVATIONS IN PAVEMENT ENGINEERING

Introduction of pavement structure with emerging materials

Emerging materials to enhance performance and functionality of pavement

Theme 7: INNOVATIONS IN RAILWAY ENGINEERING  Conventional track structures and innovations, such as embedded rail (elastomeric materials), polymer sleepers, coated ballast.
learning_objectives:
On successful completion of this module, you will be able to:

LO1. Explain the principles to design prefabricated and structural (composite) components in a circular manner for buildings and infrastructure by using conventional and novel civil engineering materials. (SE1, SE3, SE5, SE8)

LO2. Apply the advanced design aspects in structural engineering, focusing on stability problems, understanding and designing composite members, connections, detailing, external prestressing and prefabricated members with conventional construction materials (timber, steel, concrete). (SE1, SE3, SE6)

LO3. Design, analyse and optimize composite structural members, e.g. steel-concrete, timber-concrete, timber-steel beams, decks and columns, with respect to short and long term loads and environmental conditions. (SE1, SE3, SE7)

LO4. illustrate the influence of connections and detailing aspects in prefabricated and composite structures and apply this in the design and verification. (SE1, SE3, SE5)

LO5.Identify the innovative, high performance and sustainable civil engineering materials and simulate their behaviour. (SE4, SE5, SE6, SE8, SE9)

LO6. Discuss limitations and advantages of applying novel materials, advanced manufacturing and innovative systems in design of structural members and optimize design accordingly. (SE7, SE8, SE9)

LO7. Discover and justify the possibilities of applying innovative materials in real engineering problems to improve the design and behaviour of the structure or the road and railway system. (SE1, SE3, SE5, SE6, SE7, SE8, SE9)

course_name: Design of Civil Structures and Infrastructures
description:
The SE_A3 module teaches you how to design engineering (infra)structures within a realistic context: from scratch, investigating multiple variants and materials to find the most suitable design. You will make a functional and technical design, with considerable level of detail.

A3 will be organised as an engaging module:

during the first weeks of the module keynote lectures from industry and expert staff members will be organised; broad and advanced content on design methodology, and the design of buildings, bridges, rail track and roads/pavements.

in parallel you will be trained in various (soft/hard) skill-related lectures/workshops (teamwork, parametric design, presentation, setting up a clear calculation, visual communication)

the central task is a group assignment around a realistic clients brief, containing buildings, bridges, rail and/or road, and including an individual contribution of each team member in the form of a preliminary design of one structural type.

for deepening your knowledge on subjects, which is necessary for your individual contribution to the team design, various self-study content will be offered from a learning pool.

In A3, attention will be given to ethical aspects of design of engineering structures by means of addressing a realistic design context and working in a realistic team atmosphere. Considerations related to ethics are:

Which team member will take responsibility for which part of the design?

Can we guarantee that the design is safe?

Is this design addressing the societal need in a correct way?

To what extent is our global environment loaded by the presented design?

To what extent will people be affected by the construction process of this design?

Can the design be constructed safely and how?

The Core faculty module (CFM) will provide the fundamental basis for ethics, on which the course will build forth.

Structural Design is also about optimisation and graphical representation  CFM content that prepares for this will be built upon.

This module also considers topics that will continue the line of both modelling and coding from the MUDE module. MUDE: Coding skills (Python, Matlab etc.) and MUDE on modelling, data and uncertainty analysis are pre-requisites. This module will follow the lines of MUDE by analysing advanced methods with application on bridges, building, road, railway structures and circularity. The MUDE course in this aspect prepare students to understand reliable design parameters, criteria and reliable design choices out of several options.

description:
This module provides students with in-depth expertise on the analysis of the mechanical response of structures. Analytical and computational techniques are explained and applied. The module offers students the possibility to become applied mechanics specialists with the ability to use state-of-the-art computational tools and analytical tools across the structural engineering field. The module also prepares students to contribute to academic research that advances the limits of computational and analytical tools for analysis of the mechanical response of structures.

Monitoring en data science learning line: This module builds on the modelling and coding line from the MUDE, with Unit 1 focused exclusively on modelling and Unit 2 addressing a specific aspect of modelling of structures including python coding workshops. The broader theme of uncertainty is addressed in discussions of the reliability of different models.

Ethics learning line: Ethics is given attention in this module when the limits of different analysis approaches are discussed. From research perspective, being critical towards the accuracy and reliability of available methods and tools is a first step towards advancing their limits. In a pragmatic engineering environment, having the expertise to be critical of models may lead to moral dilemmas: What level of uncertainty about model reliability is acceptable? Having discussed the uncertainties of relatively high-fidelity models, what is a the good way to deal with even larger uncertainties of simpler modeling approaches? Moreover, ethical aspects of reporting in academia and engineering practice will be discussed in the module, such as acknowledgement of sources and fair representation of results.

Design: This module equips students to analyse the behaviour of materials, structures and structural elements. Analysis is an important aspect of the design cycle for civil engineering structures. Units Unit 1 and Unit 2 focus primarily on methods and their underlying formulation. Unit 3 is more applied in the sense that it provides insight in the mechanical response of structures. It will be illustrated with practical examples how this insight can be used in the design of structures. Pitfalls and best practices in structural design will be discussed in the light of the theory provided in the unit.

Unit 1 Computational modelling of structures:

Introduction to the use of the finite element method; Nonlinear finite element analysis of steel structures; Nonlinear finite element analysis of structures made of a quasi-brittle material; Application of the finite element method to solve engineering problems.

Unit 2 Advanced constitutive modelling:

Mathematical and mechanical preliminaries; Computational plasticity; Fracture models and continuum damage mechanics; Large deformation mechanics; Computational modelling of visco-elastic materials; Large deformation elasto-plasticity; Introduction to thermodynamics.

Unit 3 Advanced mechanics of structural elements:

Theory of elasticity: energy principles, closed form solutions and limitations; Theory of plasticity: frame analysis and plate analysis
learning_objectives:
On completion of this module, the student will be able to

Analyze the mechanical response of structures where that is complicated by the presence of geometric and material nonlinearity

Calculate the ultimate load of plates and frames accounting for plasticity

Explore the limits of analytical tools for evaluation of elastic stress and strain

Formulate, implement and test constitutive laws for detailed numerical analysis of the response of structures

Perform nonlinear finite element analysis for structural design verification

Unit 1:

Select an appropriate mechanical model that idealizes the physical problem of analysis of a structure (boundary conditions, loading, dimension reduction, geometric order of approximation, material model) [1]

Build an appropriate finite element model that discretizes the selected mechanical model [1, 5]

Carry out nonlinear finite element analysis for a range of different applications (steel/concrete structures, seismic response of buildings) [1,5]

Unit 2:

Select an appropriate constitutive model to account for physical phenomena of time-dependent behavior, direction dependent behavior, permanent deformations and failure in the analysis of material response [1,4]

Derive and apply the stiffness relations for orthotropic elasticity and classical laminate theory [1,4]

Understand and apply the concepts of large deformation mechanics [1]

Explain the concepts of thermodynamics and apply it to large deformation elasto-thermal material modelling [1,4]

Formulate constitutive models to describe the nonlinear response of materials

Reproduce the main steps in the derivation of analytical elaticity solutions, for example the point load on a half space, point load on a half disk, stresses around a spherical cavity in a continuum, stresses around a circular opening in a plate, moments in circular plates, stresses in curved beams, the differential equations for torsion [3]

Calculate, by hand, the ultimate load of elastic/plastic plates [1,2]

description:
This module addresses three broad topics within the Applied Dynamics of Structures. These topics are considered highly relevant for the current stage of the society development and are associated with the energy transition and modern transportation. Accordingly, the module is comprised of three units, namely:

1. Structural Response to Earthquakes
2. Dynamics of structures subjected to wind & waves
3. Dynamics of structures under moving loads

description:
Concrete is the worlds mostly used construction material. The module Concrete Structures offers a comprehensive cluster of courses that, through the application of existing knowledge and insights in new scientific developments, prepares students for the current and future challenges of society relating concrete structures. Various sectors of Civil Engineering and the entire life-span of concrete structures are covered: from the understanding and design of concrete material, the advanced modelling of concrete members taking into account the unique behaviour of concrete, to the design, maintenance of complex concrete structures, such and concrete bridges.

The course will include 5 units, namely:

B3-1: Advanced modelling of concrete structures.

B3-2: Concrete science and technology.

B3-3: Numerical modelling of concrete structures.

B3-4: Concrete structures under special loadings.

B3-5: Concrete bridges.

On completion of this module, the student will be able to: 1. Design concrete structures and members using plasticity theory and fracture mechanics for concrete. 2. Explain and design cement-based building materials and the advanced concrete mixture design methodology, further apply to design, control, and execute durable and sustainable concrete in practice. 3. Create, carry out, interpret, and document nonlinear finite element analysis of reinforced concrete structures or elements. 4. Model the behaviour of concrete members and structures subject to various environmental and anthropogenic loads, and to create appropriate design accordingly. 5. Design and assess precast and cast-in-situ concrete bridges and bridge elements considering the construction methods and the loading conditions.

description:
The module consists of 3 parallel units.
Unit 1 provides in-depth knowledge on how to design, model, analyse and critically assess results of prediction models of structural members and joints. The principles and theory of using experiments and reliability-based assisted design and verification of Steel and Composite Structures (SCS) and connections are explained and practised for monotonic and cyclic loading.
Unit 2 and Unit 3 will allow students to apply and extend their knowledge from Unit 1 in real case structures, such as bridges, support structures for renewable energy, lightweight FRP structures, cold-formed steel members, etc.


The learning line on Modelling, Data management and sensing, risk analysis is continued from the MUDE and Track base module.
Students will have the opportunity to participate in monitoring and sensing lab (or virtual) experiments during the module and evaluate data.


Ethics related to the design and reporting, construction, ownership and decommissioning of steel and composite structures are discussed throughout the module. Circumstances which lead to a collapse of structures will be discussed from (un)ethical behaviour of partners in a project. The balance between economy-safety-sustainability of construction work will be addressed, showing future engineers' responsibility.


B4 Unit 1: Fatigue and FEA of steel and FRP composite structures
Fatigue and fracture; Design and verification of steel structures and connections exposed to cyclic loading; use of FE analysis in fatigue assessment; Fatigue life prediction based on fracture mechanics; Modelling of Steel and Composite structures and design by experiments; non-linear material modelling of steel and anisotropic and layered modelling of FRP structures;

B4 Unit 2: Steel bridges and wind turbine support structures
Steel and hybrid bridges - Structural design of steel bridges - Bridge loads, traffic accounting and analysis - Design verifications of steel bridge elements - Advanced bridge analysis - Execution and details of steel bridges - Renovation and maintenance of steel bridges: Supporting structures for renewable energy - Hollow section steel joints in jacket/truss structures- Monopile supporting structures for wind turbines and connections.

B4 Unit 3: FRP composites and lightweight steel structures
Design, analysis and verification of FRP composite structures joints and details; Design and verification of lightweight, slender and cold-formed steel structures .

description:
This module will focus on the engineering of buildings as complex systems in which many facets need to be aligned in an integrated interdisciplinary design process. From an economy point of view, a share of about 70% of construction industry is involved with buildings, which makes this module very relevant for future civil engineers. The module content is grouped in three learning units:

LEARNING UNIT 1 (LU1, Architecture, Building Physics and Façades, 4 EC) will provide you with the specific building-related background knowledge that is not directly structural engineering:

contemporary and 19th century architectural styles

façade design/detailing

basics of building physics (heat transport, energy efficiency, daylight, solar shading)

building services (heating, ventilation, air-conditioning, vertical transport, water).

LEARNING UNIT 2 (LU2, Building Structures, Construction Methods and Foundations, 6 EC) is about the flow of forces in regular building structures and stability in various typologies of buildings (office, commercial, industrial, residential, etc.). Unit 2 is grouped around the following three themes:

Theme 1 (Building Structures):

advanced knowledge on the flow of forces in building structures

stability and lateral resistance and known solutions for various typologies of buildings according to their function (office, commercial, industrial, residential)

use and reuse of various building materials, to give you a clear understanding on which options are available and which solutions are appropriate for every part of the new or existing building structure

complexity of the design process and responsibilities of different partners in the design and construction chain

Theme 2 (Foundations):

Interaction with the subsoil via the foundation is an important part of the building design, and you will learn how to develop a good foundation in cooperation with the geotechnical advisor.

attention will also be paid to deep excavations, that are often required for foundation and parking garages or other underground spaces under a building.

Theme 3 (Construction methods):

The design of the building is depending on available construction methods, and by studying these, you will get a clear understanding of the limitations and options each of these methods offer.

Impact on surroundings and urban context will be addressed, as well as safety of construction, economy and material efficiency (zero-waste) on the construction site.

LEARNING UNIT 3 (LU3, Design of Spatial Structures, 5 EC) is an advanced unit in the field of special and spatial building structures, their design process, structural mechanics, structural behaviour and performance, computational modelling, combined with practical use of design- and analysis tools for structural engineering. Topics include

structures in nature

biomimetics

plates, shells and vaults

membrane and pneumatic structures

cable-nets

tensegrity structures

(space) frames

grid(shell) structures and domes

adaptive and deployable structures.

Whereas Learning Unit 2 will focus on more regular building types, Learning Unit 3 broadens the scope with an extensive introduction into complex geometries and typologies. Apart from design skills, also academic skills will be trained during this unit since the unit includes a mini conference, including the writing and presentation of scientific papers.

Working on an integrating design exercise of a realistic building that connects all three learning units, you will experience the consequences (limitations, options and uncertainties) of available design and construction methods. During the exercise, you will receive feedback from professional building engineers.

This module provides knowledge on modern tools for design, assessment, performance prediction and optimisation of engineering structures in application to transportation infrastructures, such as roads, railways, bridges, and tunnels. In this process, the entire design-construction-service cycle will be considered.

The analysis of structural behaviour commences with defining the loading conditions. Therefore, the dynamic interactions of road/track/bridge/tunnel and moving vehicles will be introduced first. The students will learn how to numerically analyse such interactions and their consequences like rutting, vibrations and noise.

The methods for analysis of the long-term behaviour of engineering structures, including wear, (rolling contact) fatigue damage, etc., will be considered as well. Additionally, the students will learn how to apply the structural reliability methods to account for the uncertainties of real life, even including the effects of the weather.

The module also focuses on critical issues related to the aging of transportation infrastructures. Topics will cover aspects of material and structural degradation due to increased dynamic loading, environmental factors, and climate change effects, and familiarize with tools to assess and predict structural durability. The use of innovative materials to enhance the performance and durability of transportation infrastructures will be also discussed.

The students will get acquainted with modern general-purpose finite element software: ANSYS, ABAQUS, PLAXIS, Discrete element methods, etc., as well as with some dedicated design software, and will use these tools to assess structural behaviour at multi-scale level.

To assure the long-term safe performance, the methods of condition monitoring of engineering structures in application to transportation infrastructures will be studied. Several non-destructive testing (NDT) technologies like Digital Image Correlation (DIC), laser scanning, and satellite data used to assess the performance and condition of infrastructure will be covered. Examples of monitoring solutions using static, moving, and crowd sensing technologies will be analysed. Application of the NDT methods for parameter identification of the numerical models will be considered as well. Combined with state-of-the-art data-analysis methods and machine learning, the monitoring information will turn into maintenance strategies.

In this module we organise excursions to companies to discuss their engineering approaches for integral design for transportation infrastructures. All knowledge will be applied to real-life case studies to be performed in close collaboration with manufacturers and engineering companies. All these will serve as preparation for MSc theses.

description:
The module consists of three parts.

The introductory part will be provided by responsible instructors covering various structural expertise focusing on sustainability aspects of the built environment in which load bearing structure is made of concrete, steel, timber or as hybrid system (steel, biobased, concrete). Different views on interpreting basic terms used in policy documents and literature relevant to CO2-neutral structures/built environments will be discussed.

In the second part, case studies of flagship projects in terms of CO2-neutral structures will be presented by architects and engineers from industry and related disciplines.

In the third part of the module, students (in a group of max 4 students) will select one of the presented case studies and provide an alternative solution with the intention to improve solution addressing weaknesses of the presented solutions with a focus on CO2 neutrality.

Critically assess and apply civil engineering technical process of generating and evaluating alternatives in a complex natural and societal environment [ILO 4].

description:
The course will contain classroom lectures to explain the aspects that have to be regarded to make a fire safe design.

The content will be delivered by experts on construction materials form TU Delft and experts from industry on fire physics, fire testing, fire safety measurements and fire safety engineers.

The content will address:

- Background of the fire safety regulations according to national and European laws.

- Introduction into fire physics. Standard and natural fire curves. Thermal loading. Theoretical and numerical methods to predict the fire development and temperature distribution in compartments.

- Explanation in the difference in Resistance to Fire and Reaction to fire, and testing methods to determine these properties.

- Smoke control and smoke propagation. Escape scenarios and human behaviour. ASET and RSET. Active and passive fire safety measurements.

- Response of construction materials steel, timber and concrete to thermal loading. Contribution of the construction material to the fire loading.

- Design and verification rules for construction materials steel, timber and fire under thermal loading.

- Fire Safety Engineering: Risk analysis to evaluate the effectiveness of fire safety measures.
learning_objectives:
Besides the verification of every structure for the Ultimate Limit State (ULS) and Serviceability Limit State (SLS), it also has to be assessed for the accidental load case fire. This load case can be governing in the design, therefore every engineer should have knowledge how to handle the load case fire and how to verify a structure based on the material response on the high occurring temperatures for the different construction materials steel, timber and concrete.

On successful completion of this module, the student will be able to:

Explain the fire physics with respect to the initation and development of a fire in structures. [ILO 1,4]

To predict the temperature development of a compartment subjected to fire loading (ILO4)

Explain the behaviour of materials and structures under fire loading.(ILO 1,7)

apply the background of the fire safety regulations on national and European level.(ILO 3)

To identify active and passive fire safety measures and how they influence the safety of the structure.(LO 7)

To apply the design and verification rules for structural safety under fire conditions for the construction materials steel, timber and concrete, and their contribution to the fire load. (ILO 1,3,9)

description:
In many countries the originally devised design life of a substantial part of the existing buildings and infrastructure has been reached or will be reached soon. These structures need to be assessed. Most often, existing structures are verified using simplified procedures based on the partial factor method which is commonly applied in design of new structures. Such assessments are often conservative and may lead to expensive renovation or unnecessary replacements of structures.

Recently, the engineering practice and the research community started to acknowledge that an assessment of existing structures is fundamentally different from designing new structures. For existing structures, it pays off to consider more advanced load and capacity models, as well as the overall structural behaviour, and to align the reliability assessment of concrete structures with all the information we have.

The result of the underlying reliability considerations is a different set of load factors for assessment, as well as a philosophy of increasing levels of approximation for assessment. More advanced models are then referred to as models with higher levels of approximation. In this elective you will learn about these types of models and associated considerations.

On the one hand we have more information about an existing concrete structure than we have for a structure which is still in the design process. E.g., the structure has shown a certain capacity over its lifetime, we have more knowledge about the loading, or we have knowledge about the actual concrete strength properties. Monitoring data and results from proof test might further contribute to the knowledge of a structure. We also must deal with higher uncertainty. E.g., corrosion levels might be unknown, and the structural behaviour of structural vintage details might be hard to quantify. A proper assessment should take all this information into account.

This elective will address the following topics:

evolution of design codes and practices,

assessment at various levels of approximation, and the link to reliability-based safety philosophies,

modelling of the structures with vintage detailing (nonconforming design),

determination material properties and the deterioration condition of structures,

methodologies to deal with involved uncertainties,

field testing, and in particular bridge load testing,

assessment studies under multiple hazards, such as seismic action,

structural impact of deteriorating mechanisms,

global structural behaviour for assessment: transverse distribution, unintended composite action, contribution of non-structural components, 

decision-making strategies

The course material of the elective will be applicable to both concrete buildings and concrete infrastructures. Most applications will be shown for concrete bridges. Since the assessment of existing concrete structures is an active research field and since codes for existing concrete structures are far from mature, this course will be updated from year to year to follow the most recent state of the research and practice.

MUDE: The first lectures of this elective will focus on the topic of safety philosophy of existing concrete structures. The influence of various sources of uncertainty, with regard to the state of information and the degradation and deterioration, will also be discussed throughout this elective.

Ethics: A discussion on the choices of the target reliability for concrete structures at different stages, namely, design, assessment, renovation is given. It will be made clear that such choice is not based on numbers but also on the ethics considerations. The topic of decision-making strategies for the assessment of existing structures will include the ethical considerations involved with this process.

Design skills: This elective will lean on general design skills of structural engineering students, which can then be applied for the analysis of existing concrete structures.

Evaluate the capacity of existing concrete structures with and without deterioration [ILO 4]

Exemplify the evolution of concrete codes and design practices and its impact on assessment [ILO 1,4]

Apply decision-making strategies for the assessment of existing bridges [ILO 5,7,10]

Appraise available test methods that can provide additional information of the structure (material properties, boundary conditions, or the bearing capacity, etc.) [ILO 5,10]

Theory:

Structural damage: what is damage? Various types of failure mechanisms. Performance criteria and codes. How often does failure occur? What are technical causes? What are human and organisational causes?

Legal aspects: liability, Insurance, Court, expert witnesses

Delft Method for Forensic Investigations: steps of investigations, life cycle, Tree House of Failures, Ring of Trustworthiness

Instruments for investigation: for example microscopy

Damage in foundations and retaining structures: e.g. deterioration of timber piles, unequal settlements, failures related to deep excavations and retaining structures

Cases with for example the following types of damage:

Damage in concrete: e.g. temporary structures, reinforcement in ridges

Damage in steel: e.g. connections and instability

Damage in timber: e.g. connections

Damage in finishing structures: e.g. leakage and connections

Damage in foundations: e.g. deterioration of timber piles, unequal settlements, building pits

Explain the Delft Method for Forensic Investigations and possible instruments for forensic investigations. Assess the usefulness of application of various instruments.

Apply the various steps of Delft Method for Forensic Investigations in a forensic investigation process.

Develop design measures to deal with important failure mechanisms.

description:

This will be taught through tools as they are currently implemented in modern software. This includes 3D modelling (e.g. Rhinoceros 3D coupled with visual programming plugins such as Grasshopper 3D) and coding (e.g. Python and COMPAS).

We will be looking at principles of designing efficient structural forms using form-finding techniques and informed by fabrication constraints. To this end, relevant digital fabrication methods for construction will be explored using computational pipelines for production using available CNC tools (e.g. 3D printing, laser cutting, CNC knitting etc).

This elective will offer you powerful toolsets to work on geometry modelling, optimisation, and evaluation of performance in structural design, as well as the natural extension of parametric models towards digital fabrication.

These skills will be directly applied in an integrated building design and manufacturing exercise/assignment carried out in groups. The module will be taught and co-taught by experts from both TU Delft, other international research institutions, and industry who have detailed knowledge of emerging research fields as well as current practice.

Design multiple alternatives for a structure and identifying the most suitable solution from an integrated and inter-disciplinary perspective [ILO 7,8].

Manufacture a (scaled) structure or building using (available) digital fabrication methods [ILO 7,8].

course_name: Contact and Interface Mechanics for Engineering Structures
description:
In this course, the students will learn the history of contact mechanics, and its relevance for different fields of modern structural engineering, followed by a basic discussion of fundamental aspects of contact mechanics.

Then numerical modeling of contact mechanics will be discussed, taking material properties into account, via the Finite Element Method (FEM) and the Boundary Element Method (BEM).

Next, the focus will shift to contact applications in structural engineering. For transport infrastructures, tire-pavement and wheel-rail interaction will be covered in depth. Aspects like surface conditions, degradation, noise will come into the picture and an experimental study with lab test-rig and deformable tire contact footprint will be presented.

Applications in the fields of civil engineering structures such as concrete, steel and composite structures are presented.

Finally, the remaining time in this course is used to work on a group assignment. This group assignment includes giving a presentation about the work done.

On completion of this module, the student will be able to:

Explain fundamental concepts of contact mechanics. [ILO 1, 2, 6, 8]

Apply contact mechanics formulations/models for engineering problems. [ILO 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8]

Implement analytical and numerical models to solve engineering level contact mechanics problems. [ILO 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8]

Analyse and interpret results of a given engineering problem. [ILO 2, 3, 4, 8, 9]

Develop methods to control interfaces in engineering structures from the perspective of lifecycle optimisation. [ILO 1, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10]

description: The course starts with discussing the fundamentals of transportation infrastructures, like fatigue analysis, degradation mechanisms and life-time prediction techniques. Then the focus will go to natural harsh conditions influencing transport infrastructure. Here the stability of soil foundations, liquefaction phenomena, and the effects of extreme conditions like strong wind, very low and very high temperatures on the (long-term) performance of roads and railways are some of the topics that this module will focus on. Moreover, the impact of disasters like earthquakes or flooding of existing infrastructure will be discussed. In addition, the influence of both increasing traffic volumes and speed on the condition of transport infrastructures will be addressed. Finally, the course will present some countermeasures against the before-mentioned harsh conditions and disasters.

Develop prevention, forecast , protection and maintenance strategies for transportation infrastructure and their supporting materials under extreme conditions. [ILO 1, 2, 3, 4, 8]

Identify and quantify the different physico-chemical degradation processes affecting transportation infrastructures using experimental data under extreme conditions. [ILO 1, 2, 3, 4]

Explain the extreme conditions transport infrastructure is exposed caused by nature and human involvement. [ILO 4, 5]

description:
In this elective, students will get acquainted with the latest technological solutions in the transportation industry facing increasing demands for passengers and freight transport, as well as challenges related to energy and climate change. The elective covers the state-of-the-art and potential technical breakthroughs that can revolutionize existing transportation infrastructure, with a focus on future resilient and green railway and road infrastructure. Backgrounds, principles, and implementations of the latest techniques and their limitations compared with the current transportation industry in terms of practicability, reliability, efficiency, and sustainability will be addressed. Leading specialists from the industry will be invited to give guest lectures to ensure the actuality of the problems discussed in this elective. Activities including laboratory and field tests, and excursions to transportation companies are planned. The following topics (not limited to) will be discussed:

1. Advanced topics on novel/sustainable designs and optimization, e.g., modular tracks, interface conditioning from the perspective of tribology, bio-mimics, smart materials, A-Train, Hyperloop, Maglev, Parcels/Pods.

2. Advanced experimental and numerical methods, e.g., nanomaterials, new ballast, discrete element method, molecular dynamics modelling.

3. Smart infrastructure, e.g., sensing, instrumentation, self-healing, platooning, MaaS equipment, digital twins, artificial passengers, cyber-security, solar roads, low-noise roads, robots for maintenance, cyber-security, railway markets, block-chain in transportation, privacy for passengers information to people in the platforms, IoT passengers as a sensor (mobile technologies, analysis of social networks, etc.), autonomous door to door transportation for passengers and freight/parcels - last mile problems.

4. Enhancing the reliability and resilience of transportation infrastructures and coping with the impact of climate change with emerging/advanced technologies for condition monitoring and decision making.

5. Energy efficiency and management, including hydrogen, fuel cells, batteries, maglev, friction modifier, friction energy reuse, automatic coupling, rolling pantograph, ATO, automated driving, ERTMS, charging station design, optimization of locations for catenary systems, and energy harvesting roads.

6. Circularity, including wheel-to wheel/LCA full loop of life cycle, construction, sustainability, CO2 and emission reduction, diesel line conversion (hybrid and hydrogen), modular design with circular materials.

7. Ethical implications of implementing the emerging technologies.

LO2: Apply advanced experimental and numerical methods to analyse and enhance the reliability and resilience of transportation infrastructures. [ILO 1, 2, 4, 5, 8]

LO3: Explain the principles of design, operation and degradation of smart transportation infrastructures. [ILO 2, 3, 9]

LO4: Apply the emerging technologies of condition monitoring and decision making to cope with the impact of climate change (including extreme weather) on transportation infrastructures. [ILO 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8]

description:
Transport Systems Design consists of five units, four of which teach practices related to the design and management of transport and traffic systems. Students should select and follow three of these four units. The fifth unit is an integrated individual project, mandatory for all students, where the content of the three chosen units should be applied to a case study. Students have the flexibility to choose the case study based on their own interests.

More specifically, the following content is covered in the units:

-          B-1 Network design: This unit focuses on designing efficient  transport networks for different modes, including a combination of them (i.e. multi-modal), for freight and passengers. Providing the principles and methods,  it explains the different elements of (multi-modal) transport networks (links, nodes, hubs, interfaces, etc.) and how to appropriately include them in the design.

-          B-2 Service design: This unit focuses on the design of transport services guided by key principles such as level of service, accessibility, inclusivity, resilience and sustainability, addressing the diverse needs of various stakeholders. It covers both strategic-level design, including service line planning, and tactical-level design, such as creating service schedules and associated vehicle circulation plans.

-          B-3 Physical infrastructure management: This unit focuses on managing road and railway infrastructures through their life cycles, balancing infrastructure requirements with operational needs of diverse users. This covers topics from asset management (which includes condition monitoring, maintenance planning, and strategies for disposal and recycling) to upgrading existing physical infrastructure using sustainable materials and innovative techniques, such as AI and IoT.

-          B-4 Traffic operations management: This unit focuses on the operational management for road traffic and other transport modes, including real-time operation of public transport services, and crowd management. Control strategies are designed to improve the traffic operations of the different modalities, covering improvements in travel time and accessibility, as well as balancing efficiency with safety and sustainability. New technologies play an important role, including automation and connectivity of vehicles.

Railway timetabling:

Microscopic and macroscopic rail traffic simulation models

Timetable design techniques and optimization models

Timetable assessment using microscopic simulation

Energy-efficient train operation

Real-time railway traffic management:

Driver Advisory Systems

Disruption management

Train delay prediction and analysis using a statistical train delay analysis tool

Railway traffic management systems

Conflict detection and resolution

Simulation-based assessment of traffic management strategies

Roles and responsibilities of railway stakeholders in planning / managing rail traffic will be tackled together with interaction processes during nominal and degraded operational conditions.

course_name: Advanced Data Science for Traffic and Transportation Engineering
description:
This project-based course is offered in close collaboration with companies (CO) and governmental organizations (GO), ensuring that student projects are grounded in real-world challenges currently faced by the transport and logistics sector.

Over the course of 8 weeks, students will develop foundational knowledge and practical skills across the full data pipeline, including data processing and analytics to visualization. These skills are directly applied to a group project based on either an assigned or chosen project. Each project is aligned with a specific challenge proposed by one of the participating external stakeholders.

To support the project development, weekly thematic sessions and lab exercises are provided. Topics include:

Data Processing and Visualization

Data Analytics and Feature Engineering

Machine Learning Methods

Additionally, students will be given access to self-learning materials to further deepen their understanding.

The course includes lectures on agile project management principles, which students are expected to apply to plan and execute their project tasks effectively. Working collaboratively in groups, students will explore and analyze real datasets to extract actionable insights for the related stakeholders. Throughout the course, they will also have the opportunity to engage in dialogue with industry experts to refine their approach and gain practical perspectives.

A key deliverable in the project is a reflection and proposal on how their solution contributes to the stakeholders. Students are expected to formulate concrete recommendations or a scalable design that outlines how their prototype could be further developed for real-world implementation, which can be finetuned in collaboration with stakeholders.

Note: A minimum of 4 students is required for the course to be offered, ensuring at least one functioning project group.
learning_objectives:

Apply steps of agile project management principles in the context of data-driven projects.

Collect the requirements from multidisciplinary stakeholders and translate them into a data science problem.

Identify, develop and evaluate the core components of a data pipeline, including data acquisition, processing, analysis, and visualization.

Apply data science tools and techniques to solve real-world challenges in engineering.

Effectively communicate data insights and solutions to both technical and non-technical stakeholders.
