description:
This course provides an introduction into the field of complex genetics. Also referred to as population genetics; generating large-scale genetic datasets and then answering relevant biological or clinical questions. The course is split in four contact days and and exam:

Day 1: Introduction to complex genetics and genome-wide association studies (genetic variation, genome-wide association studies - GWAS, applications of complex genetics).

Day 2: Biological interpretation of GWAS results (functional interpretation of genetic variants, gene regulation).

Day 3: Clinical application of GWAS results (disease risk prediction, polygenic risk scores, clinical decision-making).

Day 4: Discussion of assignments; practical examples performed in groups or extracted from literature.

Through these topics the course covers the basics of performing complex genetic studies, as well as some of the most common and currently utilized applications.
learning_objectives:
At completion of this course, the student will be able to:

1. Indicate the difference between clinical and complex/population genetics

2. Perform a complex genetic analysis (genome-wide association study)

3. Interpret complex genetic results in molecular mechanisms and biological pathways

4. Calculate polygenic risk scores and apply them to predict disease risk

5. Indicate the (possible) role of genetics in medicine

description:
Introduction: many physical phenomena can be described by differential equations. In the context of Nanobiology you can think of processes like heat dispersion, diffusion or chemical reactions. Often these equations have to be solved numerically. First, the course will discuss how a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) can be solved using numerical time integration. Then we discuss how a stationary diffusion equation can be discretized with the Finite Difference Method. Finally, we combine time integration and space discretization to numerically solve the heat equation.

The theory will be explained in 4 sessions as described below:

Lecture 1: Numerical integration and some time integration methods: Forward Euler, Backward Euler, Trapezoidal Method, Modified Euler. Implicit methods and Explicit methods. Predictor-corrector methods.

Lecture 2: Stability of time integration methods, order of accuracy and systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs).

Lecture 3: Numerical differentiation and Finite Difference Method(s). Discretization of boundary conditions and properties of the discretization matrix.

Lecture 4: Finite Difference Method (continued): (Non-constant) diffusion and the heat equation. The method of lines.


After every lecture, there is a practical session where students should be present in class to:

practice with the theory discussed during lectures using pen-and-paper exercises and Python implementations;

use Python to numerically solve given problems;

explain their Python code, implementation choices, and pen-and-paper solutions to the present instructors and/or teaching assistants in order to receive feedback;

prepare for the final assignment, which will be an oral exam.


Remark: whenever you choose not to be present in class, there are no possibilities to get extra explanation or feedback regarding the content of the lectures nor the practical sessions. This also includes the Python code and pen-and-paper exercises.
learning_objectives:
General: Given an initial value problem or boundary value problem, the student can make a motivated choice of appropriate numerical method to find a numerical approximation of the solution, and analyse the quality of the approximation.

More specifically:

The student knows, can successfully apply and can implement numerical time integration methods to solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and initial value problems, such as Forward Euler, Backward Euler, Trapezoidal Method, and Modified Euler.

The student correctly classifies methods as implicit, explicit and/or predictor-corrector method, and can analyse strengths and weaknesses.

The student correctly analyses stability and order of accuracy of time integration methods for (systems of) ODE(s).

The student correctly applies, implements and analyses the discretisation of a given diffusion equation with the Finite Difference Method.

The student correctly numerically solves the time-dependent heat equation with the method of lines.

The student can clearly explain and justify all submitted work, implementation choices, and can provide detailed elaboration on stability analysis and accuracy of all methods used during practical sessions and in the final exam.

description:
Biomedical Ultrasound elective course: 2.5 ECTS, 4th quarter.

In this course, students will receive an introduction to imaging methods and biomolecular tools that allow ultrasound to visualize cellular functions such as gene expression.

Specifically, the course will focus on the following content:

1. Genetically encoded acoustic biomolecules

2. Ultrasound imaging methods

3. Biomolecular ultrasound applications
learning_objectives:
At the end of the course, student should be able to:

1. Explain the concept of biomolecular ultrasound imaging

2. Apply image ultrasound techniques to detect acoustic biomolecules

3. Discuss strengths and limitations of biomolecular ultrasound

description: interdisciplinary independent research
learning_objectives:
At the end of the project, students will have learned to:

develop feasible research questions

applying innovative methods to the address these questions

communicate about scientific work in an effective way

write reports about their findings

description:
There is a kick off week for the first week, 8 weeks of work, and a final week when all assignments have to be handed in. This includes the final symposium of Q1.

Weekly workshops are provided by a variety of experts on four different threads: communication, collaboration, research and reflection (professional skill development). There will be substantial groupwork and self-study, it is a full time workload.

For clarification, the different ECs stated below do not represent independent courses.

In Q1

Monday mornings will consist of reflecting on previous week and planning group tasks for the coming week. A short Science Spotlight by experts in the field your project is about. Workshops on topics around skills development and research. Afternoon group study.

Tuesday: a self/group study day. Students should plan to spend this with their group working on their project.

Wednesday: a half day workshop on a professional skills topic, more group work.

Thursday: integration of what students have learned so far, writing assignments, discussions with supervisors.

Friday: symposium with all teams to share what students have learned so far, reflect on week.

Communication (~3 ECs)

There will be workshops about technical and advanced literature review, interviewing stakeholders, critical editing/feedback, data visualization, presentations, and students will use those skills in developing their research question.

Collaboration (~3 ECs):

Workshops within this thread will include teamwork, collaborative design, conflict management and resolution, peer feedback and team building.

Research (~6 ECs):

The students will work in small groups, building their knowledge, to generate a deep understanding of the biomedical/societal problem they've selected to focus. They will problem share and brainstorm with other groups on Friday afternoons . Other groups will peer review the weekly plans and ideas. Because students from different disciplines will work within the same groups, diverse knowledge and points of view will be shared to provide a transdisciplinary educational experience.

There will also be workshops related to this thread, such as perspectives and values, research funding, patents, knowledge utilisation, etc

Reflection (~3 ECs):

Reflective skills are integrated throughout the minor, in workshops, lectures and discussions. This will provide the students with skills and power to reflect on themselves, their personalities, their position within the group, their science and what they expect to gain from the Minor. Students will have reflective writing assignments.
learning_objectives:
At the end of Q1 students are able to:

1. Communicate:

a) Create an effective poster.

b) Effectively deliver a poster presentation at a research symposium for a mixed audience (peers, stakeholders and non-academics).

c) Write a research/grant proposal to clearly communicate a research plan, with background, knowledge gap, approach and impact section, including social implications.

d) Use questioning and listening techniques to improve communication in a scientific context. 

2. Collaborate:

a) Collaborate effectively with other group members, other groups and the case owners / experts of the field.

b) Use a group approach to identify problems and develop creative solutions, integrating different knowledge, perspectives and ideas.

c) Explain how intercultural differences play a role in collaboration; this includes social (language, nationality, etc.) but also professional (business vs education, medicine vs engineering) differences and apply this knowledge to the collaboration.

d) Be aware of and reflect on the various phases of the process, the challenges and problems that were encountered, and what was learned from this.

e) Evaluate different roles of members in group projects.

f) Provide constructive feedback and show openness to feedback from others.

3. Research:

a) Able to identify, analyse and integrate current knowledge about a topic from multiple sources, perspectives and methodologies, and identify knowledge gaps.

b) Formulate an adequate research question and relevant research strategy to address it.

c) Develop a helicopter view of a research topic to understand the information in different contexts, magnitude and connections.

d) Understand the dot on the horizon--Identify interesting/solvable problems, long term possibility and challenges of a research topic.

e) Create an overview of the different stakeholders that are involved in the research topic.

f) Understand research grant application processes. 

4. Reflect:

a) Discuss and write about (individual and team) experiences, processes, values.

b) Understand how personal biases influence work.

c) Ask for constructive feedback from supervisors.

description:
Q2 Block - 15 ECs:

The second half of the Minor will be developing and beginning a research plan or developing a tool/technique/algorithm that can be used to address one or more aspects or solutions to the problem. This second half of the Minor requires a student who has participated in the first half. Education will be a mix of lectures, student-organized events, interviews, workshops, groupwork and self-study.

The ECs listed is a guide to workload, not separate courses.

Communication (~2 ECs):

A series of workshops will be given by experts about how to write grant proposals, grant applications, what the institutional review process is, how to present data analysis and visualize it. Students will also practice these skills in weekly symposiums, and in developing final products.

Collaboration (~2 ECs):

There will be workshops on how to detect and correct group mistakes, data management, reproducibility. They will also further develop skills by doing active collaboration in developing and doing a project.

(Lab) Research (~9 ECs):

While the first part of the Minor involves studying the problems raised by the main overarching topic, this second part will delve into researching and finding solutions to these problems. The structure will be similar to the first part. Students will spend most of their time in labs/groups doing research about how to solve the biomedical problems raised during the first part. Students will be responsible for arranging lab opportunities (though we'll help)

Workshops include: lab budgets, sustainability in the lab, lab safety, ethics (data privacy storage, integrity), how to use available repositories.

Reflection (~2 ECs):

The self-reflection skills development will continue in this second part of the Minor but particularly focused on being reflective about the science students are doing. This is core to developing as an ethical scientist. At the end of this block, students will self-reflect on the entire process of this transdisciplinary experience and the Minor. Students will have to write a reflective journal. Topics for workshops and lectures include unconscious bias, critical thinking, troubleshooting.
learning_objectives:
Q2:

At the end of Q2 students are able to:

1. Communicate:

a) Prepare and deliver an effective research presentation / talk for a mixed audience.

b) Write an effective scientific report to communicate research (relevance, method, findings).

c) Demonstrate understanding of the scientific publishing process. 

d) Provide critical and constructive feedback on scientific reports.

e) Use questioning and listening techniques to improve communication in a scientific context. 

2. Collaborate:

a) Develop partnerships with other groups, stakeholders and scientists.

b) Process management: plan, schedule and execute the research project.

c) Identify problems and formulate solutions to collaboration-related problems 

d) Understand ethics and standard practice around credit and ownership in scientific group work.

e) Provide constructive feedback and show openness to feedback from others.

3. Research:

a) Develop research plan and gather the right tools and knowledge to complete their project.

b) Critically evaluate research strategies, and if necessary, modify and adapt these strategies.

c) Plan and (if possible) conduct an experiment based on their research.

d) Analyse outcome(s) of an experiment in a critical way.

e) Apply research ethics around reproducibility, data management and integrity.

f) Understand processes involved with institutional reviews, grant applications and scientific publications.

g) Apply ethical and philosophical considerations in performing research.

h) Able to identify, analyse and integrate current knowledge about a topic from multiple sources, perspectives and methodologies, and identify knowledge gaps. 

4. Reflect:

a) Use provided frameworks to reflect on experiences in minor.

b) Ask for constructive feedback from peers.

c) Understand how personal biases influence collaboration.

d) Reflect on transdisciplinary collaboration in such a way that it can improve collaboration.

description:
This course deals with Lagrange's and Hamilton's formalism of classical mechanics. Subjects discussed are:

- From Newton's law to Lagrangian mechanics and the least action principle. The Euler-Lagrange equations, generalized momenta.

- Constrained systems, Lagrange multipliers.

- Generalized coordinates, rigid body, inertia tensor, harmonic oscillators, Poisson brackets. Symmetries of the Lagrangian and conserved quantities.

- Hamilton's principle, Hamiltonian, Hamilton's equations, Liouville's Theorem.
learning_objectives:
1. Understanding and applying Lagrange formalism in a concrete context. Being able to derive the Euler Lagrange equations for a given Lagrangian and understand their meaning in various (biology relevant) contexts. Understand the meaning of the different terms constituting the Lagrangian.

2. Understanding the link between Hamilton and Lagrangian formalism. Understanding the meaning of Hamiltonian, being able to derive Hamilton's equations in various contexts. Understanding the role of symmetries, and being able to apply the connection with conserved quantities.

description:
This course deals with Markov processes. Subjects are:

- Discrete and continuous-time Markov processes on finite and discrete state spaces: transition probabilities, master equation, stationary distribution, ergodicity, generators.

- Diffusion processes: Brownian motion, diffusion equation, diffusion with drift, reversible diffusions, stationary distribution, Fokker-Planck equation.
learning_objectives:
By the end of the course, you should be able to:

1. Explain the theory of Markov processes in discrete and continuous time on finite and discrete state spaces.

2. Analyse a Markov process and recognize whether it has a unique/non-unique stationary distribution and whether it is ergodic.

3. Explain the theory of processes with continuous state space such as jump and diffusion processes.

4. Investigate how to model a system via a Markov process or a master equation.

5. Investigate how to model a system with a diffusion process and apply the connection between diffusion processes and partial differential equations of diffusion type.

description:
Microscopy is an essential technique in the life science and developments in microscopy have almost always led to new biological discoveries. In the course "High Resolution Imaging" we introduce the state of the art techniques to observe cells, tissue, and biological molecules at the highest possible resolution. We provide a working knowledge of various high resolution imaging techniques, present the basic principles and limitations behind these techniques, and also discuss how to prepare biological samples for the different forms of microscopy. Examples from recent scientific literature will be used to illustrate what can be and has been achieved. Targeted homework, lab demonstrations, and experimental as well as theoretical exercises will help to familiarize you with the different types of microscopes and the data they provide.

Specifically, the course includes lectures and demos on:

Superresolution fluorescence microscopy.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM).

Electron cryo-microscopy, and methods to calculate 3D structures from 2D projections.

Correlative light and electron microscopy and techniques for large-scale and volume imaging.
learning_objectives:
After completion of this course, the students should be able to:

1. Understand the basic principles and limitations for focusing light and electron beams in microscopes.

2. Explain the principles for contrast and image formation in the SEM, STEM, and TEM.

3. Understand the properties of fluorescent labels and the basic principles used in superresolution light microscopy

4. Understand the basic principles of 3D electron microscopy.

5. Explain the role of sample preparation in high-resolution microscopy, understand the steps of fixation (chemical and cryogenic), staining, embedding, sectioning, and labelling, and reproduce the main considerations for each step.

6. Estimate the limitations of each method and decide which of them would be suitable in a particular experiment.

7. Judge the validity of a microscopy approach presented in an experimental work.

description:
This advanced course focuses on the information embedded in the genome of a cell: how it is organized, accessed, interpreted, manipulated and analyzed using structural biological, genomics and proteomics approaches. The course will introduce the students to the methods for precise modification of eukaryotic and prokaryotic genomes (genomic engineering), show how they can be used to create models for fundamental research, correct genetic defects by gene therapy, and develop new strains and varieties for agriculture and biotechnology. Strengths and limitations of both state of the art (CRISPR/Cas) and historical techniques will be described.

To illustrate the required underlying principles for making informed choices during the design of a genome engineering approach, the course addresses how the structure of biomolecules defines their function, how to interpret structural information that is available in public databases, and how to use this information in the design of variants for functional studies and in mapping and interpretation of patient mutations. Furthermore, the students will learn how to analyze information encoded in the genome using genomics, transcriptomics and proteomic tools. For the latter, students will be introduced into the principles of mass spectrometry-based proteomics and will learn how to identify (mutant) proteins based on the interpretation of mass spectra in a practical course.

At the end of this course, students will be able to tackle research questions using genomics, transcriptomics and proteomics concepts in an integrated approach. The focus of this course is on application and integration of knowledge. Active participation in class assignments and discussion sessions is required.
learning_objectives:
At the completion of this course, the students will be able to:

1. Apply basic biochemical and biophysical principles to explain how protein structure determines function

2. Design structure-based mutations to explore biological function of proteins

3. Access and interpret genomic sequence and annotation using genomic browsers to address a research question

4. Conceptually plan and ethically justify a genomic engineering project using state of the art methods

5. Critically interpret the technical details and ethical implications of the genetically engineered models produced by commonly used genomic engineering techniques described in scientific publications

6. Explain the principles, methods and applications and ethical implications of genomics and transcriptomics

7. Design a typical genomics and/or transcriptomics experiment

8. Evaluate and quantify data from a typical genomics/transcriptomics experiment

9. Explain the basics of biomolecular mass spectrometry

10. Describe how mass spectrometry is used in biomedical research and biotechnology

11. Analyze data from a typical quantitative proteomics experiment

12. Design a typical (quantitative) proteomics experiment

13. Formulate gene function by integrating information from structural biology, proteomics, genomics, transcriptomics and genome engineering principles and techniques.

description:
Understanding cancer means understanding the multifaceted nature of biology. The reason for this rather blunt statement is straightforward: among the broad spectrum of diseases, cancer represents a unique didactic model as the malignant cell exploits to its own advantage the most essential biological features of the normal cell in development and adulthood. Thus, by studying the cancer cell in comparison to its normal equivalent, scientists have been able throughout the years to elucidate the molecular and cellular basis of life. That is why the study of the molecular and cellular basis of cancer is (or should be) integral part of any life science academic curriculum. The NB4040 course satisfies this need within the MSc program Nanobiology.

The general idea behind the NB4040 course is to provide the students with a basic knowledge of the biology of cancer by taking advantage of the lead provided by the seminal paper "The Hallmarks of Cancer" by D. Hanahan and R. Weinberg where the most essential features of the cancer cell have been described and discussed. The paper has already been updated in 2011 and most recently in 2022, which highlights its relevance in the cancer scientific community.

The book "The Biology of Cancer, 2nd edition" by R. A. Weinberg (Garland Science, Taylor en Francis Group, LLC, London, 2007, ISBN-10 0-8153-4078-8/ ISBN-13: 9780815340782) will form the basic textbook for the NB4040 course.

The course will start with three sessions on the cellular and molecular biology of cancer and its hallmarks. This will lay the basis for the following sessions where the focus will be on specific cancer types and their features, each covered by expert scientists and clinicians from the Erasmus MC Cancer Institute. These will include leukemia, prostate, bladder, and colon cancer. An additional session will be devoted to omics technologies and bioinformatics as essential experimental tools in cancer research.

These papers and book, together with any other reading material and the pdf's of the lectures are available for download from the Brightspace page of the course.

The format of the NB4040 is meant to satisfy different needs of the Nanobiology MSc student:

1. For those passionate about nanotechnology and its more translational and clinical applications (think of liposomes, DNA origami, nanobots, etc.), the course will highlight how each cancer type, depending on its specific hallmarks and peculiarities, and on the anatomical location of the primary lesion and of its metastases, will need specific strategies towards the development of effective targeted approaches.

2. For those who are more interested in cellular and molecular biology in homeostasis and cancer, the course will provide ample opportunities to deepen your knowledge and appreciate how even the relative relevance of each hallmark and the underlying mechanisms can substantially differ across distinct cancer forms.

In both cases, the elucidation of the hallmarks through which a cancer cell is established, progresses through different malignancy stages, and eventually metastasize distant organ sites, allows us to study and understand biology. As mentioned above, the cancer cell hijacks normal (developmental and homeostatic) programs to exploit them to its own advantage. Paradoxically, although as of today many obstacles have to be overcome to translate our current knowledge into therapies, we have nevertheless been acquiring a substantial body of fundamental knowledge in cellular and molecular biology through the study of cancer.
learning_objectives:
After completion of this course, students should have acquired a multi-disciplinary and functional knowledge of the disease cancer so to be able to address both fundamental and more translational issues (e.g. cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying fundamental hallmarks; the development of nanotechnologies towards the diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy of specific tumor types).

Apart from the textbook knowledge, the students will be able to

1. write a scientific report on a recently published cancer-related paper (based on the NewsenViews format found in Nature and all major scientific journals).

2. Understand scientific literature on recent advances in cancer biology.

3. Develop a research question based on literature research.

5. Collaborate with fellow students to prepare a presentation (and present it).

6. Critically evaluate other students' scientific presentations.

description: The course intends to train the students in the art of computational modeling, by implementing dynamical systems models. The students will be introduced to modeling through various examples and practical sessions, outlining design principles and computational requirements. Students will learn to analyze models with the concepts and tools of dynamical systems theory, such as attractors, bifurcations and parameter space analysis. The course starts with the analysis of one-dimensional dynamical systems (such as the logistic map), moving on to multiple dimensions (Lotka-Volterra and neuronal network models) and finally to spatial models, such as coupled oscillators. At the end of the course students will use 3 sessions to implement and analyze their own model of choice. They then present this model and write a report about it.
learning_objectives:
At the completion of this course, the students will be able to:

1. Describe a natural phenomenon in terms of state variables, parameters and transitions, by abstracting the relevant components of a system / phenomenon.

2. Implement the various models (in Python) from first principles.

3. Conduct parameter space analysis on dynamical behavior of their implemented models.

4. Identify and recognize relevant dynamical phenomena such as fixed-points, saddle nodes, periodic and chaotic attractors and bifurcations.

5. Characterize the stability of attractor states.

6. Find the bifurcations of simple dynamical system numerically.

7. Determine the sensitivity to initial conditions for different dynamical systems.

8. Understand the origin of synchrony in systems of coupled oscillators.

Prepare a video explainer with the results of your dynamical systems project.

description: Soft matter physics is the study of materials that are 'easily deformable, e.g. by thermal fluctuations or small shear forces. Fluids, gels and biological tissues are important examples. In this course, we study the properties of such materials with a special focus on applications in biophysics and biomaterials. Topics include macroscopic and microscopic fluid dynamics, elasticity, viscoelastic materials, polymers, mixtures, and membranes. For all of these we will build models, using the tools of statistical physics, and apply these models to biological examples, such as DNA (polymers), various tissues (viscoelastic materials), liquid-liquid phase separation, and membrane shapes and interactions. We will introduce the relevant mathematical framework where needed, using ideas from tensor calculus, differential equations and differential geometry. At the end of the course, students read and present a recent research paper on a soft matter topic, connecting what they've learned to ongoing developments.
learning_objectives:
At the completion of this course, the students will be able to:

Give an overview of the various topics that constitute soft matter.

State, explain and apply the basic laws of fluid dynamics and elasticity theory.

Explain what a constitutive equation is and derive such equations for given viscoelastic materials.

Mathematically describe polymers and membranes.

Mathematically describe multi-component systems.

Apply the above to various components of living cells.

Read and understand recent scientific literature on soft matter topics and explain the key ideas of recent papers to their peers.

description:
In this course we delve into the fascinating world of stem cells, exploring their biology, their roles in the body, and their diverse applications. Stem cells are the building blocks of life: every cell in every tissue originates from a stem cell or is a stem cell itself, residing in a specialised niche and ready to replace cells that are lost or damaged.

The course follows the journey from fundamental stem cell biology to cutting-edge biomedical applications. We will discuss a variety of topics including pluripotent stem cells and adult stem cells, cloning and reprogramming, differentiation and self-organisation into tissues and organs, regulatory niches and signalling pathways that regulate stem cells. Furthermore, we will examine how stem cells are used for disease modelling, organoid and organ-on-chip technologies, and emerging approaches in regenerative medicine and diagnostics.
learning_objectives:
By the end of this course, the students will be able to:

1. Explain key characteristics of stem cells, their microenvironment, and the major signalling pathways that regulate them.

2. Explain concepts and experimental strategies related to stem cell developmental potency, cloning and reprogramming, lineage tracing and differentiation.

3. Explain the rationale behind the use of stem cells for disease modelling and regenerative therapies.

4. Describe and reflect on ethical issues and policy questions associated with human embryo and stem cell research.

5. Critically read, interpret, and present recent scientific journal articles about stem cells.

description:
The cell nucleus is not just a repository of genetic information but a dynamic regulatory hub where molecular mechanisms govern gene expression and cell fate. In this course, we explore how transcriptional regulators, chromatin remodelers, and histone modifications encode and transmit regulatory signals—translating environmental and developmental cues into stable or reversible gene expression states. We examine how these molecular switches orchestrate processes such as stem cell differentiation, lineage commitment, and how their dysregulation contributes to diseases like cancer. Particular emphasis is placed on the physical principles underlying nuclear organization, transcriptional regulation, and epigenetic memory. Students will integrate concepts from molecular biology and biophysics to gain a systems-level understanding of nuclear function in health and disease.

Course Outline:

Structure and Function of Nuclear Components:
Explore the roles of key nuclear elements, including DNA, RNA, nucleoli, nuclear bodies, speckles, and the nuclear membrane, in maintaining cellular integrity and regulation.

Organization of Genetic Information in the Nucleus:
Investigate how DNA is packaged from histones to higher-order chromatin structures, and how specialized regions such as centromeres and telomeres contribute to genome stability and function.

Chromatin Dynamics and Gene Regulation:
Examine how chromatin is dynamically remodeled by chromatin regulators, including remodelers and transcription factors, to activate or silence specific genes. Emphasis on the molecular mechanisms governing transcriptional control.

Nuclear-Cytoplasmic Communication:
Delve into the mechanisms of nuclear transport and the role of nuclear pores in mediating communication between the nucleus and cytoplasm, focusing on the regulation of protein and RNA trafficking.

Key Methodologies for Studying Nuclear Processes:
Review cutting-edge techniques used to study nuclear dynamics, such as ChIP-seq, single-molecule imaging, and live-cell assays, and their application in uncovering nuclear function.

Breakthrough Discoveries in Nuclear Biology:
Discuss landmark discoveries that have shaped our current understanding of nuclear processes, from chromatin structure to nuclear transport, and their implications for cellular function and disease.

For a preview of the course content you can find links to Youtube animations in the "course content" section on Brightspace.
learning_objectives:
Learning goals of the course:

Generally, you will improve your skills to critical evaluate scientific experiments and their presentation in publications and and train your presentation skills by discussing your evaluation in the class. Since these assignments are performed in groups, you will also train your teamwork and time management skills.

Related to the specific content of the course you will be able at completion of the course to:

describe the basic principles of gene regulation, chromatin organization and chromatin re-organizing processes.

relate the functions of different nuclear components (for example the nuclear lamina) with gene regulation.

describe the basic principles of nuclear transport.

explain which role phase separation might play for nuclear processes.

describe at least one human pathogenic condition that is related to structural malfunctions in the cell nucleus.

interpret experimental results obtained with methods and technologies to study nuclear processes and be able to select appropriate techniques to address questions around the major principles discussed.

description: In this advanced elective, we first cover the necessary mathematical tools from tensor calculus and differential geometry to be able to describe physical systems where geometry is important. We then move on to two important applications: (bio)membranes as two-dimensional surfaces living in three-dimensional space, and the four-dimensional spacetime of general relativity. This is a 'reading course', meaning that the students study the relevant material by themselves, work on the associated problems together, and meet once a week with the instructor to discuss their progress and ask any questions they have.
learning_objectives:
At the completion of this course, the students will be able to:

Explain what tensors are, and use them in calculations, both in index notation and index-free form.

Describe the geometry of objects in any dimension with the curvature tensor.

Explain where the various terms in the Canham-Helfrich energy of the biological membrane come from, and use this energy to calculate membrane shapes.

Explain where the various terms in the Einstein equation of general relativity come from, and use this equation to calculate the geodesics of stars and black holes.

Use the large-scale description of the universe to discuss its possible evolution scenarios.

description:
Even the simplest organism is more complex than the most sophisticated man-made device. How did biological evolution build such intricate machines, and could we build such organisms ourselves? In this course, we will examine how to engineer the properties of existing organisms. In doing so, we will consider the both the successes and failures of modern synthetic biology in its efforts to apply general engineering principles to biology. Through lectures and interactive discussion of recent research articles, we will develop an integrated view of biological behavior, evolution, and the state-of-the-art of bio-engineering.

We will explore how we can use modern genetic engineering tools to engineer the properties of organisms. We will study basic tools and advanced synthetic-biology approaches that can be used to engineer biological solutions for real-world problems. A background in biology will be appropriate preparation for participating students.

Throughout the course you will get the opportunity to study, present, and discuss recent articles from the scientific literature on cutting-edge discoveries and techniques. Specific topics include: real-time experimental evolution, the modern genetic toolbox, feedback control and logic gates, design properties and construction principles of synthetic biology circuits and networks, and the debugging and optimization of engineered networks.
learning_objectives:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

1. Summarize how living systems work in terms of structural and functional concepts at multiple levels of biological organization.

2. Identify why living systems are engineerable.

3. Describe the limitations of the use of engineering approaches learned from other fields when applied to biology.

4. Apply design principles to create new biological functions.

5. Improve and debug the results of genetic engineering by utilizing specific genetic and evolutionary principles.

6. Critically evaluate literature papers in the fields of synthetic biology.

7. Assess the social and safety implications of genetic engineering and directed evolution projects.

8. Engage in constructive scientific discussions

description: The importance of viruses for the evolution of life is paramount. The pandemic caused by SARS-Cov-2 has underlined the impact viruses can have on all areas of human society. In this course we will discuss the principles that viruses employ to infect bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes. We will discuss how viruses evolve and look at the main mechanisms of immune defense of hosts, including CRISPR-Cas, adaptive immunity and RNAi. We will discuss bacterial, archaeal and eukaryotic viruses through a series of lectures, masterclasses, and a final poster presentation. We will invite leading virologists in the Netherlands for a masterclass to bring in cutting edge insights into virus biology.
learning_objectives:
At the completion of this course, the students will be able to:

1. Give an overview of how various types of viruses infect their hosts

2. Explain molecular mechanisms involved in distinct steps in virus reproduction/life cycles, such as virus attachment, entry, replication

3. Explain molecular mechanisms of host immunity and immune evasion by viruses

4. Critically select, review, discuss and present research papers in virology

5. Formulate relevant research questions based on scientific papers in virology.

course_name: AI and Machine Learning for Biomedical Sciences
description: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles and practical applications of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning methods (ML) in the context of nanobiology and biophysics. The course covers key methods such as deep learning, supervised and unsupervised learning, and their applications to protein structure prediction, bioimage analysis, and biological data interpretation. Students will explore the capabilities and limitations of AI tools, address ethical considerations in AI-driven biological research, and gain hands-on experience through computational practicals. The course consists of lectures, coursework, and guided programming assignments.
learning_objectives:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

Understand key AI/ML concepts relevant to biological data analysis, including supervised and unsupervised learning, neural networks, generative models and model evaluation

Apply AI methods to real-world problems in nanobiology, such as protein structure prediction and microscopy image analysis

Critically assess the capabilities and limitations of AI tools in the biological sciences.

Implement and interpret computational models using Python-based tools

Critically reflect on ethical and societal implications of AI in biological research

Collaborate in problem-solving tasks that integrate computational and biological knowledge

Introductions and expectations, how to find seminars, form groups, what should be included in a report.

description:
Nanobiology MSc students are required to do a broadening research project in addition to their MEP. The company internship is one of the options available to students to fulfill this requirement.

Students can schedule their broadening research project at any point in their Master programme, before or after their MEP.

The internship comprises 15 ECTS, or the equivalent of about 10 weeks of full-time work. The company internship should be carried out in a Nanobiology related company where MSc Nanobiology knowledge is necessary for the project.

The goals of a company internship are:

To become familiar with a professional working environment for a Nanobiology graduate.

To apply academic knowledge and skills, acquired in the degree course, to a project in an industrial setting.

To participate in a project in a professional working environment.

To get practical training on the job.

The company internship is supervised by an internal (Nanobiology Green list) and an external (company) supervisor. The company supervisor is responsible for day-to-day supervision. The student will report to their Nanobiology supervisor on a regular basis about progress made on the project. Both supervisors will evaluate the final report and give a grade; the final grade is ultimately decided by the internal supervisor.

Students must complete one research project, either broadening or Master End Project in the research group of a Nanobiology Greenlist supervisor. Doing a company internship means that students must do their MEP in a Nanobiology GreenList research group. Students may not do both projects with the same GreenList supervisor, this includes 2nd supervisor for Internships.

The student is responsible for finding an internship position. Students are advised to start the orientation process at least 4 months in advance if planning to stay in the Netherlands, and at least 6 months if planning to go abroad. The Internship Office has an assisting, coordinating and administrative role.
learning_objectives: To obtain practical experience in company related project work, to further develop communication skills, master research techniques, and broaden scientific thinking and reasoning.

description:
Nanobiology MSc students are required to do a broadening research project in addition to their MEP. The Academic Research Project is one of the options available to students to fulfill this requirement.

The research project comprises 15 ECTS, or the equivalent of 10 weeks of full-time work.
The student may do their work in an academic research group at any approved university or research institute.

The student will work as a member of a University research group and collaborate with other students, PhD students, postdocs, technicians and group leaders.

Work on a specific research topic of the student's choice, doing experiments or simulations and generating new ideas for further research.

Apply knowledge from the Master phase to the research subject.

Practical training in the group / lab to obtain new skills necessary for the project.

Participate in lab activities, group meetings, journal clubs, etc.

If the project is done at an external institute or research group outside the Nanobiology programme, it is supervised by an internal (Nanobiology green list) and an external supervisor. The Nanobiology supervisor must approve the initial project before beginning. The supervisor from the external institution is responsible for day-to-day supervision. During the project the student will report to the Nanobiology supervisor on a regular basis about progress made on the project. If a project is done externally, students must do their MEP in the research group of a Nanobiology GreenList supervisor.

If the project is done in the group of a Nanobiology (green list) supervisor, it is guided by this supervisor, with a second Nanobiology green list member from a different research group for the evaluation.

For Broadening research projects which require a GreenList supervisor, students may not have the same GreenList supervisor for their MEP and their Broadening research project.
learning_objectives: To obtain practical experience in scientific research, to collect data, to practice communication skills, master research techniques, and further develop scientific thinking and reasoning.

description:
A structured approach will greatly increase the chances of success in a scientific research project. The first step of such an approach is to write a proposal. The proposal is a ‘birds-eye, big-picture’ level document including background, hypothesis, general methods and plan. You have written such a proposal in the Project Development Course.

The next step is to create a structured project plan to increase the chances of success in your research project. Planning ahead and discussing your plan with your supervisor will help you set realistic goals, ensure that you have enough time to carry out the tasks required to reach those goals, avoid common pitfalls, and get the most out of your time in a research group. Making a realistic and feasible plan will moreover be a key skill you will need in any job. The preparation phase is therefore an essential step towards a successful MEP.

We strongly recommend that you NOT rush the planning phase because of the attraction of getting started in the lab. Planning your project well, thinking through pitfalls, alternate hypotheses, necessary skills, writing plan will help your project be much more successful. Also spend the time to make sure you have a clear mutual understanding of expectations, benchmarks, and communication channels. Important that benchmarks are about work accomplished not getting results.
learning_objectives:
At the end of the MEP-PREP course, the student will be able to:

Formulate a research question on a scientific topic in the field of Nanobiology.

Formulate hypotheses about possible answers to the research question.

Make a detailed critical planning for a large research project including precise (experimental / simulation) design and necessary resources

Be able to discuss expectations with supervisors and create shared expectations.

Write a data management plan.

Identify meaningful and achievable benchmarks in a research process.

Identify relevant milestone documents to ensure research is on track

Reflect on a proposed project to identify potential risks and possible ways to address those risks.

Identify skill weaknesses and knowledge gaps to complete the project and make a plan to address them.

Be ready to start their MEP.

description: Interdisciplinary independent research on current topics with scientific or societal relevance.
learning_objectives:
At the end of the project, students will have learned to:

develop feasible research questions,

apply innovative methods to the address these questions,

communicate about scientific work in an effective way,

write reports about their findings

description:
The Master End Project (MEP) is usually conducted in the second year of the MSc. It will take approximately 30 weeks, and is conducted in a research group on the Nanobiology GreenList. The research project comprises 42 ECTS and includes writing a Master's thesis, presenting the work and defending it orally.

During your MEP, you work as a member of a research group and collaborate with other students, PhD students, postdocs, technicians and group leaders. You will be working on a specific research topic of your choice, doing experiments, simulations, or theoretical work, and generating new ideas for further research. You are expected to implement the knowledge from the Bachelor and Master phase and apply that knowledge to the research subject. If the research project is outside the Nanobiology programme GreenList, you need to have both an internal (GreenList) and external supervisor. Projects outside the GreenList must be approved by the Board of Examiners prior to beginning.

The research project is concluded by submission and defense of the MSc thesis. The thesis will take the form of a full-length research article, suitable for publication in an international journal. In contrast to a regular article manuscript, the MSc thesis will include a more elaborate introduction, describing the scientific background of the study, and the methods section will be expanded to include a complete and detailed description of all methods that have been applied. The MSc thesis should demonstrate the ability of the student to organize and present results and knowledge in a form required for publication of a scientific article.

The defense of the thesis will take about 30 minutes, and will be preceded by a public presentation (of also roughly 30 minutes) on the aim, results and conclusions of the thesis work.A research project can be followed with a supervisor on the Nanobiology GreenList that can be found on the Brightspace page of the Thesis office Applied Science. With approval from the Board of Examiners, students may apply to do a project outside the Nanobiology programme.

When planning research projects, students must do either their MEP or their Broadening Research Project internal to the Nanobiology programme, they can do both. Please see the programme page for Broadening Research Projects to see which allowed projects are considered internal and other rules about the projects.
learning_objectives:
At the completion of this course the student will be able to:

Perform laboratory or theoretical research,

Design and execute a research project including experiments, data collection and analysis

Report on their methods and findings in both oral and written form,

Demonstrate scientific thinking and reasoning, including critical reflection on their work,

Work collaboratively in a research environment including giving and receiving feedback,

Reflect on the ethical and social implications of their research.

description:
Offshore structures are exposed to cyclic mechanical loading; forces and moments, both environment (wind, waves) and service (operations, machinery) induced. The response in terms of stress, strain or energy is cyclic by nature accordingly, meaning fatigue, a cyclic loading en response induced local, progressive, structural damage mechanism is a governing limit state. To be able to assess the offshore structure integrity en longevity in this matter, course contents include:

Fatigue fundamentals, i.e. physics and damage process phenomena in:

materials at defect locations (stress concentrations at micro- and meso-scale); different sources and different stages in the fatigue en fracture process (crack initiation, growth and propagation, fracture).

structures at notch locations (stress concentrations at macro-scale) as part of structural members or at the member connections; particular attention will be paid to arc-welded joints in that respect, since marine structures are predominantly assemblies consisting of plates, shells and tubular members.

Macroscopic (notch) stress concentrations, distributions and intensities:

as part of structural members.

at (welded) structural member connections, consisting of a cyclic mechanical- and quasi-constant thermal residual part.

Fatigue resistance:

materials (plane geometries)

structures (notched geometries: welded joints) at small-, large- and full-scale

testing (measurement techniques)

damage criterion life time relations in different ranges (low-, mid- and high-cycle fatigue); formulations and parameter estimates using regression analysis (least squares- and likelihood approaches).

short- and long crack growth relations.

Fatigue assessment concepts:

damage criteria using an intact geometry parameter (nominal stress-, structural hot spot stress- and effective notch stress/ strain concept).

damage criteria using a cracked geometry parameter (crack tip stress intensity- and equivalent stress concept).

Particular attention will be paid to analytical formulations and numerical approaches; concept capabilities and limitations.

Fatigue influence factors: material and geometry (strength, surface integrity, volume, welding improvement techniques), environment (temperature, corrosion), loading en response (min/max ratio, mean stress, amplitude variability (time domain analysis, cycle counting, spectral approaches, scatter diagrams, cumulative damage hypotheses), multi-axiality including proportionality (in-phase, out-of-phase).

Fatigue reliability for (risk based) inspection and maintenance purposes: time dependent limit state functions, (joint) design variable statistics, level 1, 2 and 3 analysis, 1st and 2nd order analytical reliability methods and Monte Carlo simulation.

Structure integrity en longevity: fatigue strength calculation and life time estimation for assessment and design using different (design) philosophies, concepts, rules, standards and guidance.
learning_objectives:
Theory (fundamentals):

to identify and describe the fatigue physics and damage process phenomena in materials en structures

to establish and calculate the macroscopic fatigue characteristic structural response parameters

to investigate fatigue resistance testing considerations and characterise damage criterion life time relations

to model fatigue physics mathematically based on different damage criteria developed in the course of time

to assess fatigue resistance consequences of relevant influence factors and incorporate models in fatigue damage criteria

to examine 1st and 2nd order as well as Monte Carlo simulation based reliability methods at level 1, 2 and 3 for (risk based) inspection and maintenance purposes

Validation (experiments):

to evaluate dedicated fatigue testing techniquest

to analyse and process measurement data and establish fatigue resistance parameters

Application (engineering):

to identify and classify fatigue sensitive locations in structures

to select an appropriate fatigue assessment concept

to establish and improve marine structure integrity en longevity, i.e. to calculate the fatigue strength and corresponding life time estimate for analysis and design purposes

hydrostatics / floating stability

laws of fluid mechanics

potential flow

constant real (viscous) flow

wave spectra

description: This course introduces students to the offshore renewable resources of the ocean environment and the technologies for renewable energy conversion, with the main purpose of developing comprehension of the first principles of offshore renewables engineering. description:
This course treats the mechanics of slender structures. First, simple cases are treated in which analytical solutions of single elements are possible. The goal is to explain physics and the basics of the methods. Thereafter, the focus is shifted towards more design-type assignments in which the students apply the solution methods in more complex systems consisting of combined one-dimensional structural elements and plates together with complex boundary/interface conditions. The course covers:

- Formulation of governing equations of one-dimensional and two-dimensional slender structures.

- Statics and dynamics of cables, rods, shear beams and beams in bending.

- Statics and dynamics of plates in bending.

- Statics and dynamics of combinations of one-dimensional slender structures.

In addition, students are trained on transferable skills, relevant for their professional development.
learning_objectives:
After this course, you should be able to:

1. Identify the relevant mechanical principles in terms of one-dimensional slender structures and plates of offshore systems

2. Formulate the governing equations of motions of one-dimensional slender structures and plates

3. Determine the response of one-dimensional slender structures and plates to static and dynamic loads

4. Assess the implications of simplifications of physical principles and corresponding assumptions on the analysis of offshore en dredging engineering systems

5. Perform an analysis of personal characteristics in terms of core qualifies, pitfalls, allergies and opportunities in relation to others, within the context of a professional environment

6. Evaluate alternative positions in discussions by taking up and evolving arguments brought in by others, recognizing moral values underlying own and alternative opinions, distinguishing personal opinions and factual judgments

7. Articulate a moral framework for the analysis of the impact of own work based on personal values and professional guiding principles

description:
This course entails the seabed preparation processes that are typically encountered in dredging and marine construction. These seabed alterations are typically due to mechanical or hydraulic action, but could also happen due to natural processes occurring. The following content will be treated during the course:

- Introduction to dredging engineering and dredging equipment
- Intro to soil mechanics
- Cutting mechanisms
- Generic cutting model
- Cutting of saturated sand
- Clay cutting
- Rock cutting
- Settling velocity
- Sedimentation en (high speed) erosion
- Jetting in sand and clay
- Breaching
- Turbidity currents
learning_objectives:
By the end of this course, the students will be able to:

- Explain the fundamental principles that govern rapid deformation of (submerged) soils
- Apply the physical principles that govern excavation processes in dredging engineering
- Evaluate the factors that affect the excavation process, including soil conditions and equipment used (mechanical, hydraulic or hybrid).
- Assess the strengths and limitations of different models and assumptions used to simplify the analysis of the excavation and seabed intervention processes.

course_name: Numerical Methods for Offshore and Dredging Engineering
description:
This course concerns the numerical methods that can be used to analyse offshore en dredging engineering systems (structures and operations). During this course, you are trained to perform a numerical experiment, including the design of algorithms. Following through the different steps of study design, pre-analysis, data collection, post-analysis, validation and interpretation, you gain experience in drawing relevant conclusions and reflecting critically on the research activities performed.

After a training on relevant numerical methods, covering both computational fluid and structural dynamics, you will conduct a numerical experiment using your self-developed algorithm in Python or Matlab. Following the FAIR principles, you will learn how to analyse and visualize your obtained data to draw scientifically relevant conclusions.

The course offers multiple numerical assignments to conduct in small groups. You can express your motivated preference for a specific assignment through the individual reflection portfolio of the course OE44195. Your allocation to a specific assignment will be based on both your motivation and practical considerations.
learning_objectives:
After this course, you should be able to:

Define a methodical approach to answer scientific research questions in the domain of offshore en dredging engineering, including the selection of appropriate methods and tools.

Conduct numerical experiments in a reproducible way, including the design of algorithms, using relevant numerical methodologies to analyze the working principles of offshore en dredging engineering systems.

Draw scientifically relevant conclusions (and the range of applicability thereof) from data obtained with numerical experiments using coherent interpretation techniques.

Disseminate data retrieved from numerical experiments required to answer research questions in a findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable manner.

Demonstrate academic integrity, implying commitment to honest and moral behaviour in an academic setting.

Evaluate collaboration and team performance in terms of clear targets, productivity, sharing of responsibilities and accountability, using constructive feedback.

Update the personal development plan in a reflective and responsive manner, based on monitoring of development using self-assessment and feedback from peers and supervisors

description:
This course equips you with the critical skills necessary to conduct novel research in offshore and dredging engineering, with a focus on physical experimentation. You will follow a structured process, including conception of the experiments, design, pre-analysis, data collection, post-analysis, and validation. Through this, you will gain experience in interpreting collected data, drawing meaningful conclusions, and reflecting critically on your research activities.

After training on relevant experimental methodologies, such as Pi theorem, scaling laws, measurement techniques and signal processing, as well as on safety in the labs, physical experiments will be carried out in a relevant lab. Following the FAIR principles, you will learn how to analyse and visualize your obtained data to draw scientifically relevant conclusions.

The course offers multiple experimental set-ups to conduct experiments in small groups. You can express your motivated preference for a specific set-up through the individual reflection portfolio of the course OE44195. Your allocation to a specific setup will be based on both your motivation and practical considerations.
learning_objectives:

Define a methodical approach to answer scientific research questions in the domain of offshore en dredging engineering, including the selection of appropriate methods and tools

Conduct physical experiments in a reproducible way using relevant experimental methodologies to analyze the working principles of offshore en dredging engineering systems

Draw scientifically relevant conclusions (and the range of applicability thereof) from experimental data using coherent interpretation techniques

Disseminate data retrieved from research required to answer research questions in a findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable manner

Demonstrate academic integrity, implying commitment to honest and moral behaviour in an academic setting

course_name: Reflection for Offshore and Dredging Engineers
description:
Your study is not just about grades and exams. You have chosen the master Offshore en Dredging Engineering to become a knowledgeable and skillful engineering professional. To this end, you will participate in all courses, and demonstrate your skills and understandings in exams and projects.

Becoming an engineering professional involves more than demonstrating your performance in exams and projects. Each of us has her/his personal talents and preferences, and we all suffer from ineptitudes in certain areas. Being effective in the professional field requires a good level of self-awareness. On which aspects can you be a leader and for which domains can you better rely on the expertise of others?

The course Reflection for Offshore en Dredging Engineers aims to open your eyes for all non-technical aspect that contribute to your success as engineering professional. Understanding your strengths and weaknesses helps you formulating goals for self-development and makes you an effective team player.

Running in parallel with all your course work in the first year of your master, the course will help you sharpen your thoughts regarding the projects and elective courses you intend to follow. You are invited to motivate your preferred projects for the second semester and your selection of elective courses for the first quarter of the second year.
learning_objectives:
Your reflection on your development as offshore en dredging engineer contributes to your proof that you meet the following exit qualifications of the programme:

- Self-development: Develop competences and knowledge to function in varying professional environments.
- Academic communication: Communicate professional and scientific judgments effectively.
- Collaborative problem-solving: Collaborate in international, multi-cultural and multi-disciplinary teams.
- Ethical Intelligence: Demonstrate the ability to critically assess the societal and environmental implications of their engineering solutions.

description: This course will introduce the students to the technical aspects and detailed understanding of offshore developments (e.g. renewable energy farms, deep-sea mining, seabed preparations). The course builds on fundamental knowledge addressed in the first semester with project management techniques, as well as applied design methodologies. The students will participate in a realistic project teamwork, working on actual cases with stakeholder analysis, risk management assessment and modelling, including an overview of the project development of safe and reliable offshore technologies. In this course, students can choose from different development projects to participate in (currently two projects available).
learning_objectives:
After this course, students should be able to:

Define the design space of a new or modified offshore en dredging engineering development, based on a functional and requirements analysis, and accounting for the full life-cycle

Select design solutions in a methodological and transparent manner, based on an analysis of the life-cycle performance in terms or functional, societal and economical value, including sustainability and circularity

Perform risk analyses, accounting for health, safety and environmental risks, and including possible mitigation measures

Create a plan for professional development, based on individual goals obtained from self-assessment and feedback from peers and supervisors

Articulate assumptions, boundary conditions and limitations of (design) methods, distinguishing concept-based and application-based approaches, to put results, conclusions and recommendations into perspective

Execute well-planned projects, based on principles of project management and time management

Create ethical plausible measures for reduction of impact or mitigation of adverse effects

description: The course addresses relevant topics in Soil Mechanics and Geotechnical Engineering related to offshore energy harvesting, including renewables and oil & gas. The core subject is the analysis and design of foundation systems for offshore structures. The course will start with an in-depth introduction to soil behaviour, including the response of soils to environmental cyclic loading. Then, essential concepts about marine site investigation are discussed and followed by an introduction to soil-foundation-structure interaction effects. Then the course is brought to a conclusion by addressing the analysis/design of both shallow and deep offshore foundations.

The primary objective of this course is to enable students to produce a conceptual engineering design for offshore structures. During this course, students gain a thorough theoretical understanding of the design process, its structuring, available design methodologies and the philosophy behind the design codes.

Throughout the course students work on a group design project, where each student team designs an offshore jacket support structure for wind energy applications from scratch up to a preliminary design by performing a full design-cycle. This design-cycle includes:

The design and assembly of the structure geometry and the structural configuration, including a natural frequency analysis,

Determining and assessing the permanent and environmental loads, including both hydrodynamics and wind, on the structure,

The design, analysis and evaluation of its foundation,

The analysis of the jacket structure by using structural mechanics approaches, and

The evaluation of the jacket structure against ULS and, if applicable, FLS design criteria.

Through this group design project, students will not only learn to judge their design against ULS and FLS design criteria, but they will also develop an instinct on how to best modify and improve their design based on both static and dynamic structural analyses. Thereby, students will learn how to analyse and evaluate the dimensioning and performance of structural components for strength and stability. Furthermore, students learn to predict how changing (parts of) their design will influence the corresponding loads and based on their insight in these loads, be able to defend their design choices. Moreover, students will learn what the practical implications of their design choices are for operations and other feasibility and life-cycle aspects. To reinforce the understanding of these aspects, the course program also includes a visit to an offshore structures fabrication yard.

During this course, students will additionally learn how to collaborate effectively in a team and develop skills and competences to motivate their assumptions and provide argumentation of their design choices by accounting for relevant moral values, norms and principles.
learning_objectives:
After a successful participation in this course, students are able to:

Define the design space and generate sound preliminary designs and design solutions for new or modified offshore structures based on functional requirements, its interaction with the environment and accounting for the full life-cycle of the structure, and to do so in a methodological and transparent manner.

Analyse principles of ultimate resistance and fatigue relevant for the design of offshore structures, using available scientific knowledge.

Evaluate the limit states of designs of offshore structures, using an applicable safety philosophy (deterministic, probabilistic) based on valid design standards.

Perform statistically sound and context-based analysis and verification of the structural health of offshore structures, including possible mitigation measures.

Effectively collaborate and communicate with the aim to execute a design project based on principles of project and time management, and to generate and optimize offshore structures designs.

Critically reflect on your own design and that of your peers, and the reliability of offshore structures and its structural components in general by articulating assumptions, boundary conditions and limitations of (design) methods to put results, conclusions and recommendations into perspective.

Translate current natural and societal needs into possible technical designs of offshore structures by accounting for relevant moral values, norms and principles.

This course contributes to the final attainments of the Offshore en Dredging Engineering program on Constructive Design (1-4), Collaborative Problem-Solving, Self-Development and Academic Communication (5-6), and Ethical Intelligence (7).

description: In this course, students will undertake a research exercise to develop/enhance their research skills. The topic of the research exercise will be identified jointly by the student and their daily supervisor. The exercise may include various tasks such as literature review, data collection, data analysis, and hypothesis testing, all aimed at addressing specific research questions. This course will provide students with experience in conducting research, enabling them to apply theoretical knowledge in a practical context and gain a deeper understanding of how to conduct scientific research.
learning_objectives:
Depending on the research exercise, the student will be able to conduct a set of the following research activities:

Survey the state-of-the-art knowledge pertaining to the problem at hand and identify relevant knowledge gaps.

Formulate research questions to be addressed within the allocated time for research.

Define a systematic approach to address the formulated research questions.

Execute the necessary tasks according to the defined approach.

Draw scientifically valid conclusions based on the findings.

description:
This course serves as preparation for your master graduation project (OE54035). You are expected to do a review of the available literature for your intended topic of graduation, which result in the framework for your research. The report should consist of the following components:

A background description, or a description of the field.

A general problem statement. Why further research for this field is needed?

A description of the method of literature retrieval. What search engines did you use? What search strings and how did you define these? How many publications did you find and how many were useful?

An overview of the available relevant literature. What research have been done? What problems have been considered? What are the recent developments? Other sources you could use are interviews, discussions with an expert panel, simple benchmark calculations etc.

A specific research objective, research question or hypothesis. What should be the outcome of your research?

A description of your research approach. How do you intend to reach your objective?

For your literature research you should make use of recognized scientific sources. Correct, consistent and complete referencing in accordance with an accepted academic style is expected. It is possible to use oral sources, for instance by means of expert interviews. In this case, written documentations of the interview should be added as an appendix to the literature review. Online search engines and generative AI tools can be helpful in collecting information and improving your writing style. Using such tools does not take away your responsibility for the content of your report.

A summary of your literature review can serve as the introduction of your graduation report.

The procedure to find a topic for your literature review and graduation is as follows:

- Contact the professor, or other academic staff members, who works on a topic of your interest to see if there is a project available that you might like. TU Delft is frequently contacted by problem owners for such projects, but this is not guaranteed. In a discussion you can both find out what subject interests you and if there is a project available that relates to that subject. In most cases there is a rough problem description available of about half a page (A4). If not, most academic staff members can tell you where to search or who to contact to help find a suitable project.
- Another option is to contact a problem owner (company/PhD student/Staff Member) yourself (e.g. through your own network). If they agree to take you as a graduation student on a subject you find interesting, you should write a short description of about half a page (A4) to discuss with the specialization prof. This is usually sufficient to check if a problem is a viable subject to graduate on.
- Based on the initial description and discussions with all involved parties, you should extend the description to a more detailed Plan of Approach that ensures that both you and your supervisory team agree on what you will do. If all parties agree with your Plan of Approach the initial phase is concluded and it is time to set the date for a kick-off meeting. Usually at this point, you should also be assigned a daily supervisor (the problem owner) and an academic supervisor (TU Delft).

It is advised to start about 3 months in advance with these preparations.

This course concerns the final part of the master programme Offshore en Dredging Engineering and follows on completion of the course OE54010-22 Literature Review (or the Specialization Project for EWEM-OE students).

During the MSc thesis project, you will work individually on the execution of your experiment (physical, numerical, or other) that you designed to answer your research question. You will collect and analyze the resulting data, draw scientifically relevant conclusions and provide recommendations for further research. You will perform your activities under the guidance of a daily supervisor (problem owner, as defined under OE54010-22) and a academic supervisor (who could be the problem owner).

Throughout your project, you will organize meetings with your supervisory team, during which you present your progress and bring up points for discussion. These meetings serve as an opportunity to receive feedback as well. The scheduling of the meetings, as well as the organization of the feedback process should be discussed with your supervisory team.

The total duration of the MSc thesis project is approximately 25 weeks. In consultation with your supervisory team, it is possible to deviate from this. At the end of the 25 weeks, you submit a final draft of your thesis report and organize a so-called greenlight meeting. During this meeting, you present your work to your committee, who then decides whether you are ready to graduate (i.e. your work can be graded as 6.0 or higher). If the level of your work is insufficient, you will have a second opportunity to schedule a green light meeting, under the conditions agreed upon with your supervisory team. You also have the right to request feedback to improve your work towards the defense ceremony, even if a green light is granted.

After receiving a green light, you can schedule your defense date and submit a Form 5 to the Study Programme Administration (spa-me@tudelft.nl), which is available at the following link: https://www.tudelft.nl/en/student/me-student-portal/education/related/student-forms/msc-forms/.

At the defense ceremony, you will present your work to the public (family, friends, peers) and the assessment committee. The public and the committee are invited to ask questions about your work. After the presentation and the Q&A, the assessment committee will decide upon your final grade, which will be communicated in public.

If you undertake the graduation project at a company, a graduation agreement should be signed. In this respect, the template of the TUD-ME graduation agreement should be used, which is available at the following link: https://www.tudelft.nl/en/student/me-student-portal/education/related/student-forms/msc-forms/.
