Design

The main objective for the assignment is to create a design, thereby following a methodological approach and using all the necessary tools and calculations to converge to a most suitable design.

Experimental

The main objective for the assignment is to acquire experience in designing, building a testing methodology and measuring the relevant parameters. In scientific research experiments have to be repeatable in order to be valid, this means that the experiments have to have the same results when performed by a third party.

Computer/Programming

The main objective for the assignment is to acquire experience in designing and building a representative environment for experiments. The test environment can be a computer or physical model and should be designed "to purpose" which means the performance indicators are relevant and the results accurate enough to answer the research question.

description:
The MSc-thesis work is the final assignment in the MSc-program, during which a student either further develops the theoretical knowledge gained in the literature survey, or applies it in the form of computer simulations or in the form of experiments (depending on the chosen project). The student will set up and carry out a research project in the field of Systems and Control. The subject of research can be provided by the staff or a company, however it is also possible to propose another project. The final project can be carried out within the framework of ongoing research at the university, within a company, within a research institute or at another university.

See also
https://brightspace.tudelft.nl/d2l/le/content/43131/viewContent/3004041/View
This project also encompasses 2 formal colloquium presentations (Mid-term colloquium and Final MSc colloquium). The students have to attend 15 student colloquia (including those where they give their own presentations). Attendance is monitored.

Colloquia sessions are organized throughout the year and are published on the DCSC website and communicated to 2nd year students by email.

Workshops with fellow students will be organized by individual staff members or by several staff members together. Your thesis supervisor will discuss this with you.

Every S&C MSc Thesis project needs to have an MSc advisor involved who approves the project, serves in the final exam committee, and is a staff member of DCSC .The student may receive daily supervision from a DCSC staff member, a staff member from another department/faculty, a company supervisor (if applicable), or from a PhD student.

If a student undertakes the graduation project at a company, an additional graduation agreement should be signed. In this respect, the template of the TUD-ME graduation agreement should be used, which is available at the following link: https://www.tudelft.nl/studenten/me-studentenportal/onderwijs/gerelateerd/formulieren/msc-formulieren
learning_objectives:
Formulate a formal/mathematical description of the problem setup

Describe and reflect on alternative formulations, establish fallback options (contingency planning)

Construct a research plan to be executed as part of the thesis project, and specify further details of the research objectives

Propose at least one approach as a potential solution to solve the problem

Mid-term colloquium: Present the detailed problem formulation and a proposed approach in front of an audience

Develop new methods, or extend/modify/compare existing methods in a novel way to address the research question

Implement, evaluate, and if needed, perform several (re-)design cycles of the developed techniques either in numerical simulation or based on an experimental setup

Engage in scientific discussions with peers (attend colloquia)

Write a scientific report (thesis) presenting and discussing the motivation, problem setup, approach, and results/conclusions.

Present an overview of the developed methods, the obtained results and research findings, together with the corresponding conclusions in front of an audience (final presentation)

Defend the performed research and its findings in front of a committee of experts.

course_name: Introduction to Design in Complex Systems
description: This is an intensive, structured one-week programme. The aim of the activities in this course is to engage you in forming a learning community with your peers and instructors, to introduce you to the TPM mindset, and to support you in developing a skill set that is needed for designing in socio-technical systems. As such, this course is an introduction to the other design-related courses in the COSEM MSc programme: SEN1121, 1131, 1141, 1151 and 1161. The course consists of a mix of lectures and collaborative project work. Lectures introduce the basic vocabulary, concepts, analytical and design methods that are useful for designing technical structures, institutions and stakeholder processes. Daily assignments are related to a real-world design problem and challenge students to apply these concepts and methods. At the end of the week, teams present an intervention of their own creation in response to the real-world problem presented to them to peers and instructors.

The course introduces design and systems thinking in complex sociotechnical systems in line with the core orientation of the CoSem MSc programme. Students learn important concepts related to complex systems engineering and how to apply these to different cases. The goal of the course is to master the correct vocabulary and to learn how to look at complex socio-technical systems.

The course consists of three parts:

Part 1 - Design thinking

This part covers the basics of designing interventions in complex socio-technical systems. Topics discussed include analyses vs design, design cycles, design approaches, and scientific design.

Part 2 - Systems thinking

This part covers an introduction to systems thinking and to complex systems/complexly science. Topics discussed include systems thinking, complex socio-technical systems, and complex systems properties.

Part 3 - Design in Complex Systems

This final part combines the two previous parts and focuses on design in complex systems. It covers topics such as systemic design, transdisciplinary design and research, systems modeling and simulation, and project and risk management.
learning_objectives:
After completion of the course, a student is able to

- use and differentiate between concepts and terminology related to the design of complex sociotechnical systems

- properly define and apply concepts related to design thinking, systems thinking and complex systems

- structure and coordinate a design process for a complex sociotechnical system

course_name: Institutional Economics for Designing in Socio-technical Systems
description:
This course provides fundamental concepts from the field of Institutional Economics that are instrumental for the design of institutions in socio-technical systems. Relevant frameworks and theories will be elaborated in relation to the design of socio-technical systems. The fundamentals of institutional economics will be applied to concrete design challenges, like the transition to sustainable infrastructures. It will be demonstrated how to relate Institutional Economics to interdisciplinary research challenges, including engineering, political science, law and philosophy. This provides interesting perspectives to other courses in the curriculum. Typical questions that are addressed in this module include:

What is the specific contribution of Institutional Economics to the design of socio-technical systems?

How to frame and interpret design challenges from an Institutional Economic perspective?

What is is an institutional design?

How can institutional designs be related to the technical design of complex systems?

How to operationalize concepts from institutional economics and apply them to empirical design challenges?
learning_objectives:
After the completion of the course, the student is able to:

to understand and analyse complex institutional arrangements from an Institutional Economic perspective

reflect on the possible contribution of Institutional Economics in addressing different design challenges

apply approaches from Institutional Economics to concrete design challenges

position and apply different approaches from Institutional Economics to interdisciplinary design challenges.

establish a coherent institutional design given the features of the technical system(s) embedded in their socio-political environment

description:
The TPM Master on Complex Systems Engineering combines three major perspectives: Technology, Institutions and Actors. The course ‘Managing multi-actor decision-making’ (SEN114), focuses on actors and more specifically their interests, needs, values, relations and processes of decision making.

In many cases, a ‘traditional’ top down, linear development of a systems engineering design is no longer possible due to interdependencies between collaborating actors: including different sets of expertise from different academic disciplines, and engineering traditions. Therefore, engineering designs for complex socio-technical systems are often being developed at negotiation tables, in cocreation sessions, and decided upon in various (institutionalized) decision making arenas.  

This course teaches future engineers a variety of advanced decision making and governance processes to analyse and develop decision making processes that better include multi-actor perspectives in the design of complex-socio-technical systems. These processes include ‘stakeholder management’, and more advanced forms of governance such as transition management and collaborative and adaptive governance.

Students will

(1) acquire knowledge about the concepts and methods to analyse the formal roles, interests, problem framing and sources of power of individual and collective actors in the system- as well as their interdependencies and networks.

(2) acquire knowledge about the concepts and methods to design forms of multi-actor decision making and governance that are aiming to realize change in the decision making process and through that in coping with complex, wicked socio-technical systems.

Based on three real -life cases in the areas of energy, mobility, and digitalization, students will apply theories and methods and develop skills to identify stakeholders, their networks and their type of interactions in order to design and manage decision making processes about engineering interventions that contribute to positive change. Often this means a process design and management that encourages interdependent actors to move from negotiations to more collaborative and adaptive forms of governing.
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course, students will be able to

explain why actors in networks behave as they do, and how their behaviour evolves

describe different network structures and their practical implications

assess the designability of institutions, systems, policies and technologies

argue why certain process managerial tactics might work under which conditions

create case-specific process managerial tactics to anticipate complex decision-making.

assess the quality of process designs

reflect on multi-actor decision-making in light of broader scientific and public policy trends and debates

description:
Suppose we want to switch to a hydrogen based economy in which fuel cell cars are used as power plants. Or suppose we want a fully automated inland terminal. And what about the construction of multifunctional dikes? You cannot 'just' realize that but you have to be aware of the relevant legal and institutional framework. That framework will enable you to make things happen, but it can also contain constraints.

This course focuses on the legal and institutional framework to take into account with that kind of projects. Are there for instance legal instruments to force people to switch to fuel cell cars? And to what institutional layer do those instruments belong? Are they easy to change? Or: can the government subsidize the transition to a fully automated inland terminal? What are the constraints? And can we work around those constraints? Or: what exactly has to be studied for the environmental impact assessment regarding the dike? Does an environmental impact assessment have to be conducted at all?

Students are requested to form groups and select a case. Then, the group will present its case in an elevator pitch to all the students and make an initial outline for the legal and institutional aspects of the case. On the basis of those pitches, we will dive into the world of law in order to see what defines the design space for those projects, what areas of law are relevant, whether the law forms a barrier or not and how the law can be used to realize those projects. Next to these group assignments, which will be finalized by a group paper, there will be an individual exam.
learning_objectives:
At the end of the course, students are able to:

- Relate legal instruments to the institutional framework

- Work with the law as a system

- Relate the legal instruments to the institutional framework

- Identify the legal borders of the design space regarding a socio technical system

- Identify relevant law for a socio technical system

- Apply relevant law to a socio technical system and identify barriers and opportunities

- Deal with legal language

description:
This course is a ten-week, capstone project; students work in teams of 5 persons. Teams are formed by the module-manager based on student's preferences.

Teams work under supervision. Students are encouraged to also consult with experts and stakeholders from the field.

Early in week 1, students receive their specified assignment, namely the design of an intervention that enables stakeholders to implement a recent policy decision related to energy transition, mobility, or digitalisation in the Metropole the Hague-Rotterdam. Starting in week 1, the design team analyses the problem situation, frames the design problem, and then designs, evaluates and communicates suitable interventions. The final product comprises the lay-out of an intervention that implements the policy decision, namely: basic but well-aligned technical and institutional designs, a design for a stakeholder process that supports the realization of the intervention (including process rules), and other products needed to communicate these designs.

Deliverables are (1) A team report that documents all steps in the design process, including products that inform stakeholders about the results of the design process. (2) An individual reflection paragraph.
learning_objectives:
After completion of the course, the student should be able to design interventions for real-world, socio-technical systems. This ability is exhibited through the following capacities - students will be able to:

LO 1. Frame a complex problem using the analysis of the technical, institution and multi-actor processes aspects of a system

LO 2. Generate design alternatives for the technical, institutional and multi-actor aspects an integrated intervention

LO 3. Able to evaluate and select between chosen design alternatives and make this process explicit, based on acquired knowledge and theory throughout the design process

LO 4. Communicate the intervention to stakeholders by demonstrating perspectival agility

LO 5. Articulating the team's strategies for phasing of the design process, including choice and use of available methods, tools, theory

LO 6. Communicate the process of analysis and designing orally, in writing and graphically, working in a team setting

LO 7. Reflect on their individual rationale for making design choices and work processes and demonstrate the consequences of this reflection within the course

description:
This course has two focus points: 1. agent-based modelling and 2. complex adaptive systems theory for ABM.

Firstly, you will develop agent-based modelling skills by creating an agent-based model in a small group. This course is not meant as an introduction to basic programming, or a thorough introduction to Python/Mesa, but will rather focus on understanding the concepts of agent-based modelling and how model design choices affect the model created and how it can be used. Additional reading materials are provided for self-study in getting up to speed in basic programming, Python, and Mesa, as well as refresher exercises in the practical sessions. There will be a weekly lecture focused on agent-based modelling theory. In addition, there will be a weekly practical session focused on further developing your agent-based modelling skills.

Secondly, there will be weekly lectures focusing on complex adaptive systems theory for agent-based models. Different characteristics of these systems, theoretical concepts and their applications will be discussed. Further reading will be offered to broaden your view and deepen your understanding.
learning_objectives:
After following this course, the student can:

1. understand, modify and create agent-based simulations in Python with the Mesa library.

2. identify relevant properties of a system and determine whether the system can be classified as a complex adaptive system or not.

3. apply the definitions of complex adaptive system properties, as listed in the course topics, to different types of socio-technical systems and agent-based models

4. reflect on the traditional engineering systems thinking from the complex adaptive systems-perspective and understand the implications of changing the traditional perspective.

description:
If one wants to design effective (transport) systems, one needs to understand the behavior of -future- users of these systems, e.g. the market share of a new public transport service. If one wants to design effective (transport) policies, one needs to know how people will respond to these policies, e.g. impact of a tax incentive on electric vehicle sales. This course sets out to provide students with in-depth knowledge and hands-on experience with behavioral theories, mathematical models, and statistical methods, and data collection methods that have proved very effective in understanding and predicting human choice behavior.

Importantly, this course takes a quantitative (i.e., mathematical and statistical) perspective on choice behavior; this is quite different from the usual perspective in behavioral science courses, which tends to be more qualitative. More specifically, we formalize behavioral theories into mathematical models, which we then estimate on empirical datasets using cutting-edge statistical methods. In combination, the estimated econometric 'choice models' support rigorous analysis and forecasts of quantitative phenomena, thereby playing a crucial role in private and public sector policy development.

The theories, models, and methods that are taught in this course are applicable -and have been used- throughout a wide variety of domains, including but not limited to Transportation, Health, Marketing, Environment and Energy, and Political sciences. As such, our course optimally prepares students for a wide range of (quantitative, empirical) topics for their graduation projects.

The course will cover both canonical (and Nobel Prize-winning) methods, which are grounded in theories of choice behavior, as well as more recently proposed methods which are based on machine learning.
learning_objectives:
Students will acquire in-depth knowledge concerning the below-mentioned theories, models, and methods, as well as the skills to use them in their research. Finally, they will acquire an understanding of the usefulness and limitations of these theories, models, and methods; and an understanding of how they can and should be used in combination.

Knowledge transfer will take the form of a series of lectures, whereas skills will be (further) developed in tailor-made computer exercises (a.k.a. lab sessions). Specifically, during the computer exercises, students will learn how to design a statistically optimal choice experiment, and how to analyze data obtained from such experiments. In addition, they will learn how to interpret the outcomes of such analyses and how to use them to evaluate and design policies.

- Choice behavior modeling (van Cranenburgh)

o Discrete choice theory and the Logit model

o Mixed Logit models

o Machine learning approaches for discrete choice analysis

- Stated Choice data collection methods (Molin)

o Data-collection paradigms

o Stated choice experiments

o Efficient design approaches.

course_name: Mixed Research Methods for Multi-actor Systems
description:
The course Mixed Research Methods for Multi-Actor Systems will teach you how to design and perform research. In this course, you will learn how to research a multi-actor system using a mixed-methods research methodology that combines qualitative and quantitative approaches.

The design of multi-actor systems requires an in-depth understanding of the way technologies and innovations are both shaped and received by public and private actors. This requires insight in both the institutional context and the preference and behaviour of involved actors. A mixed-methods research design could facilitate getting this understanding, because the combination of qualitative and quantitative methods ensures that the advantages of each approach are exploited while compensating their disadvantages.

In small groups you will execute all steps of a research project in the controlled environment of the classroom. The course focusses on the choices that you need to make as a researcher throughout the research process, from research design to interpretation of results. We will go through all steps of the inductive research cycle, from problem definition and research design to reporting. We therefore 'simulate' the environment in which empirical data will be collected.

During the course, you will learn how to apply this in a mixed-research methods study combining two selected research methods: the Case Study and Gaming Research. By using these methods and by practicing with several data collection instruments that are key to this type of research (e.g. interviews, surveys, document analysis), you will learn when and how to apply these tools. After following this course, you will understand how both methods as part of a mixed-methods research design can greatly strengthen findings and thus, ultimately, the design of multi-actor systems.
learning_objectives:
After following this course you should be able to:

1. Appraise the differences between different qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods research designs

2. Develop and justify a mixed method approach that fits your research problem, , including suitable research questions

3. Design, execute and interpret gaming research, using a given game

4. Design, execute and interpret case study research to analyse a practical situation

5. Evaluate and integrate the findings from both research approaches

7. Reflect on the (mixed-methods) research approach.

6. Write a research paper

description:
In our highly connected world, networks exist in a multitude of contexts and domains, for example, in infrastructure, supply chains, transport, information, and social networks. These are socio-technical systems that consist of a large number of components and actors organized into a network. Analysing and managing such systems is a complex endeavour.

This course provides an introduction to the analysis of networked systems and the design of interventions that aim to improve their efficiency. The analysis is based on graph theory, which studies structural network properties. Topics covered include, amongst other material, the following:

- Network metrics

- Social networks

- Formation and evolution of networks

- Complex networks

- Optimal trees

- Community detection

- Example cases from critical infrastructures and epidemic
learning_objectives:
Networked systems often have a high degree of complexity, both in terms of structure and in terms of their social and institutional environment. In this course, we aim to provide you with theoretical knowledge and practical skills that enable you to reason about networked systems and design mechanisms for improving their efficiency.

After taking the module the student will be able to:

Analyze structural properties of networked systems using graph theory.

Apply a range of tools (Gephi, various Python libraries) for analysis of networked systems.

Design a new mechanism that can be used as a basis for interventions in networked systems.

description: This module provides students with an in-depth overview of the state of the art in a research challenge related to socio-technical systems design, by conducting and reporting a structured literature review. In addition, workshops are provided in which issues of scientific integrity are addressed. The module can inspire students in selecting electives and their topic of the master thesis project in the second year of the CoSEM programme, in relation to the research themes at the TPM Faculty. The students are supervised in small groups by a research theme leader based on their preferences for a research theme.

course_name: Engineering Optimisation and Integrating Renewables in Electricity Markets
description: This course is an introduction to mathematical optimisation modelling applied to diverse problems in planning and operating energy systems, in particular energy systems with a high share of variable (weather-dependent) wind and solar generation. We will go from a solid theoretical grounding in formulating different kinds of optimisation problems, to practical strategies to solve them under real-world conditions. To do so, we will formulate problems in Python using the Pyomo optimisation package.
learning_objectives:
After completing the course, you should be able to:

- LO1: Explain the challenges in planning and operating renewable energy systems and the role of mathematical optimisation in addressing these challenges

- LO2: Formulate linear, mixed-integer, and non-linear optimisation problems

- LO3: Apply different methods to deal with parametric uncertainty in optimisation

- LO4: Determine and justify the choice of an optimisation approach to formulate an energy system decision problem

- LO5: Formulate and solve optimisation problems using Python

course_name: Electricity and Gas: Market Design and Policy Issues
description:
Electricity market design

Electricity market economics; investment theory

Capacity mechanisms

Energy network regulation

Electricity distribution network congestion management

Transmission network congestion management

North Sea energy system

Natural gas and hydrogen market design

ETS: market design, development towards a zero-carbon system (negative emissions etc.)

Long-term market design, current policy dilemmas

Electricity market simulation game.

Power market modeling exercise.
learning_objectives: At the end of this course, students should be able to analyze energy policy issues from a technical, economic, and institutional perspective, to make informed choices regarding market design and policy options and to develop improvements to these options. In this course, the students' technical, economic and policy making skills are applied to the complex reality of regulation and market design in electricity and gas/hydrogen sectors.

description:
The course challenges students to tackle an integrated energy system design problem through a modelling project. Students must envision a creative integrated energy system design problem. Hence, they evaluate the expected performance of one or more promising system designs for the defined problem.

The design challenge is complex and requires students to: take into account dynamics on the short and long term; tap into relevant knowledge on technological developments; consider various parts of the value chain, in terms of energy, mass, financial and information flows; and address the multi-actor and multi-level complexities.

Students must perform the above analyses with a set of quantitative modelling tools made available for this course, some used in earlier courses in the Energy Track, some developed by research institutes and companies, and others used in ongoing academic research at the faculty.
learning_objectives:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

Conceptualise key processes that affect the performance of an integrated energy system and their interactions

Develop a multi-model strategy for the design of integrated energy systems

Apply multi-models to generate quantitative results on system design options

Discuss the design space of integrated energy systems in light of uncertainty

Reflect on aspects that lie outside the design space

description:
This module addresses the changing technological and societal characteristics of future energy systems.

Contemporary energy systems are confronted with technical and socio-economic developments, such as the climate crisis, renewable technologies, ICT-based control innovations, energy scarcity and environmental concerns. These changes will affect operational roles and responsibilities, market structures and actors' interests, and business models for energy services. Moreover, they may require new forms of governance to ensure reliable operations that meet socio-economic performance criteria. The course discusses the technical and socio-economic aspects of future energy systems, dealing with issues like the integration of new forms of distributive solar PV or large-scale off-shore wind energy into existing networks, various forms of sustainable energy sources, alternative energy carriers, storage methods, and the dynamics of transition processes.
learning_objectives:
At the end of this module the students know:

- Which technical and societal developments can be expected in the energy sector.

- How new energy technologies and societal developments may reshape operational roles and responsibilities, energy markets and business models, and governance arrangements.

- How to compare and analyze future energy systems, develop plausible transition paths towards them, and estimate the potential of new energy technologies within various scenarios.

At the end of this module the students can:

- Formulate descriptions of the technical and societal characteristics of future energy systems.

- Make a conceptual design of an energy system, given certain demands.

- Formulate a balanced advice on issues in the energy sector.

description:
More and more data is available using various sources like databases, social media or the Internet of Things (IoT). Information sharing requires the integration of these systems. The ability to execute and process data is a key capability required by public and private organizations. The large variety of heterogeneous data, applications and business processes results in a complex and fragmented landscape that need to be dealt with when architecting and engineering new systems. Path dependencies and legacy block the easy integration, whereas at the same time new technologies appear that need to be integrated in the complex systems landscape.

The purpose of this course is to teach the architectural design of innovative and large-scale ICT infrastructures and services in the light of the challenges imposed by the requirements from the system's physical, economic and social environment. Emphasis will be put on the concepts and role of ICT-architecture and modelling in order to properly design ICT solutions within a multi-actor context. For this purpose application and data integration technologies and information and system quality theories will be addressed.
learning_objectives:
-The student is familiar with the state-of-the-art knowledge of ICT-architecting, design and governance within the field of large-scale ICT-systems within a multi-actor context

-The student is able to describe basic concepts related to architecting and designing large and complex ICT-infrastructures and service systems within a multi-actor context.

-The student should master architecture theories, methods and tools with the ability to combine and switch between them when dealing with complex ICT-problems.

-The student is able to structure and analyze problems and identify dilemmas arising during the design process with regard to designing large ICT-systems within a multi-actor context.

-The student is able to apply system engineering and architecture-based approaches, methods and tools to deal with problems with regard to designing large ICT-systems.

-The student is able to report about the use of architectural concepts, methods and tools for translating business needs into ICT-designs within constellation of public and private actors.

description:
AI, Internet-of-Things, Mobile apps, Cloud Edge computing are enabling a range of new ICT services. Since these services are typically offered in ecosystems of interdependent actors, designing services that add value for users as well as ecosystem stakeholders is challenging.

In this course, you learn how to design practical ICT services and develop a valorization plan. The course contains two main parts. In the first part, it is about designing innovative services that meet the needs of users. You will design service mockups and interview users to test your ideas. In the second part, it is about bringing that service idea to reality. You will design a valorization plan that specifies how to deal with external technologies, stakeholders and revenues.

The course is practical and hands-on: you will create, test and plan your service ideas. At the same time, you will learn how to support design choices using relevant kernel and design theories.
learning_objectives:
After the course, you are able to:

- Analyze practical ICT services by applying concepts of design science research, action design research, agile development and service engineering

- Evaluate practical requirements and make informed choices on supporting technologies and platforms, with specific attention to autonomous driving, healthcare IoT, AI, XR, and edge computing technologies

- Evaluate an ICT-enabled service concept through semi-structured interviews

- Design and illustrate a value-added service concept driven by ICT

- Design a valorization plan that explicitly covers how and when to involve external stakeholders in a design process and integrate the ICT service with value network

description:
In recent years data has become the fuel of most digitalized organizations. Data Analytics is a powerful tool to observe, predict, diagnose issues within the organization and inform decision-making to solve these issues. It also helps explore, identify opportunities and assist in improving organizational processes.

But 'with great power comes great responsibility'. Data is seldom objective. It often represents a biased view of the world. When we base our observations and decisions upon this data, we need to be aware of this bias to avoid undesirable impacts. Besides, the way we frame, interpret, and act upon data analytics results can have negative externalities. A responsible data analytics project should account for and mitigate these harmful impacts and externalities.

In this course, you will master important tools and techniques used in data analysis projects with a particular focus on the data scientist competencies. Data science can be defined as the computational skills of extracting meaningful insights from raw data and then effectively communicating those insights to generate value. You will apply data science tools and methods to answer real-life questions. You learn how to select data, preprocess data, and analyze and interpret results using basic statistics and machine learning techniques implemented in Python.

You will be invited to think critically about the field of Data Analytics and Machin Learning and understand the potential harmful externalities of the tools you are using in this course. You also will practice methods to identify and mitigate some of these externalities.
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course, you will be able to:

LO1 Explain different roles and steps involved in a responsible data analytics project.

LO2 Select the adequate data science tools and methods to address a real-life sociotechnical problem.

LO3 Interpret the output of a data analytics project.

LO4 Implement scripts (collecting, cleaning, and preprocessing data) and models (statistical and basic ML) in python to carry out a data analytics project.

LO5 Implement fairness measures to identify and mitigate harmful societal and ethical externalities of data analytics (bias, inclusiveness, framing results, designing models, etc.)

description:
Digital platforms offer innovative ways to organize business and social processes. The rise of digital platforms is transforming entire industries (such as marketplaces for data sharing, Airbnb in the hospitality industry, and Uber in the personal transport industry). This leads to new and potentially disruptive business models. But these platforms also influence social processes, such as the way we interact with businesses and peers.

In this module, we explore the design variables of digital platforms from a designer's perspective: if you were to develop a new digital platform, which aspects/elements would you need to decide upon for this type of highly dynamic sociotechnical complex systems throughout their life cycle?

A tentative list of aspects that we explore are: the technical architecture of the platform; (distributed) platform control and governance; data platforms; the ecosystem and business models; generativity and openness of platforms; data spaces(what they are, what exists today, and why data sharing matters); joining data spaces (connectors, taxonomies/ontologies, interoperability standards, and onboarding challenges); motivations and the role of regulatory bodies; tools for data sovereignty and usage control; access control and data-sharing policies (e.g., ABAC) with context-aware decision-making; and open issues in data spaces. The bottom line is: how to develop an integrated platform design that takes these aspects into account?”
learning_objectives:
After taking this module, the student should be able to

develop an analytical framework for conducting analyses of digital platforms, using academic literature in the field of platform design  (Part 1)

formulate technical design principles to develop a digital platform architecture and enablers (e.g., access control technologies, identity management); (Part 1 and 2)

identify and evaluate the mechanisms that are used in platform design (e.g., openness, control, governance) (Part 1)

(re-)design a business model (including governance) and technical architecture for a digital platform and enablers, taking into account the context of a specific domain (Part 1: platform; Part 2: enablers)

evaluate the required data flows and sources for a given digital platform (Part 2)

recommend technological enablers for a digital platform in a data spaces context (Part 2)

course_name: Advanced Evaluation Methods for Transport Policy Decision-making
description: Transport policies are almost always controversial. Several methods are applied worldwide to support decision-making in transport. Nowadays, societal cost-benefit analysis (CBA) is the most prominent and well-known transport policy appraisal methods. In this course you will learn about the newest scientific developments in these appraisal methods. Additionally, you will learn about new appraisal methods such as Participatory Value Evaluation.
learning_objectives:
Describe and explain traditional evaluation methods (e.g. CBA) and non-traditional evaluation methods such as PVE.

Apply a CBA and a PVE

Explain and understand the pros, cons and ethical critiques of different evaluation methods for different evaluation circumstances

Analyse the pros and cons of applying various evaluation methods for the assessment of a specific case study.

Argue why an (combination of) evaluation methods is most applicable for a policy maker to deploy.

Provide recommendations to a policy maker about further research and how to use results of the evaluation method that you suggested.

Write a coherent academic essay in which arguments are underpinned with academic literature.

description:
In this course students learn how to perform travel behaviour research and how to translate the findings from such research into recommendations for transport policy design.

The students will acquire knowledge about six modelling paradigms in travel behaviour research, namely the econometric, psychological, geographical, biographical, marketing and sociological paradigm. The strengths and weaknesses of each paradigm will be discussed. In addition, three state-of-the-art methods to analyse travel behaviour (structural equation models, latent class choice models and latent class clusters models) will be treated. These methods figure prominently within the six modelling paradigms. For each method there will be a group assignment (so 3 in total). These group assignments will count for 50% of the grade.
learning_objectives:
After this course the students will be able:

(1) to carry out travel behavior research using three state-of-the-art statistical methods, namely structural equation modeling, latent class cluster analysis and latent class choice models.

(2) to translate the study findings to recommendations for transport policy design.

course_name: Analysis and Design of Freight and Logistic Systems
description:
- Global and local megatrends in freight transportation

- Recap of logistics and freight transport policy

- Introduction to freight transport demand modelling

- Design of multimodal freight networks including terminals

- Lectures on theory and a practical modelling assignment

- External speakers: Panteia and Signifiance on freight models in practice
learning_objectives:
At the end of the course, the student can:

- Reproduce and explain the analysis and design framework for the freight transport system, including its background in supply chain management (demand), basic design elements (network, policy) and related quantitative models.

- Select and combine relevant parts of this framework for various freight transport analysis and design problems.

- Provide functional and mathematical specification of a freight transport demand and network design model.

- Implement and apply an empirical freight demand and supply model for a practical freight network design problem.

description:
The transport and logistics systems are continuously changing due to the introduction innovative concepts in vehicles, infrastructure, and services. Examples range from the introduction of the car, to e-bikes or fat bikes, UAVs, high speed train (vehicles), Uber, GPS tracking, satellite navigation, or crowd monitoring and AI (services), to charging facilities for electric driving (infrastructure). But many innovations fail and are never adopted despite being promising. Others have undesired consequences that may undermine the resilience of the (transport) system or create unwanted cascading effects into other systems or services.

Therefore, policy-makers, investors, start-ups and transport providers need to understand the chances for success and the implications of the innovations they pursue.
learning_objectives:
By the end of the course, you should be able to:

LO1: explain the main frameworks that describe the impact of innovations.

LO2: analyse the main pathways that link transport and logistics innovations, and their societal impacts within the system (e.g., accessibility, safety, and environment).

LO3: analyse the success and failure factors of candidate transport and logistic innovations using a combination of frameworks from the literature.

LO4: examine the role of resilience capabilities of candidate transport and logistics innovations in reducing effects of unanticipated events.

LO5: develop a conceptual model that illustrates the impacts of a candidate transport and logistics innovation.

course_name: Systems Science for Health and Care
description:
In this course, students will explore the fundamentals of health systems science, learning how to analyse and assess challenges in health & care by applying a systems perspective and systems science methods.

Students will begin by identifying the environmental, social, and technical components of health systems, examining the macro-, meso-, and microsystem perspectives, and practicing habits of a systems thinker within the health & care context. Key topics include the drivers of health systems, their key actors, organizational and regulatory frameworks, and the role of the (built) environment and infrastructure. The course also addresses the interactions between these system elements and their collective impact on health outcomes.

Students will be introduced to systems science methods and their application in health & care, such as descriptive, normative, and prescriptive modelling approaches. The course includes hands-on exercises where students will engage in small, controlled modelling practices using select machine learning algorithms and game theory concepts. These exercises will help students understand how these methods can inform decision-making in health & care systems. Healthcare-specific methods like epidemiology and evidence-based principles will also be taught, equipping students with the knowledge foundation necessary to address challenges in this domain.

As part of the course, students will work in small groups on a given health & care challenge. Through problem-structuring approaches, stakeholder interviews, and document analysis, they will apply systems methods to analyse the problem, propose evidence-based solutions, and reflect on the engagement of stakeholders for co-design and future adoption. Practical exercises will include working with existing quantitative and qualitative data to address the specific challenge.

By the end of the course, students will understand what “health systems science” entails, including the constituents, dynamics, and complexity of health systems, and be equipped with the tools to design interventions for this domain.

Topics covered are:

-       Global and National Health & Care challenges and threats

-       How systems thinking and systems science methods can be utilized to solve systems challenges in health & care.

-       Drivers in the Health & Care domain including the key actors, regulations, (built) environment and (financial) infrastructure

-       Safety in health care (pathways to harm in health & care and how systems methods and engineering can reduce harm through health care)

-       Health methods: Epidemiology, and knowledge fundament including the principles of ‘evidence-based’ approaches in medicine and healthcare research.

-       Systems methods as applied in Health & Care, specifically:

o   Evolutionary Game Theory to Understand and Target Evolving Diseases

o    Machine learning principles for clinical and organizational decision-support systems, with hands-on practice using select algorithms and working with provided datasets to model and analyse specific health & care scenarios.
learning_objectives:
LO1: Explain the necessity of systems thinking and systems science in addressing challenges and threats in the Health & Care domain.

LO2: Examine how key actors, organization and regulations, infrastructure and (built) environment impact the performance of health & care systems at micro-, meso-, and macro- levels.

LO3: Demonstrate basic competency in implementing and interpreting small-scale models using machine learning and game theory, evaluating their relevance and limitations in solving health & care challenges.

LO4: Assess, through application-exercises, the opportunities and limitations of healthcare - and systems science methods to address complex health & care challenges

LO5: Apply a systems science method to investigate a health & care challenge, evaluate potential interventions, and construct evidence-based solutions tailored to address its complexities.

description:
In this course, we examine when and why a systems perspective, along with systems science methods and successive design of innovations for health and disease, can contribute to improving individual health & well-being. In the theoretical part we will explain how the current standard-of-care approaches in health care evolved (knowledge base), identify its strengths and shortcomings, and explore where and how a systems approach can address specific limitations. We explore methods and technologies that enable personalized, patient-centered, value-driven, and safe care. Medical decision-making, on both diagnosis and treatment, is a key element in care and depends on understanding disease (mechanism), understanding the context, and seeing options for (human-centered) interventions. Both in the diagnostic trajectory as in designing or choosing treatment options, decision support systems can be of significant help and constitutes a key element of this course. The ethics of health technologies and the potential impact of integrating such solutions in care delivery on persons or society are discussed as an integral part of the innovation process. In the project part, we practice designing interventions for individual health and well-being, by taking a systems perspective on disease dynamics and/or finding novel intervention opportunities. These can be diagnostic tools, novel treatment strategies or technologies such as decision tools. Teachings from the theoretical part will be integrated into the project where applicable.

Topics covered are:

-        Key aspects of quality of care, including safety of care, concepts of personalised and patient-centered care, and (shared) decision-making.

-        The relevance of medical and societal paradigms on health, well-being and disease in finding solutions for what can be considered ‘good care’.

-        Knowledge base in health care, including research (methods) in medicine, with consideration of the ethics of (developing) health technology, clinical research and patient care.

-        Understanding and modelling disease as a complex evolving dynamic system between an agent (cause(s) of disease), host (patient) and treatment. This concept, and its implications in the context of potential systems-based health interventions is explained using a small variety of use cases including oncology, infectious disease and neurological disorders.

-        Design interventions that contribute to individual health & well-being
learning_objectives:
After following this course, you are able to:

LO1: Discuss key elements of personalised, patient-centered and safe care

LO2: Critically evaluate the knowledge base of health care and medical research, and the ethics of medical research and (technological) health interventions

LO3: Examine what role systems science-based approaches (can) have in improving individual patient care in the context of clinical decision-making on diagnosis and treatment

LO4: Analyse the context and ethical aspects of health technologies designed for individual health and well-being.

LO5: Design an intervention to improve individual health & well-being in a responsible manner.

course_name: Innovation and transitions in healthcare systems
description:
Health(care) systems globally aspire towards the same goals: to provide effective, safe, patient-centered, equitable care, which is sustainable for the future. Healthcare faces multiple challenges, including resource scarcity and rising costs, the problem of unsafe care, and significant circularity concerns through its energy consumption and waste production. How can we facilitate the transition towards a healthcare system that is able to rise to these challenges and deliver good quality care for all?

To answer these questions, we look at the meso-level of health systems: focusing on healthcare provision, quality, assessment, decision-making and financing. You’ll learn what it takes to create change/transition in healthcare systems, and how analytical techniques (such as economic evaluation or MCDM) can help inform and evaluate such changes.

Topics covered are: 

Drivers in health & care and the identification of healthcare actors, regulations and infrastructure in any country or domain within healthcare.

The dimensions of quality of care (is care safe, effective, efficient, timely, patient-centred and equitable) and how quality of care can be assessed. An emphasis is put organisational aspects of quality and safety in healthcare systems and how to create interventions for improvement. 

Methods used in daily practice to assess and evaluate healthcare system performance and the value of alternative interventions / policies in healthcare systems, such as those used in Health Technology Assessment. 

The impact of technology and technological advances in healthcare systems, and the multi-faceted approaches needed for the introduction of such technologies (optimising the balance between safety, efficiency, effectiveness, patient-centredness, and future sustainability) including methods such as Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM). 

The domain specific challenges in adoption and implementation and methods to overcome these, including implementation science, transdisciplinary approaches, and participatory and engagement research for health & care. 

Digital information systems including methods to improve security and accessibility of health data for personal and institutional use, and as part of research, quality assessment and improvement.  

Financing of (parts of the) healthcare system, and the impact of financial incentives on outcomes such as accessibility, quality and costs of care.
learning_objectives:
After following this course, you are able to: 

LO1: Appraise healthcare systems and its constituents, including actors, regulations and (built) environment, as a sociotechnical dynamic system using systems science methods 

LO2: Evaluate the knowledge-fundament of healthcare research, including the principles of health technology assessment (HTA), quality improvement (QI) and implementation science 

LO3: Assess mechanisms of harm to patients due to the design and functioning of healthcare systems (blunt-end) and institutional process designs (sharp-end), to propose interventions to improve 

LO4: Evaluate healthcare system performance, such as in accessibility, affordability, resilience and sustainability, applying systems science methods and propose (technological) interventions to its support or improvement 

LO5: Explore the nexus between health and non-health systems with respect to the relevance for logistics and resource management in healthcare

description:
In this course, students will learn how our health and healthcare systems are shaped by broader sociotechnical structures, and how this complexity can be analysed to improve the design of effective interventions. This includes examining the nexus between non-health systems that affect our health (e.g. the energy, transportation, food, and education systems), with an emphasis on the health challenges, risks and threats these systems pose to society, but also the opportunities that arise due to the interrelatedness between other systems and health. We draw on concepts such as the social determinants of health (SDH), systems safety, and public health. The challenges encompass the geopolitical complexities at the intersection of healthcare and other critical systems, influencing the manufacturing of medicines, global vaccine distribution, allocation of hospital resources, and the mobility of skilled professionals. At the same time, we highlight how these interconnected systems—such as food, transportation, economic, and educational policies—also present opportunities to advance public health. This course emphasizes the importance of understanding how health systems are shaped by—and interact with—a wide range of societal, economic, environmental, and infrastructural forces. We appraise the role of national and international governments, assess their decision-making processes and enhance the design of solutions, interventions and/or policies to improve health for all.  

 

Topics covered include: 

• The meaning of Global Health, One Health and Planetary Health and what governance strategies are in place to enable good health for all.

• Values and disparities, discussing health inequities and inequalities, health literacy, and the distribution of care and resources globally

• Application of epidemiological analysis to analyse environmental, social and economic determinants of health.

• Application of systems analyses to analyse interdependencies between systems, and analysing potential solutions using simulation modelling techniques (depending on students’ backgrounds)
learning_objectives:
After following this course, you will be able to:  

LO1: Analyse how people’s health and the health(care) systems are influenced by environmental and social determinants of health

LO2: Apply systems science methods for addressing societal health challenges and threats

LO3: Design interventions on a national and international level for societal health challenges and threats.

After concluding this course the student should be able to develop a master thesis research proposal, that demonstrates:

societal relevance

academic relevance based on a structured literature review

the link between the research proposal and the MSc program in which it is conducted;

a well-formulated main research question and choice of research approach

a structured list of sub questions, each linked with research methods, data requirements and data analysis tools

a research flow diagram, a feasible time schedule and a reference list that contains complete bibliographic details

a feasible research planning, including a conscious and justifiable choice of research methods, a research flow diagram and an accompanying, feasible time schedule

In addition, the student should be able to:

do serious and high quality peer reviewing

provide solid argumentation for all choices made in the master thesis research proposal

description:
Summary

The Master's Thesis Project covers a period of 21 weeks and consists of an individual academic research project.

Summary

The simulation game design project offers conceptual insights as well as hands on experience with simulation-gaming (SG). SG is an established field of practice with proven value for instance in the field of spatial and urban planning, ecology, engineering and design, public administration, business management, learning, research and consultancy. The staggering growth and success of the video gaming industry has triggered the interest in simulation games - from paper based games to video games for learning and policy making - even more. Besides creativity and enthusiasm, there are no entry requirements. In this course, students acquire advanced knowledge in, and experience with, designing simulation games for serious use, i.e. for policy- and decision support, organization and management and professional learning.
learning_objectives:
After completion of this course the student will have acquired knowledge and insights about:

The history, backgrounds, key-concepts, formats and applications of simulation games.

After completion of this course the student will be able to:

1. Design a (prototype) of a simulation game to be used for learning, research or intervention

2. Apply a game design cycle (or systematic design steps)

3. Define, conceptualize and construct the various game components

4. Facilitate simple simulation games

Give the participant theoretical and practical insight and application skills into supply chain management-associated theories and their applications, through:

Understanding the functioning of business logistics sub-systems and their interrelations with other subsystems (marketing, sales, R&D, production, finance).

Decomposing the logistics function in its basic functionalities and analyze and optimize them.

Judging a wide variety of the material, information, and money flows within and between companies.

Positioning supply chain management in the perspective of the functioning of companies.

Formulate, comment, and judge the criteria and constraints of how companies can develop and maintain their position as an adequate supply chain member.

Structure, analyze, and develop skills to find improvements in the strategic position of enterprises using reference models, and other modeling techniques.

Design and develop supply chain frameworks to facilitate the analyses of supply chains.

Have a thorough insight into the differences and commonalities between supply chains of consumables and durable products.

Develop an analytic approach to find requirements for supply chain re-design.

Understand the supply chain as a ‘fulfillment structure’  for the collaboration between companies for new business ventures to cope with problems and opportunities.

Understand the potential of Logistics and Supply Chain Innovations for continuous improvement of businesses.

Suggested and developed supply chain (re)design directions for the future of companies as supply chain partners.

description:
Summary

Gaming gives students and company representatives the opportunity to learn and participate in supply chain problems in an informal way. It helps to see each others positions and discuss a wide range of issues during game play or afterwards in facilitates sessions. Topics for games that student will play, analyze, design and develop are based on setting and trade-off that occur in supply chains and where companies have to make appropriate decisions (see below in italic).

Supply chain management is about the exchange of product, information and money between companies that are part of a supply chains or demand/supply-network. Supply chain management contributes to the competitive strength of companies and supply chains in the market place. The supply chain management co-ordinates and controls operational business value adding processes in and between companies. For a large extent supply chain management determines the position of companies in the supply chain and marketplace and the flexibility of companies to respond to market changes and determines the efficiency of the internal processes within companies, as well as the inter-company processes. Logistical and supply chain decision-making frequently relates to situations in which conflicting wishes and desires from various parts of organizations have to be brought together cohesively. Gaining insight into the performance indicators of a company, its logistical costs, customer expectations and the opportunities to improve these aspects is of vital importance for the survivability of companies.

Based on earlier gained knowledge (see text in italic) and additional required domain related knowledge groups will during sequential lectures design and develop a realistic and playable serious supply chain game/session (board game, card game, role playing game etc) for a (hypothetical) client.
learning_objectives:
This course gives students knowledge and understanding in theoretical and practical issues concerning the design, development and execution of supply chain serious gaming sessions (game and facilitation). The fundamentals of game design and its application area supply chain analysis and management will discussed and practiced. Important and problematic logistics and supply chain issues and opportunities for innovations to improve the supply chain from a multi-stakeholder and multi-perspective will be explained and related to game sessions design alternatives.

Upon completion of this course the student should be able to:

Elaborate on how companies can develop and maintain their position as an adequate supply chain member.

Understand important logistics and supply chain trade-offs that are suitable to incorporate in supply chain games.

Suggested and develop supply chain (re)design directions for the future of the companies in a supply chain that need awareness between supply chain partners that can be facilitated by means of game sessions.

Demonstrate that they can decompose logistics and supply chain activities in meaningful game elements.

Understand the fundamentals of strategic game design approaches and elaborate on reality, meaning and play aspects and their relationships.

Develop a practical descriptive and prescriptive design method for game session design.

Design, development a functional supply chain game session and be able to demonstrate and assess its play-ability.

description: A transition to renewable energy is needed for our climate and welfare. In this course, you will learn how to assess the potential for energy reduction and the potential of renewable energy sources like hydropower, wind, solar, biomass, geothermal and other environmental sources of heat. The content is an introduction to the tracks in the Sustainable Energy Technology Masters that are organized around the energy carriers heat and electricity. You will be introduced to assessing the energy balance of a country or region and its importance to understand the opportunities and challenges for the transition to renewable energy. The basic principles of energy transition models will be discussed. The physical and chemical principles that determine the impact of our energy consumption on the earth's climate are briefly discussed, as well. This course gives an overview of the most important renewable energy sources, the challenges to incorporate those in power supply, heating and cooling systems and the need for storage. You'll learn how to integrate sources, storage and transportation of (thermal) energy in an energy system, and take an engineering approach to look for solutions and design a 100% sustainable energy system.
learning_objectives:
Using physical principles you will be able to:

quantify, compare and evaluate the use of energy in transport, building, heating/cooling and manufacturing

quantify, compare and evaluate the generation of Renewable Energy: how much can you generate from all the different sources? (Hydropower, Wind Energy, Solar Energy, Biomass, Tidal Energy, Wave Energy, geothermal, environmental sources of heat)

quantify, compare and evaluate the power density and energy density of various storage technologies

You will be able to analyse:

large scale energy infrastructure using energy balances and identify corresponding climate effects of such energy infrastructure.

the capacity factor, system efficiency, energy pay back time, circularity aspects of energy systems.

In addition, after this course you will be able to make basic quantification an evaluation of the impact of planet earth's albedo, radiative forcing, greenhouse gas emissions on the climate of the planet (temperature, sea levels).

You will be able to recognize, quantify and evaluate the technological principles and challenges for various Renewable Energy technologies

After this course you will be able to identify and evaluate feasible options for a 100% renewable energy system.
faculty: Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science

course_name: Economics and Regulation of Sustainable Energy Systems
description:
This course is a general introduction to energy economics. In this course, you learn the essentials of how actors in the energy system make economic decisions, when markets work well and when they may fail, and what options the government has to remedy market failures. Specifically, the following topics are addressed:

Introduction to energy (electricity) markets: perfect competition; oligopoly

Rational (and irrational) market behaviour; ABM ?

Investment decision making; LCOE

Opportunity costing / discounting; NPV; IRR; discount rate

Markets, (perfect) competition and market failure (esp. externalities en lock-in)

Private costs, external cost and social cost; empirical evidence (related to energy)

LCOE; discounting; private discount rate; IRR and NPV

Social cost-benefit analysis; social discount rate
faculty: Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science

description: This course is an introduction to mathematical optimisation modelling applied to diverse problems in planning and operating energy systems, in particular energy systems with a high share of variable (weather-dependent) wind and solar generation. We will go from a solid theoretical grounding in formulating different kinds of optimisation problems, to practical strategies to solve them under real-world conditions. To do so, we will formulate problems in Matlab using the YALMIP optimisation package.
learning_objectives:
After completing the course, you should be able to:

- LO1: Explain the challenges in planning and operating renewable energy systems and the role of mathematical optimisation in addressing these challenges

- LO2: Formulate linear, mixed-integer, and non-linear optimisation problems

- LO3: Apply different methods to deal with parametric uncertainty in optimisation

- LO4: Determine and justify the choice of an optimisation approach to formulate an energy system decision problem

- LO5: Formulate and solve optimisation problems using Matlab
faculty: Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science

description:
Intelligent Electrical Power Grids - a.k.a. Smart Grids - are the "smartified" version of our electricity infrastructure. By adding controls, communication, and other digital elements these grids are expected to be more flexible, robust, efficient, and capable in order to satisfy the requirements of the future: hosting more renewable sources, catering for an active demand side, or implementing flexible peer-to-peer energy markets.

Working with Smart Grids requires knowledge in a variety of disciplines out of electrical engineering, computer science, and mathematics. Of great importance is modeling and simulation, since Smart Grids show a level of complexity and heterogeneity that often can not be covered by analytical methods. In this course you will learn how to describe and assess a Smart Grid, mainly by using numerical tools.

You will use various modeling and simulation tools to investigate the properties of smart power grids. Each practical results in a short report. In the end, an electronic exam will be done.

This course is part of the Power track of the SET master and can also be chosen by EE master students.

Understanding of power flow is expected. Slides and exercises to check if you are up for it are provide on Brightspace.
learning_objectives:
After this course students are able to

LO1: Describe the smart functions of energy management systems ​

LO2: Deploy software-based models for steady-state and market performance analysis ​

LO3: Synthesize operational scenarios for insecurity risk identification ​

LO4: Apply data analytics and optimization for intelligent flexibility management ​

LO5: Solve operational security threats of systems (e.g. TSO-DSO, offshore/onshore systems, large/small size hubs) with different characteristics​
faculty: Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science

description:
In this course you will learn about the following aspects of biomass conversion based on thermo-chemical conversion technologies.

- Biomass Characterisation (biomass types, properties, analyses)

- Pretreatment (harvesting, size reduction, drying, torrefaction)

- Thermochemical conversion (combustion, gasification, pyrolysis and hydrothermal processing; reactor types)

- Transportation fuels / biorefinery

- Reactor Engineering (mass & mole balances, ideal reactors)

- Process design (structured design approach, economics)
learning_objectives:
During this course, the students will gain knowledge of and insight into energy conversion technologies based on biomass thermo-chemical conversion processes for a wide range of applications, such as supply of electricity, heat and fuels. They will be provided with practical problems to solve and projects to perform in this field.

By the end of this course, you should be able to:

LO1: Evaluate fuel characterization techniques based on the chemical composition of biomass.

LO2: Solve (design) problems related to the thermo-chemical conversion of biomass fuels by applying the principles of reaction kinetics, transport phenomena and idealised model reactors (well-stirred reactor and plug flow reactor) equations.

LO3: Evaluate the techno-economic feasibility of various thermochemical conversion processes using different economic indicators such as NPV, POT, and ROI.

LO4: Defend, both orally and in writing, the concepts underlying thermochemical processes.
faculty: Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science

description:
In a renewable energy future energy storage is an additional necessary means to match the supply and demand of energy.

- Week 1: Future energy generation systems, the combination of sources on a large scale.

Group work 1: program in Matlab a numerical model for energy generation, with flexible input of PV, solar heat, wind, hydro, biofuel

- Week 2: Future energy use possibilities: look into current typical use patterns of the different sectors, and look into possible changes: electrification, different sources, etc.

Group work 2: program in Matlab typical use patterns for the different sectors

- Week 3: Estimate the possibilities for 'demand response' in the different sectors and program this in Matlab. Deduce the resulting demand for short term and long term storage. Determine the demand for transport of energy and estimate possible transport losses.

Group work 3: program in Matlab the different magnitudes for demand response, short and long storage throughout the year.

- Week 4: Storage methods introduction, pumped hydro, mechanical, compressed air, deployment possibilities.

Group work 4: calculate different factors for energy density, capacity, timescale of storage. Investigate approximate efficiency.

- Week 5: Thermal storage, high T and low T. Combined heat and power possibilities.

Group work 5: Investigate energy densities, efficiencies, capacities, exergies.

- Week 6: Biomass and biofuels, future prospects for storage. Introduction to scalable chemical energy storage methods: batteries and fuels. What would electrification of the chemical industry mean.

Group work: investigate biofuel resources, calculate efficiencies and compare to solar PV and electrolysis numbers.

- Week 7: Hand in report and model. Group presentations of the model calculations (where each group has different boundary conditions). Discuss how the boundary conditions influence the outcome of the storage demand.
learning_objectives:
At the end of the lectures and group work the students should be able to:

- Reproduce and reflect on the role of storage in a renewable energy based society.

- Explain how different timescales for energy storage are relevant for the future system.

- List and explain the different storage solutions in terms of typical energy density, cost and efficiency.

- Tell about the different drivers for energy conversion including demand for storage, and demand for transport of energy.

- Reflect on the energy efficiency of intermediate storage.
faculty: Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science

description: Hydrogen is a vital element in the energy transition. While sustainable energy sources such as solar and wind plants will power the planet, this energy needs to be converted in chemical bonds to provide storage, fuel and resources to our future energy system. Hydrogen is the most simple chemical bond that can be made by (electro)chemistry. Hence, we will discuss the various (electro-)chemical ways that hydrogen can be produced and discuss the main impediments for the implementation of this technology. Once the hydrogen is produced it will need to be stored and converted. Hence, we will discuss the basics of different storage methods: as a gas, liquid, adsorbed or absorbed inside appropriate solids. Furthermore, the use of hydrogen as a fuel in several types of fuel cells will be discussed.
learning_objectives:
After this course students:

Students are able to distinguish the various sustainable methods to produce hydrogen, assess their pro/cons and describe their operation in thermodynamic terms.

Students have a basic understanding of the physical nature of hydrogen and are able to assess the various ways of storing it.

Students have a basic understanding of various fuel cell technologies and are able to assess their efficiency and describe their operation in thermodynamic terms.
faculty: Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science

Compare thermochemical and electrochemical conversion processes and their current technology readiness levels
