The project will require students to analyze financial feasibility, market potential, ethical considerations, safety risks, and the broader economic impact of the innovation.

Through research, case studies, and expert feedback, students will learn to navigate the complexities of innovation-driven decision-making in a corporate environment. The final deliverable—a professional Innovation Plan—will outline a strategic roadmap for the company’s innovation, including financial projections, risk assessments, marketing strategies, and other recommendations. This course emphasizes collaborative problem-solving, critical thinking, and strategic decision-making, preparing students for careers at the intersection of business and engineering.
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course, you will be able to:

LO1: Apply fundamental concepts of innovation management, finance, marketing, ethics, and management of risk and safety to evaluate business innovation challenges.

LO2: Integrate innovation management, finance, marketing, ethics, and management of risk and safety perspectives to evaluate business innovation challenges.

LO3: Collaborate in multidisciplinary teams to develop and communicate a comprehensive innovation plan.

description: In this course, you will ideate, prototype and validate your solution concept. We will follow the book "Testing Business Ideas: Field Guide for Rapid Experimentation by Alexander Osterwalder and David J Bland". We will also make use of various methods, tools and techniques to aid in your product/service development (such as Assumptions Table, Morphological Analysis, Risk Analysis etc.). In addition, this course will also have guest lectures to bring more insight into product design and prototyping.
learning_objectives:
- To conduct primary market research (minimum 10 interviews) with stakeholders (end-users, government employees, business owners etc.) to validate the problem faced by the customers

- Design 10 conceptual solutions as product/service ideas for the identified problem using morphological analysis

- Build a prototype of the winning concept to test with end-users in a real-world setting

- Design a validation study for the built prototype to test and receive feedback from at least 3 end-users

- Evaluate the feedback to draw reasonable conclusions on the product/service ideas

description:
This course provides an engaging, practice-oriented introduction to the fundamental principles of Business-to-Business (B2B) Marketing, specifically tailored for engineering and entrepreneurial contexts. The course Business Marketing for Engineers focuses on how technical professionals and future engineers can understand markets, customer needs, and competitive dynamics to create value through effective marketing strategies.

Through an interactive and learner-led learning approach, students are encouraged to take ownership of their learning journey by working on real-world cases, developing a strategic marketing plan, and actively participating in class discussions. Interactivity, peer learning, and application of theory to practice are central to the course philosophy.

Topics covered:

The course unfolds across five key themes, reflecting the end-to-end journey of marketing strategy from foundational concepts to future trends:

Introduction to B2B Marketing and Customer Value: Understanding marketing fundamentals, customer orientation, segmentation, and the role of value propositions in engineering-based ventures.

Marketing Strategy and Positioning: Exploring how companies craft strategic marketing approaches that align with their value creation logic, competitive environment, and innovation potential.

Customer Behavior and Go-to-Market Design: Examining customer decision-making in B2B contexts, including organizational buying behavior, sales approaches, and route-to-market strategies.

Sales, Communication, and Relationship Management: Learning how to build long-term customer relationships through effective sales strategies, communication planning, and CRM practices.

Emerging Trends in B2B Marketing: Investigating the evolving role of digital technologies, service innovation, sustainability, and ecosystems in shaping modern marketing and business models.

Each lecture combines conceptual grounding with real-world application through case discussions, activities, and student-led reflections.
learning_objectives:
After completing this course, students will be able to:

Understand the relevance and core functions of marketing in technology-based organizations.

Analyze marketing processes and identify areas for strategic improvement.

Segment markets, select customer groups, and craft value propositions tailored to their needs.

Design and evaluate marketing and sales strategies that support customer relationships and business growth.

Apply relevant marketing metrics to assess customer performance and marketing effectiveness.

Reflect on emerging developments in B2B marketing, including digital transformation, service innovation, and ecosystem thinking.

description: This course focuses on startup financing. We cover finance tools and concepts that are essential to an entrepreneur when creating a financing strategy. We go over the techniques for setting up and evaluating a financial model and cover the principles of sound financial management. We study fundraising strategy and the entrepreneurial finance industry: the sources of startup funding (e.g. Venture Capital), motivations of entrepreneurs and investors, and negotiations and contracts between them. We also explore latest developments in entrepreneurial finance (e.g. crowdfunding).

This part of the minor MedTech Based Entrepreneurship has the character of a project or internship.

During the total integration course and the bar is set high, because you always have to get the best out of yourself as an entrepreneur. The self-strengthening cooperation between students and teachers is of great importance in this regard. Self-reliance, proactive behavior and an entrepreneurial attitude contribute to the end result. The intention is that the students prepare themselves to be able to set up their own business or carry out an assignment for a start-up in the MedTech sector. You must literally and figuratively leave the campus.

Three process steps form the basis of the integration course: exploring, experimenting and implementing.

In the first quarter the emphasis is on exploring and experimenting with an eye for implementation.

During the second quarter (TBM044b) the focus shifts to experimenting and implementation, while an open and exploratory attitude remains important. It also offers the space for personal coaching and guidance.

Each group of 4 or 5 students will go through the following steps:

1. Consider multiple ideas for your own startup or client

2. Designing and developing a technological innovation

3. Developing business models

4. Testing the ideas and business models in practice (Validation with stakeholders)

5. Prepare a marketing plan

6. Describe the operational plan

7. Making a financial plan

8. Process points 3, 5, 6 and 7 into a business plan

9. Pitching the end result
learning_objectives:
The course is supported by lectures that connect to the above subjects.

At the end of this course the students are able to do the following:

1. Thinking up different business models

2. Drawing up a business plan

3. Holding a sales and technical pitch (part 2)

4. Working together as an entrepreneurial team

Beside:

+ Evaluate own work and that of fellow students

+ Critical analysis and constructive feedback

+ Critically considering alternative solutions

+ Orally presenting conclusions and discussing them

+ Argument and contribute in discussions

description:
This course is the second part of the Integration Project within the MedTech-Based Entrepreneurship minor. Building on the foundation from Part 1, you now move into experimentation and implementation. The focus is on testing, validating, and refining your MedTech startup or client project using real-world input.

You will continue working in teams to further develop your product, business model, and system fit. This phase emphasizes deeper engagement with stakeholders—gathering feedback to improve your solution and strengthen your business case. You’ll also assess how your innovation impacts patients, healthcare providers, and the broader system, while considering safety, ethical, and regulatory aspects.

There is room for personal coaching, team reflection, and applying your knowledge from across the minor (including medical design, finance, and health systems). You will revise and complete your marketing and operational plans, and develop a clear communication strategy, including visual materials for different target groups.

This phase ends with two major deliverables: a professional business plan and a set of tailored pitches that clearly explain your innovation’s value to different stakeholders.

Key outcomes of Integration Project 2:

Refine your innovation based on feedback from real stakeholders

Evaluate the impact, safety, and system fit of your solution within healthcare

Create a website/ brochure to communicate your concept to patients, hospitals, or other key users

Finalize and present a strong, professional business plan

Deliver clear and convincing sales and technical pitches, tailored to different audiences
learning_objectives:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Evaluate the feasibility, safety, and system-level impact of a MedTech innovation on patients, care providers, and the healthcare system

Apply stakeholder feedback to refine the product, business model, and implementation strategy

Revise and improve marketing and operational plans based on practical insights and real-world constraints

Create a coherent and professional business plan that integrates technical, operational, and strategic components

Design clear and targeted communication materials (e.g. website or brochure) for key stakeholders such as patients or hospitals

Deliver tailored and persuasive sales and technical pitches to different audiences

Reflect on team collaboration, coaching feedback, and personal performance to support continuous improvement

description:
To solve complex problems, argumentation skills are crucial for engineers. Not only during your studies, but also in your career, you will need to justify design choices, deliberate with (potential) clients or write project proposals and (grant) applications. You can only persuade a potential client of your brilliant design if you are able to articulate its strengths through convincing arguments

Critical thinking not only helps engineers identify and avoid pitfalls in their own work, but also enables them to recognise fallacies and weaknesses in the work of others. Therefore, in the course "Argumentation: Analysis and Reasoning", you will learn to unravel others' arguments as well as construct strong and persuasive arguments of your own.

Defending (policy) proposals in meetings, negotiations or informal settings, persuading a client of a design or advice, or defending your thesis: both during and after your studies, you should be able to present your knowledge and ideas in a convincing way.

In the course Persuasion and Debate, you will learn to apply insights from rhetoric (the skill of persuasion) in debates. We will discuss how you can use the stock issues to defend and attack propositions. Furthermore, you will learn how to structure your arguments clearly and how to present them strategically, for instance by using stylistic devices (figures of speech) or framing. Additionally, we will discuss how you can critically respond to your opponent by countering their arguments and refuting fallacies. All of this will be achieved through extensive practice in various debate formats.

Health systems worldwide face significant challenges in delivering adequate, accessible, and efficient care. In this course, students will explore the potential of Digital Health Technologies (DHTs)—including digital health apps, platforms, wearables/ smartwatches, AI-driven analytics, and conversational agents—to enhance healthcare by making it more inclusive, patient-centered and effective.

Students will examine how DHTs can empower patients in self-care, support clinical decision-making, and reduce the burden on healthcare services. However, the adoption of these technologies also raises critical ethical and social challenges, such as concerns about equity and inclusivity, patient safety, patient trust, and engagement. Without careful design, DHTs risk reinforcing disparities and facing resistance from both patients and healthcare providers.

Students will evaluate how to address these challenges, including using methods such as user-centered design, participatory methods, universal design, ethical analysis and stakeholder analysis, ensuring that diverse perspectives and ethical principles are incorporated throughout the design process of digital health applications. Through real-life case studies, students will learn about successful development of DHTs, while also highlighting key ethical and social barriers.

Students will analyze a digital health case study using a combination of guidelines for ethics in AI for healthcare, user-centered, and responsible design principles, and stakeholder analysis. Imagine you are advising a digital health start-up on navigating the ethical and social complexities of DHT development—what strategies would you recommend?

This course provides a critical perspective on the role of digital health technologies in the future of healthcare.
learning_objectives:
By the end of the course, students should be able to:

1.     Evaluate key digital health applications, such as apps and websites, AI-driven diagnostics and chatbots, and how they are used in healthcare delivery   

2.     Assess ethical and social challenges associated with digital health applications, including issues of equity, inclusivity, and trust in digital health solutions.

3.     Analyze how ethical and social considerations can be integrated into real-world digital health applications.

4.     Develop recommendations for relevant stakeholders such as app developers, policy makers, health practitioners, and patient organizations for navigating ethical and social challenges in digital health applications.

description: This course is part of the Minor Programme MedTech-Based Entrepreneurship. It merges foundational principles of medical design with advanced applications and innovations. Students explore theoretical frameworks, design methodologies, regulatory considerations, and technological integration in the development of medical products and systems. Key themes include creative problem solving, user-centered design, and the application of design methods to real-world case studies across the lifecycle of medical products.
learning_objectives:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

Understand and apply core design principles in healthcare contexts.

Identify and analyze user needs, regulatory requirements, and technology trends.

Develop prototypes addressing real-world medical challenges.

Apply iterative design processes to refine solutions based on feedback.

Communicate design concepts effectively to stakeholders.

Evaluate the feasibility and impact of innovations in clinical settings

description: A key part of the course content is understanding what the SDGs are and how they can be instrumental in reaching a more sustainable society at large. The course analyzes the genesis of the SDGs and key points in their development. One major component is examining case studies of how organizations are taking action to address the SDGs and the challenges they face. This means analyzing how these goals are being pursued and the difficulties encountered by organizations. It also involves considering existing gaps and feasible solutions to close these gaps. Students will critically appraise the efforts of specific companies, synthesizing their findings into a report and group presentation. This practical application allows students to see the SDGs in action in the corporate world. Another facet of the course is guest lectures from experts in relevant fields. Hearing diverse perspectives from professionals working on sustainable development issues helps expand students' understanding beyond theoretical concepts. The external visit/s likely provide a similar experiential learning opportunity.
learning_objectives:
Evaluate the role and importance of the SDGs by considering regional and local contexts.

Synthesize the multifaceted SDG-related problems and their interrelations given real existing situations.

Through specific case studies, compare various solutions and points of view related to SDG challenges and open questions.

description:
Course description

Accordingly, it makes a case for organisational transformation to tackle the SDG challenge through collaboration across public, private, and community organisations. Consequently, students learn the principles of organizational theory as a basis for identifying different levels of responsibility to address sustainability issues and exploring partnerships across the State, Market, and Civil Society. The course provides the theoretical basis for understanding when an organization has responsibility and when it can take responsibility to overcome these issues and their negative impact on its stakeholders and society at large.

This theoretical basis provides practical tools for matching sustainability issues, organizational responsibilities, and inter-organizational arrangements, with an emphasis on the South Holland and Dutch contexts. Hence, the course focuses on SDG challenges and inter-organizational opportunities within the economic, social, political, and environmental dimensions of development, shaping ongoing economic, societal, and environmental challenges in the region. Overall, students are expected to develop solid theoretical,  practical skills, and professional criteria to identify leverage points for roads of transformation and partnership for sustainability by identifying individual and inter-organizational responsibilities.
learning_objectives:
After taking this course, you will be able to:

·         Identify the eight organizational archetypes across the State, Market, and Civil Society Sectors

·         Identify the four levels of responsibility for sustainability according to the principles of Social Triangulation Theory

·         Interpret SDG challenges in South Holland as a problem of organizational and inter-organizational responsibility according to the principles of Social Triangulation Theory

·         Identify inter-organizational partnerships matching the distinctive characteristics of SDG challenges within the ongoing development path of South Holland.

·         Identify weaknesses of the Social Triangulation Theory to address SDG challenges in South Holland.

course_name: Project Module 1: Diagnosing Challenges and Opportunities with System Thinking
description:
SDGs challenges are typical wicked problems characterised by complexity, ambiguity, multi-framing, and diverse views. Accordingly, this challenge-based learning module teaches students to identify, develop, and take ownership of a compelling, concrete, and actionable SDG challenge, blending systems thinking with the insights from Social Triangulation Theory. It also guides them in applying tools, enabling them to contextualise their learning experience with the SDG actionable challenge grounded in complex and inter-organizational theory. SDG challenges are co-defined with partner organisations based in South Holland, including public, private, profit, and non-profit organisations. Corresponding tools are put into action for students to suggest roadmaps for transformation. As a challenge-based module, this course focuses on guiding the engagement and investigation of the SDG actionable challenge with the partner organisation (client). The process includes:

·         The co-definition of the SDG challenge and the ambition for sustainable impact with the partner organisation (client).

·         The overall characterisation of the challenge context, considering the SDG nexus approach and the perspective of long-term value linked to the regional development partner in South Holland.

·         The identification of a complex-sensitive theory of change, including the characterisation of challenge, matching the levels of organizational responsibility of involved actors, and possibilities of collaboration and partnership.

The outcomes of the course to be delivered are

·         A fresh view of the SDG challenge of the client organization as a matter of (inter) organizational responsibility across state, market, and civil society.

·         A screen of new potential partners to share responsibility in tackling the SDG challenge.

·         A system map showing how partnering drives responsibility for change in tackling the client SDG challenge.
learning_objectives:
By the end of this course, you should be able to:

·         Assume collective responsibility with peers to provide high-quality inputs to real organizations on sustainability challenges and opportunities

·         Engage with real organizations in identifying, analysing, and diagnosing actionable SDG challenges in the province of South Holland

·         Articulate insights from Social Triangulation Theory into complex-sensitive theories of change using System Dynamics

·         Synthesizing empirical facts, visions, and ideas into effective visualizations to pitch priorities and possible roadmaps for actionable change.

course_name: Sustainability In Action: Legal Frameworks for ESG&SDG's
description: We live in challenging times. The consequences of climate change, loss of biodiversity, and other problems related to sustainability are becoming increasingly visible. The call to combat those problems is getting louder, and the ambitions in this area are increasing. The European Union aims to be the first climate-neutral continent by 2050 and has set an ambitious policy for a fair and inclusive transition, a so-called just transition, attempting to enable a shift towards sustainable growth throughout different segments of society. Additionally, the UN SDGs provide a comprehensive framework aimed at addressing a broad range of interconnected global challenges. Achieving these goals requires profound legal transformations and behavioural changes from different actors, such as governments, institutions, and organizations worldwide. These changes influence multiple domains, such as environmental regulations, corporate governance structures, labour laws, and human rights protection. The legal landscape is continuously adapting to address these evolving demands, making it essential to understand how legal frameworks interact with and advance broader sustainability objectives. As sustainability becomes an integral part of regulatory and societal expectations, existing questions of how organisations are directed, how decisions are made, and how accountability is ensured are being revisited through the lens of environmental and social responsibility. This course examines the role of corporate governance and associated legal frameworks in influencing how organisations address sustainability challenges. Students will engage with foundational principles of corporate governance and the essentials of company law. The course will expand key theoretical perspectives introduced in Q1 theory courses, including agency theory and stakeholder theory, to facilitate a deeper understanding of organisational relationships and accountability. Building on this foundation, students will analyse various corporate governance structures, mechanisms, and instruments that are specifically designed to advance ESG-objectives and contribute to the realisation of the SDGs.
learning_objectives: By the end of this course, you should be able to: Understand and explain the role of corporate governance and legal frameworks in driving sustainability initiatives, including ESG and SDG implementation; Identify agency conflicts and develop strategies to mitigate them within organisations; Critically assess the shift from ‘talking’ to ‘walking’ in corporate governance and identify practical instruments that enable organisations to move from passive intentions to proactive sustainability efforts; Address and evaluate sustainable corporate governance challenges and provide advice or solutions to cases.

course_name: Project Module 2: Integrating Legal Solutions for Impact Driven Development
description: Complex issues require sophisticated and well-designed solutions. This course will focus on the creation of a partnership arrangement or policy document aimed at approaching the SDG challenge(s) in the chosen organisation. Whilst forming and drafting the arrangement/policy, the project groups will get acquainted with different topics in the sphere of law and governance. Depending on the challenges faced by the organisations, the project groups can encounter different obstacles, such as the involvement of a widespread group of stakeholders or the navigation of an opaque set of rules and regulations. Through a multifaceted approach, students will develop the (professional and theoretical) skills necessary to identify and address these complexities, ensuring a comprehensive and strategic response to the legal aspects of their organisation's sustainability challenges.
learning_objectives: By the end of this course, you should be able to: Systematically analyse the legal challenge faced by your organisation; Design a partnership arrangement or policy document in groups for your organisation to reach its SDG ambition; Understand criteria for partner selection and additional considerations to be made when selecting partners, such as power disparities and partnering principles; Identify and consider stakeholders in the creation of your partnership arrangements; Deliver a substantive presentation in groups on the partnership arrangement, including the legal aspects of the challenges faced by the organisation and a profound motivation on the choice for certain solutions/provisions within the arrangement.

course_name: Project Module 3: Sustainable Business Model and Entrepreneurship
description:
In this course, you are expected to build a business case for an SDG-oriented organisation. In the previous modules, the cornerstones of an SDG case were presented. The question now arises: how do you create a grounded SDG business case for your organisation? This course will support you with this challenge. At the end of this course, you will be professionally competent as an ‘SDG-model builder/ambassador/change agent’ who can describe and diagnose a real-life organisation on its SDG orientation and help it develop its attainable/challenging SDG business case.

 

You will work in teams, and you will follow up on the opportunities identified in Q1 around the four levels of intervention. The course begins by articulating these opportunities into business cases for sustainability  (Chapter 8), as a grounding step for transition to sustainable business model innovation. That means you will identify the current business model using a Business Model Canvas and propose a new, sustainable business innovation using a Business Model Canvas (+). Here, you will learn business dynamics and the difference between the adaptation of existing business models (Levels 1, 2, and 3), and full transition (Level 4).  Overall, we discuss an organisation's sustainable value proposition from the perspective of dealing with wicked problems by means of business within new economies. For example, we will showcase the emergence of the circular economy and its circular business model as an illustration of how actors can collaborate in shaping new business ecosystems (level 4).  Therefore, you will have an integrative view on business model innovation, the dynamics of business models, and the Circular Business Model, and consider environmental and social costs and benefits. These insights will feed your work in the Project Module 2: Integrating Legal Solutions for Impact-Driven Development for discussing partnership agreements.
learning_objectives:
·         Identify business cases for sustainability out the insights from SDGs challenges and opportunities

·         Understand and apply Business Model canvas for their organization

·         Explain the Transition to Sustainable Business Model Innovation

·         Understand and Apply the business case for sustainable business and model innovation in a Business Model Canvas (+)

description:
This course will discuss risk in a broad sense. Based on lectures and accounts of major accidents, a discussion is initiated on a topic related to engineering risk management in organisations. Major accidents and cause-effect mechanisms will be explained through short videos and longer documentaries on safety issues and risk mitigation. The students will be made familiar with several accidents that had a significant contribution to the field of safety science in general and risk management in organisations in particular.

Risk is conceptualized as a topic of uncertainty and possible loss from different perspectives (both safety and security). Topics are further elaborated, and theories/models/metaphors are taught by means of interactive discussions and tested by poll exercises. The effects of different justice concepts (restorative versus retributive) on risk reduction and safety reporting are introduced.

Throughout the course, several accidents and lessons learned will be explained. This includes the Titan submersible accident, which happened in the year 2023. The accidents will be used as a basis for active participation from the students concerning the course contents.

The following topics are discussed:

Introduction and definition of risk concepts, such as hazard, loss, probability, frequency, threat

Similarities and differences between safety and security risk

Risk theories, models, concepts

Risk assessment and risk mitigation methods

Aspects of safe human performance, including cognitive bias and the role of operational procedures

Organisational aspects such as safety management systems, reporting systems, and safety learning principles

Restorative versus distributive justice as different approaches for organisational risk management
learning_objectives:
After this course, you will be able to:

Reflect on a variety of risk reduction measures and organizational responsibilities that result from learning from previous accidents.

Apply acquired risk knowledge (acquired models, attitudes, concepts, risk reduction elements, methods, etc.) that lead to the mitigation of safety/security issues.

Be able to explain the differences and similarities between managing safety and security risks.

Discuss presented examples or theoretical approaches to manage safe human performance and organisational responsibilities to obtain a safer workplace.

Appraise the differences between retributive and restorative justice as different approaches for organisational risk management, both in theory, and applied to practical examples.

course_name: Writing a Bachelor’s Thesis in English
description: This course is designed for students who are in the process of writing their Bachelor's thesis. The main focus is on thesis structure and the writing process, with particular attention paid to effective organization of ideas, precision of formulation and academic style. The course will also include discussion of the use of AI tools in the writing process, addressing both their potential and limitations. Aspects of the writing process will be supported by weekly reading and writing assignments.
learning_objectives: Through interactive lectures, students will gain a clear understanding of thesis structure and the organisation of chapters. By working in peer review groups, they will learn to give and receive constructive feedback to improve the quality and clarity of their writing. By the end of the course, students will be more critical of their own writing and know how to edit their work independently.

course_name: Process Management and Decision-making in Project Environment
description:
This course is only accessible as an elective if you have demonstrable knowledge of project management (by way of pass on a project management course on BSc or MSc level)

Projects are generally managed with a strong focus on predicting the schedule, budget, scope resources and tasks. That phase of predicting is then followed by a strong focus on controlling the works towards the predicted outcome (predict and control).

However, many projects have to deal with significant uncertainties, leading to surprises in the execution of the project. Process management offers a different view on projects, focussed on dealing with surprises by preparing for them and committing parties to the project (prepare and commit). It can help steer the project from separated task orientation to an integrated goal orientation.

The course introduces the students to the way in which process management can be used in projects and how that translates to contracts, structures and day-to-day management.

This course is part of the minor project management. (Please contact the module manager in case you would like to follow this course outside the minor program).
learning_objectives:
Understand how complexity and uncertainties reveal themselves in projects and how to be prepared for them.

Understand the role and forms of process management in managing complex projects, as an addition to standard project management tools.

description: This course teaches programming in Python on an intermediate level.
learning_objectives:
After completion of this course, the student is able to:

1. Implement Python programs based on a given natural-language description.

2. Write code that follows Python's code style guidelines.

3. Make use of basic data structures such as strings, lists, dictionaries, tuples, and sets.

4. Implement reading and writing data from/to different file formats.

5. Apply object-oriented programming concepts such as inheritance, operator overloading, and properties.

6. Apply functional programming concepts such as list comprehensions, structural pattern matching and higher-order functions, as well as iterators and generators.

Apply array programming concepts, including universal functions and broadcasting.

8. Understand and write type hints.

description:
Algorithms and Data Structures teaches you how to choose the right algorithm and the right data structure for your problem. It teaches you how to analyse algorithms and data structures and how you can use this information to make your choice.

You will also learn how to implement various algorithms and data structures that you will often need when programming.

In the final lecture we will discuss problem complexity instead of the algorithm complexity we discussed until then.
learning_objectives:
After this course, you should be able to:

Analyse standard data structures and algorithms

Using natural language for recursive code

Using big-Oh, big-Omega and big-Theta notation for iterative code

Implement standard data structures and algorithms using those data structures

Select the right data structure and algorithm for a problem, given the run time requirements

Prove that a problem is part of P and/or NP

description:
This course provides an introduction to databases technologies, as well as a comprehensive overview of the principles and practices of software engineering. It also introduces the software development life cycle and various development methodologies.

Databases Topics:

- Overview of Database Concepts, Models, and Architectures
Introduces the purpose and structure of databases, covering the evolution from file based systems to modern database technologies. It includes an overview of relational databases where data is organized using tables, keys, and relationships to ensure data integrity and consistency. It also provides a brief introduction to non relational databases, which offer flexible data models suitable for specific needs like scalability or complex relationships. Additionally, it outlines the common architectural setups used in database systems and briefly introduces the key languages used to interact with databases.

- The Relational Model and Database Design Theory
Covers the formal structure of relational databases, including relations, attributes, tuples, primary and foreign keys, and integrity constraints. Emphasis is placed on conceptual schema design using Entity Relationship (ER) modeling and the process that follows, translating the conceptual schema into a logical relational schema suitable for implementation.

- Database Normalization
Focuses on organizing data in relational tables to eliminate redundancy and prevent anomalies. Includes normal forms, how to identify repeating groups or functional dependencies, and how to apply normalization techniques to improve data consistency and maintainability.

- Structured Query Language (SQL)
Introduces the core language used to interact with relational databases. Topics include defining schema structures (CREATE, ALTER), enforcing constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY), modifying data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), and querying. Also includes the use of joins, aggregate functions, and filtering in order to retrieve and manipulate data effectively.

 


Software Engineering Topics:


- Introduction to Software Engineering

Definition and importance of software engineering

Overview of the software development life cycle (SDLC)

Software engineering methodologies (Waterfall, Agile, Scrum)

- Requirements Engineering

Requirements elicitation techniques

Requirements specification and documentation

Requirements validation and management

- Software Construction

Explain and apply coding standards

Best practices for software solutions
learning_objectives:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Perform data modeling by designing Entity Relationship diagrams and translating them into normalized relational schemas that enforce data integrity.

Build logical database schemas based on application requirements, applying normalization principles to ensure clarity, consistency, and non redundancy.

Design and implement SQL operations to define, manipulate, and query data structures, including table creation, data updates, and queries, utilizing constraints, join operations, and aggregate functions to support effective data management and analysis.

Explain the software development life cycle (SDLC) and different methodologies.

Gather and analyze software requirements.

Explain and apply coding standards and best practices for software solutions

description:

6. Clustering.

7. Dimensionality reduction.

description:
Note: TIL40202-20 TIL Research project will be replaced by TIL5055 TIL Thesis Preparation. In Q1 25-26 TIL4020-20 TIL Research Project will be offered for the last time. TIL5055 TIL Thesis Preparation will be offered every quarter from Q2 25-26.

This course teaches TIL students how to design and manage scientific research in the TIL domain. TIL students will become Master of Science. This means that they have to be able to do and manage scientific research. However, what is scientific research actually? What is the difference between scientific research and consultancy research? What is the role of scientific theory (or theories) in scientific research? What is the role of scientific literature in scientific research? In this course these kinds of questions are addressed using literature and insights from teachers experienced in doing TIL related research and from fellow TIL-students who just finished their master thesis. In this course also writing a good quality conclusion and discussion section is taught.

The course TIL4030 Research en Design introduces, discusses and practices research en design methodologies in the Transport, Infrastructure and Logistics domain on the basis of cases and problems along the four Specialisations in the MSc TIL program. Through workshops, exercises, an integrated design exercise (in Q1) and a research project (Q2) students bring the knowledge and skills into practice.

For more info, see brightspace or MSc TIL website section 4.

Course content p0 (preparation):

See study goals

Course content p1 (Vision and Scope):

In P1 you write your PVS. It is based on a small literature study and discussions with your commissioner, the course coordinator and if time-wise possible, also your TUD supervisors.

Ideally, you start working on it as soon as the course coordinator approves your commissioner and topic; week x.6 or earlier. It should be ready by the end of week x.9.

Baseline: You choose a design/systems engineering method to structure your project and build your story-line. On top of it you use other scientific methods and tools in support of the Problem analysis, Literature overview, Stakeholder analysis, Design requirements analysis, Designs, Evaluation.

[Problem analysis]

The problem as defined by the commissioner is a starting point for your actual definition of the problem:

"Problem analysis [..] involves identifying the overriding problem and establishing the causes and effects related to that problem. A key element of this analysis will ensure that root causes, not just the symptoms of the problem, are identified and subsequently addressed in the project design. Projects that only address the effects of the problem, and not its underlying causes, are unlikely to produce sustainable benefits." (1)

Problem analysis involves

A short literature review to see if there are theories that deal with the stated problem, to choose appropriate research and design tools, to elaborate relevant topics and to define the research gap.

Study of the commissioner's organisation and its context. This allows you to collect qualitative (interviews, brainstorms) and quantitative data (data collected by the commissioner and your own measurements).

Stakeholder analysis with a choice of (a coalition of) main stakeholders.

This material helps you to scope your project, modify your research questions, specify requirements and constraint for your designs.

Requirements analysis: Wat are key requirements, constraints and (if applicable) kpi to be fulfilled in the designs? These are not given by the commissioner, but established by your team.

[Design]

The design phase is meant to develop and evaluate possible solutions (alternatives) to reduce or solve the problem(s) as identified in the problem analysis, to choose the one(s) best fitting with the requirements analysis. You then evaluate the design(s) based on the same (or subset of these) criteria.

[Technical perspective]

The project suits a technical university, hence it should have some technical perspective/application/component, which should be elaborated to a sufficient extent. Examples are RFID or barcodes, sorting or transport equipment in a warehouse or the use of driver assist tools in a car, fuel technology. A model is regarded as a practical tool, not as technical perspective.

[Project choice: Balance science-practice]

No consultancy-style projects = do exactly what the commissioner wants. As an academic you should be critical towards any information you receive and follow your own line when discussing and advising the commissioner.

The course format does not allow you to learn new theories, methods or apply unfamiliar software.

In case of software, you will not develop a real software tool, but you can help the commissioner by building a preliminary design.

[Available topics]

Not all fields and topics can be chosen. This depends on available commissioners and options for supervision at the TUD. The company list on Brightspace may change. The course coordinator will also assess the risk level of each project based on previous experiences. https://www.elo.iastate.edu/engl-309/problem-analysis/

Course content p2 (Analysis and Design):

This is an advanced course in applied systems/design engineering. The PVS was written in P1. It is amended in the kick-off meeting. This amended PVS is your initial guidance for the content and planning of the project. You do not rewrite your PVS after the kick-off meeting, but use the comments in your draft project report.

A project contains the following 3 building blocks:

A current state analysis:

an extensive research problem analysis of the organisation and its context

literature analysis with research gap

stakeholder analysis to study relationships among stakeholders and search for common ground for your later designs

requirements and constraints analysis as a basis for your design alternatives and for the filtering and evaluation of your designs

A future state analysis:

description of ideal future situation

one or more conceptual designs taking care of the results of the requirements analysis

one or more preliminary designs which are usually filtered (by a morphological analysis or other tool)

choosing the best final design(s)

detailing of the best final design(s)

Evaluation, conclusions and recommendations:

final evaluation of developed (detailed) designs

conclusions, recommendations for science and practice

[implementation advice]

In appendix

technical details (statistics, PDL/simulation, unused cases or scenarios, ..)

team reflection about final results, project experience, experts and literature,

supervision and the course itself

logbook (detailed weekly activities by each team member)

PVS (kick-off version)

By email

individual reflections

The goal of each project is to provide the commissioner with a dedicated advice on how to improve its business or policy process or product. A project is finished with a complete project report, which is defended in a final presentation and defense meeting.

Read the extensive Course Manual on Brightspace.

A complete overview of the course without login can be found here: https://www.tudelft.nl/en/student/faculties/ceg-student-portal/education/master/transport-infrastructure-logistics/programme-2022-2023/4-projects/til-design-project/.

In p2 (Analysis and Design) students learn:

To carry out a full-scale problem analysis using relevant scientific tools and methods on the foundation of a systems engineering approach. The problem analysis will be finished with a set of design requirements, criteria, constraints and where applicable KPI's.

To develop and evaluate one or more design(s) (a set of complementary measures, solutions or tools) to deal with the problem as scoped earlier. To write a (final) report with appendices. This may also contain an implementation advice. You present and defend (final) project results during P2 and in particular in the Final Presentation and Defense meeting.

As a team, you cooperate to reach the project goals in an effective and pleasant manner. You organize weekly supervision meeting with your commissioner supervisors and the TUD supervisors (independently). You keep your TUD supervisors informed about planning and team dynamics. This demands sound project management. You inform the course coordinator in case of more structural team issues.

description:
The patient is the centre of the medical universe around which all our work revolves and towards which all our efforts tend William Murphy, 1934 Nobel Prize winner.

The Technical Medicine Professional, like medical doctors, should approach patients from multiple perspectives ranging from large-scale prevention to individual patient care. In collaboration, both professionals should be able to conceptualize care around patients and use technology to improve the diagnostic and treatment process. In this process, the medical interview and physical examination are specific skills which play an essential role in the communication between (potential) patients and healthcare providers. It is used to guide patients from complaint to diagnosis and treatment in a structured form, keeping in mind the patient profile (background, age, expectations, desires, etc). As such, it forms the basis of treatment relationships in most healthcare contexts and determines where technology can be used to improve patient outcomes.

This case-based course addresses communication skills in a healthcare context, the diagnostic process, patient treatment and follow-up. Students will learn where (the development of) technology can be helpful and how it is integrated in modern patient care. The first cases will focus on basic communication skills and physical examination, the latter cases will focus on integration of technology into patient-care.

Topics include:

- The medical interview

- Physical examination

- Communication skills in a healthcare context

- The diagnostic process

- From diagnosis to treatment

- Conceptualizing medical problems into technological solutions

description:
In the BSc Klinische Technology, molecular imaging has already been introduced in the module “Imaging bij grote ziektebeelden”. In this MSc course the physics, acquisition techniques and signal processing underlying various molecular imaging techniques such as PET, SPECT, optical imaging, and spectroscopy will be explored, whereas diagnostic and therapeutic applications, both in clinical practice and preclinical research, will be outlined as well.

 

The following topics will be covered:

Basic principles of gamma radiation, PET and SPECT, optical imaging, and spectroscopy

The indications for the different modalities

The pharmacodynamics and the development of tracers Issues of image quality, especially related to resolution, signal to noise ratio, quantitative and dynamic imaging.

 

Molecular imaging is a scientific field that emerged at the beginning of the twenty-first century. This field originated from the field of radiopharmacology due to the requirement for improved understanding of molecular mechanisms and pathways in organisms and cells. Therefore, the field of molecular imaging itself focuses on imaging techniques that enable non-invasive visualization of cellular function and molecular processes, with the objective to improve the understanding of disease mechanisms, diagnosis and prognosis of disease, patient stratification, and evaluation of treatment response. Many of these techniques are now being applied in the fields of oncology, neurology, and cardiovascular diseases for the purpose of research and within the clinical arena.

 

Molecular imaging differs from traditional imaging in that specific probes are used to visualize specific targets or molecular pathways. This in contrast to conventional imaging techniques that rely on differences in physical properties (e.g. density or water content) to image the anatomy of a biological system. Imaging probes can interact or be altered according to the state of a biological system. Detection of these probes makes it possible to either qualitatively or even quantitatively assess the state of such biological systems. Imaging probes encompass a wide range of biological agents (e.g. enzymes substrates, antibodies) and can either be administered or be endogenous to the system.

 

Molecular imaging can be categorized into a number of different groups, depending on how a specific technique is used to assess the state of a biological system (e.g. magnetic resonance, optical detection, emission tomography). Although many molecular imaging techniques can be used to image living cells and organisms without perturbing the biological system, other techniques such as mass spectrometry used in the operating theatre, are more destructive techniques.

 

This course will focus on different molecular imaging techniques and their application in clinical practice as well as in preclinical research. Although many MRI techniques can be categorized under molecular imaging as well, these are discussed in the course Advanced Imaging Techniques and, therefore, fall outside the scope of the present course.
